Summary: Section 5 requires the Director of Economic Development to file an electronic report with the Legislature by July 1, 2026, and annually thereafter, detailing (1) the percentage and (2) the total dollar amount of economic development funds awarded to (a) individuals starting new businesses or (b) individuals/entities providing services to businesses established within the prior five years whose principal place of business is in Nebraska. Section 5 requires the Director of Economic Development to file an electronic report with the Legislature by July 1, 2026, and annually thereafter, detailing (1) the percentage and (2) the total dollar amount of economic development funds awarded to (a) individuals starting new businesses or (b) individuals/entities providing services to businesses established within the prior five years whose principal place of business is in Nebraska. Beginning July 1, 2026, the Department of Economic Development is encouraged to award five percent of "economic development funds" — defined as the amounts budgeted for economic development programs administered by the Department, including community development block grants — to those recipients. No specific appropriations are altered.
Additions: Requires the Director of Economic Development to file an annual electronic report to the Legislature (first due July 1, 2026) showing: (a) the percentage of economic development funds awarded to (i) individuals starting new businesses and (ii) individuals/entities providing services to businesses es… 
Requires the Director of Economic Development to file an annual electronic report to the Legislature (first due July 1, 2026) showing: (a) the percentage of economic development funds awarded to (i) individuals starting new businesses and (ii) individuals/entities providing services to businesses established within the past five years (in-state); and (b) the total dollar amounts for those awards. Beginning July 1, 2026, the Department of Economic Development is encouraged (not required) to allocate 5% of its "economic development funds"—defined as amounts budgeted for DED programs, including community development block grants—to those startups and service providers. No mandated appropriations or required budget reallocations are imposed.

Summary: LB101 amends the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act to add an explicit right to jury trial and bar rental-agreement waivers of rights under state or federal law. Procedural changes affect courts and court officers: complaints for restitution file with the clerk of the district or county court and may demand a jury; summonses must notify defendants of the right to a jury trial; courts (including county court) must inform defendants of tha… 
LB101 amends the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act to add an explicit right to jury trial and bar rental-agreement waivers of rights under state or federal law. Procedural changes affect courts and court officers: complaints for restitution file with the clerk of the district or county court and may demand a jury; summonses must notify defendants of the right to a jury trial; courts (including county court) must inform defendants of that right at first appearance and inquire about jury demand; courts schedule jury trials as practicable and may require rent deposits if a tenant obtains a continuance. If restitution is awarded, the court must declare forfeiture and may direct the sheriff or constable to restore possession within ten days; plaintiffs must follow the Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds that complaints may demand a jury trial and requires courts to inform defendants of the right to and opportunity to demand a jury trial at first appearance; county courts must ask whether the defendant elects a jury or bench trial. Timelines: bench trials set 10–14 days after summons; jury tria… 
Adds that complaints may demand a jury trial and requires courts to inform defendants of the right to and opportunity to demand a jury trial at first appearance; county courts must ask whether the defendant elects a jury or bench trial. Timelines: bench trials set 10–14 days after summons; jury trials scheduled as soon as practicable. If a tenant requests a continuance of a jury trial beyond the initial date, the court may require the tenant to deposit accrued rental payments with the clerk of the court. Agencies mentioned: courts generally, county courts, and the clerk of the court. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB102 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §43‑513 for the Aid to Dependent Children program. Effective July 1, 2026, the bill sets the standard of need at $1,132.50 for a single individual plus $393 for each additional individual in the ADC unit. Beginning July 1, 2026, the standard will be adjusted annually each July 1 based on the Consumer Price Index rate of growth as determined by the U.S. Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics for the previous calendar year. The standard is used to calculate ADC benefits; payments remain capped by §43‑512. The original §43‑513 is repealed. No funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes are specified.
Additions: Adds a definition of "standard of need" as the regular recurring monthly amount used in the initial income test for aid to dependent children (ADC), tied to the "Budget the Gap Methodology" in section 68-1713. Establishes an effective date of July 1, 2026, and sets the standard at $1,132.50 for a si… 
Adds a definition of "standard of need" as the regular recurring monthly amount used in the initial income test for aid to dependent children (ADC), tied to the "Budget the Gap Methodology" in section 68-1713. Establishes an effective date of July 1, 2026, and sets the standard at $1,132.50 for a single individual plus $393 for each additional person in the ADC unit. Confirms the standard is used to calculate a unit's ADC benefit amount. No specific government agency or department is named in the added text, and there are no new funding, appropriations, or budget allocation changes included.

Summary: LB103 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §27-412 (Nebraska Evidence Rules) governing admissibility of evidence in sexual-misconduct cases. LB103 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §27-412 (Nebraska Evidence Rules) governing admissibility of evidence in sexual-misconduct cases. It narrows permissible evidence (retaining exceptions for evidence showing another source of physical evidence, similar prior conduct with the accused to prove consent, and evidence required by constitutional rights), requires a party to file a written motion (generally ≥15 days before trial) and serve all parties and notify the victim/guardian, and directs the trial court to hold an in camera hearing before admitting such evidence. The bill bars questioning a victim during any pretrial hearing or proceeding (including depositions) on matters inadmissible under the section. No state agency appropriations or funding changes are included.
Additions: Adds subsection (5) stating that a victim of sexual assault may not be questioned during any pretrial hearing or proceeding—including depositions—about matters that are inadmissible under this section. No government agencies or departments are referenced, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budgetary changes in the added text.

LB104 designates "Department" as the Department of Health and Human Services and requires the department to fund only home visitation programs that (1) include periodic in‑home visits for families with children age five or younger or pregnant persons, (2) provide visits by nurses, social workers, early‑childhood/health professionals or supervised lay workers, and (3) are evidence‑based as defined in the bill. Funded program dollars may be used for workforce purposes and to assist programs/individuals in obtaining and maintaining provider certification. The department may adopt rules to implement the Act and must submit electronic reports to the Legislature (by Feb 15, 2026, and through Feb 15, 2028) with program, outcomes, demographic, and expenditure data. The bill contains no specific appropriations or budget allocations.
Additions: Creates the "Family Home Visitation Act," defines "Department" as the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), and requires DHHS to fund only evidence‑based, periodic home‑visitation programs for pregnant people and families with children ≤5. Funded programs must use nurses, social workers, o… 
Creates the "Family Home Visitation Act," defines "Department" as the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), and requires DHHS to fund only evidence‑based, periodic home‑visitation programs for pregnant people and families with children ≤5. Funded programs must use nurses, social workers, other professionals or trained/supervised lay workers and target specified outcomes (maternal/infant health, parenting, child development, family well‑being, economic self‑sufficiency, reduced maltreatment, school readiness). Evidence‑based criteria and fidelity requirements are specified. State funds may be used for workforce supports and provider certification/recertification. DHHS may adopt rules and must submit electronic reports (due by Feb 15, 2026 and Feb 15, 2028) including total funds expended. No specific appropriations or new dollar amounts are included.

Summary: LB105 amends statutes governing public power and public power and irrigation districts. Key state actors: - Nebraska Power Review Board: retains authority to approve district petitions dividing territory into election subdivisions, and to approve adding board representation from counties outside a district’s chartered territory. - Secretary of State: the bill removes a prior requirement for Secretary of State approval of precinct divisions/opera… 
LB105 amends statutes governing public power and public power and irrigation districts. Key state actors:

- Nebraska Power Review Board: retains authority to approve district petitions dividing territory into election subdivisions, and to approve adding board representation from counties outside a district’s chartered territory.
- Secretary of State: the bill removes a prior requirement for Secretary of State approval of precinct divisions/operating-area boundary changes, but districts must still transmit division/certification information with the election certification provided under section 70-611.
- County election officials (election commissioners or county clerks): boards must follow precinct lines those officials create after each decennial census.

Budgetary effect: districts are liable for any additional election costs caused by precinct divisions or customer certifications and must pay county statements within 30 days. The act takes effect immediately due to an emergency clause.
Additions: Adds or clarifies language concerning "the boundary lines of whole or divided voting precincts," including the phrase "operating area" alongside "either whole or divided." No state or local agency or department is referenced, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes.

LB106 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §60-6,257 to revise motor vehicle window-tint standards. It prohibits tinting that substantially impairs the driver's view or the ability to see into the vehicle and sets numeric limits: front side and rear (behind front seat) windows may not have luminous reflectance greater than 20% or light transmission less than 20%. Windshield sunscreening remains restricted below/above the AS-1 line. The bill references federal safety glazing standards (49 C.F.R. §571.205) for campers, motor homes, pickup covers and similar equipment. The bill repeals the prior version of §60-6,257. No state agencies, appropriations, or budget changes are specified.

Summary: The bill explicitly grants the Department of Revenue authority to recapture a previously enacted home‑purchase income tax credit if the claimant sells, transfers, or stops using the residence as a primary residence within five years of the taxable year the credit was claimed. Separately, it amends the Property Tax Credit Act, specifying minimum relief amounts through tax year 2024 (e.g., $275M for 2020–2022; $360M for 2023; $395M for 2024), direc… 
The bill explicitly grants the Department of Revenue authority to recapture a previously enacted home‑purchase income tax credit if the claimant sells, transfers, or stops using the residence as a primary residence within five years of the taxable year the credit was claimed. Separately, it amends the Property Tax Credit Act, specifying minimum relief amounts through tax year 2024 (e.g., $275M for 2020–2022; $360M for 2023; $395M for 2024), directs past transfers from the General Fund to the Property Tax Credit Cash Fund ($105M by Aug 1, 2007; $115M by Aug 1, 2008), and preserves legislative authority to transfer funds from the Property Tax Credit Cash Fund to the General Fund. No other provisions explicitly mention the Department of Revenue.
Additions: Creates a new refundable renter's income tax credit, effective for tax years beginning (or deemed to begin) on or after Jan. 1, 2025. The credit applies to Nebraska residents who rent their primary residence and equals the greater of 4% of annual rent or $200, capped at $1,000. It is a refundable cr… 
Creates a new refundable renter's income tax credit, effective for tax years beginning (or deemed to begin) on or after Jan. 1, 2025. The credit applies to Nebraska residents who rent their primary residence and equals the greater of 4% of annual rent or $200, capped at $1,000. It is a refundable credit against tax under the Nebraska Revenue Act of 1967. Department of Revenue implications: administer, calculate, process refunds, and update forms/filing systems to accommodate the new credit. The text contains no explicit changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department.

Bill amends the Cities of the First Class Firefighters Retirement Act to change contribution rates and offsets administered through the Firefighters Retirement System/Fund. Employee contributions rise on a schedule to 12.7% (effective Oct. 1, 2026) unless the firefighter is employed by a city over 60,000 population in a county over 100,000 and covered by an absolute coverage group—those remain at 6.5% beginning March 1, 2025. Employer (city) contributions rise to 15% by Oct. 1, 2026, with the same large-city/county exception keeping contributions at 13% for affected firefighters starting March 1, 2025. Beginning July 20, 2024, a 6.2% offset to contributions applies for firefighters and cities covered by absolute coverage groups, except for the large-city/county combination. Cities continue to pick up employee contributions (IRC 414(h) treatment) and must fund additional amounts into the unallocated employer account as needed. IRS and Internal Revenue Code provisions referenced. Emergency clause: effective on passage.
Additions: Adds mandatory contributions to the firefighters’ retirement system, effective March 1, 2025. Firefighters employed by a “city of the first class” (city >60,000 population in a county >100,000), who participate in the retirement system and are in an “absolute coverage group,” must contribute 6.5% of… 
Adds mandatory contributions to the firefighters’ retirement system, effective March 1, 2025. Firefighters employed by a “city of the first class” (city >60,000 population in a county >100,000), who participate in the retirement system and are in an “absolute coverage group,” must contribute 6.5% of salary to the retirement system. Those cities must contribute 13% of each such participating firefighter’s periodic salary to the retirement system. No other state agencies or specific appropriations/budget line items are referenced; the change is limited to employee and municipal contribution rates to the retirement system.

LB109 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §§44-4606 and 44-4610 to regulate pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) and insurer/health plan provisions concerning clinician‑administered drugs. It (1) bars PBM contract clauses that restrict pharmacists or pharmacies from disclosing treatment, authorization, cost, or PBM practice information to covered persons; (2) preserves disclosure to the director, law enforcement, or state/federal officials (subject to confidentiality protections); (3) prohibits PBM termination/penalties for reporting PBM practices or sharing contracts with the director under the Pharmacy Benefit Manager Licensure and Regulation Act; (4) requires patient cost-sharing be the lesser of plan cost-share or cash price and count toward deductibles/out‑of‑pocket limits per 42 U.S.C. 300gg‑6; and (5) limits PBM restrictions on retail community pharmacy choice. The bill includes severability and repeals the original sections. No funding or appropriation changes are included.
Additions: Adds provisions restricting pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs): PBMs may not limit a covered person's ability to choose how a retail community pharmacy dispenses or delivers prescription drugs and may not prohibit a retail community pharmacy (text continues). Lists permitted settings for administration/dispensing as a physician's office, hospital outpatient infusion center, pharmacy, or other clinical setting. LB10 amends section 71-7455, R.R.S. Neb. It requires wholesale drug distributors (other than the original finished-form manufacturer) to verify all pedigree transactions before further distribution. The bill authorizes "the department" to receive prescription drugs and supplies directly under the Prescription Drug Donation Program Act and to dispense them via licensed personnel during, or while preparing for, a Governor-declared state of emergency. The department may also receive and distribute donated drugs and supplies to individuals impacted by such an emergency. The original section is repealed and the act takes effect immediately due to an emergency clause. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are specified.

Summary: LB110 prohibits a health care provider from performing a pelvic examination on a patient who is anesthetized or unconscious in a hospital or medical clinic without prior written consent, except when (1) an authorized decisionmaker has given written consent, (2) the exam is necessary for emergency diagnosis or treatment, or (3) a court orders the exam for evidence collection. LB110 prohibits a health care provider from performing a pelvic examination on a patient who is anesthetized or unconscious in a hospital or medical clinic without prior written consent, except when (1) an authorized decisionmaker has given written consent, (2) the exam is necessary for emergency diagnosis or treatment, or (3) a court orders the exam for evidence collection. Violations are subject to discipline under the Uniform Credentialing Act. If such an exam is performed, the patient must be notified in writing prior to discharge. The bill contains no provisions for funding, appropriations, or budgetary changes.
Additions: Adds a prohibition on performing pelvic exams on anesthetized or unconscious patients in hospitals or clinics without prior written consent, except when: (a) an authorized decision‑maker has given written consent; (b) the exam is needed for emergency diagnosis or treatment; or (c) a court orders the… 
Adds a prohibition on performing pelvic exams on anesthetized or unconscious patients in hospitals or clinics without prior written consent, except when: (a) an authorized decision‑maker has given written consent; (b) the exam is needed for emergency diagnosis or treatment; or (c) a court orders the exam for evidence collection. Violations are subject to discipline under the Uniform Credentialing Act (i.e., professional licensing/credentialing authorities). Requires written patient notification prior to discharge if such an exam was performed while the patient was unconscious or anesthetized. No agencies are newly created or renamed and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes included.

Summary: LB111 regulates insurers' use of nonoriginal equipment manufacturer (non‑OEM/aftermarket) parts in motor vehicle repairs. It (1) defines insurer, consumer, consumer care, non‑OEM, and part (excluding tires/windshields/windows) with cross‑references to sections 60‑2701 and 60‑1401.10; (2) bars insurers from requiring non‑OEM parts that lack permanent manufacturer identification or that are inferior in fit/performance (including modification costs)… 
LB111 regulates insurers' use of nonoriginal equipment manufacturer (non‑OEM/aftermarket) parts in motor vehicle repairs. It (1) defines insurer, consumer, consumer care, non‑OEM, and part (excluding tires/windshields/windows) with cross‑references to sections 60‑2701 and 60‑1401.10; (2) bars insurers from requiring non‑OEM parts that lack permanent manufacturer identification or that are inferior in fit/performance (including modification costs); (3) requires written consumer consent before using non‑OEM parts and forbids charging consumers the price difference to use OEM parts; (4) mandates a specified notice in repair estimates and clear identification of any non‑OEM parts; (5) prohibits requiring aftermarket parts for vehicles manufactured within 36 months of damage; and (6) makes violations Class I misdemeanors. No state agencies or budgetary appropriations are named or affected.
Additions: Added provisions define terms and impose consumer-protection rules on insurers regarding non‑original equipment manufacturer (non‑OEM/aftermarket) parts: insurers may not require use of non‑OEM parts that lack permanent manufacturer identification or are inferior in fit/performance; must notify cons… 
Added provisions define terms and impose consumer-protection rules on insurers regarding non‑original equipment manufacturer (non‑OEM/aftermarket) parts: insurers may not require use of non‑OEM parts that lack permanent manufacturer identification or are inferior in fit/performance; must notify consumers in ≥10‑point font and obtain written consent before using non‑OEM parts; must identify any non‑OEM part in repair estimates; may not force aftermarket parts for vehicles manufactured within 36 months of damage; may include a standard policy notice for older vehicles. Violations are a Class I misdemeanor. No specific government agencies or departments are referenced, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes.

Summary: LB112 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 60‑171 and 60‑173 concerning salvage‑branded motor vehicle titles. It (1) revises definitions—expanding "salvage" to include owner‑voluntary designation and vehicles deemed "structurally totaled" and defining "structurally totaled"; (2) clarifies insurer duties to obtain an owner’s certificate of title, surrender it to the county treasurer, and apply for a salvage‑branded certificate when a total‑loss settlement is… 
LB112 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 60‑171 and 60‑173 concerning salvage‑branded motor vehicle titles. It (1) revises definitions—expanding "salvage" to include owner‑voluntary designation and vehicles deemed "structurally totaled" and defining "structurally totaled"; (2) clarifies insurer duties to obtain an owner’s certificate of title, surrender it to the county treasurer, and apply for a salvage‑branded certificate when a total‑loss settlement is paid (or to notify the department if the owner retains the vehicle); (3) requires the department to immediately enter a salvage brand into the computerized vehicle record and to accept insurer electronic reports via the department’s electronic reporting system once the director implements it; and (4) allows insurers to apply for a salvage title without an endorsed owner title after 30 days if they submit an affidavit documenting attempted title retrieval and settlement evidence. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. Original sections are repealed.
Additions: Adds a definition of "structurally totaled vehicle," referencing "consumer care" as defined in §60-1401.10. A vehicle is structurally totaled if a facility that performs consumer care and the insurer at the time of damage deem it so, based on a kink or crease in a frame rail, unibody, or structural… 
Adds a definition of "structurally totaled vehicle," referencing "consumer care" as defined in §60-1401.10. A vehicle is structurally totaled if a facility that performs consumer care and the insurer at the time of damage deem it so, based on a kink or crease in a frame rail, unibody, or structural component (e.g., engine cradle, rear differential). Excludes totals due solely to hail or cosmetic damage, and excludes vehicles whose repair costs do not exceed 75% of actual cash value. No state agencies, departments, or funding/appropriation changes are specified.

LB113 amends multiple liquor statutes and shifts regulatory duties between the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission (the commission) and local governing bodies (city/village/county clerks). Key agency actions: the commission may authorize rickhouses and offsite storage, adopt rules on distribution rights, receive and process entertainment-district and license endorsement applications, and must notify local clerks of entertainment-district applications. Local governing bodies may designate/revoke entertainment districts, file such actions with the commission, impose occupation taxes, cancel licenses for cause, set criteria for temporary expansions, and collect an additional $300 entertainment-district license fee payable to the local clerk. The bill contains no statewide appropriations or other budget allocations.

LB114 amends multiple Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) provisions for driver records and creates a fund for a new operator’s license system. Key DMV provisions:

- DMV may furnish certified driving-record abstracts for $3 each. Revenue from subsections (1)–(5) is remitted to the State Treasurer and credited 41 2/3% to the Department of Motor Vehicles Cash Fund, 25% to the General Fund, and 33 1/3% to the Records Management Cash Fund.
- Monitoring-service searches are charged $0.30 each; $0.24 per search is credited to the DMV Cash Fund and $0.06 as provided in subsection (2).
- Driver-header extracts are $30 per 1,000 records, credited to the DMV Cash Fund. For certain record requests $2 per individual record and $22 per 1,000 (for requests over 2,000) are credited to the License Plate Cash Fund.
- Creates the Operator’s License Services System Replacement and Maintenance Fund (funded by amounts credited under §60-483) to build/maintain a new operator’s license services system; implementation by July 1, 2032. Investment earnings in the fund are credited to the General Fund beginning October 1, 2024. Act operative July 1, 2025; emergency clause included.

LB120 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §60‑484.02 regarding the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV). Key DMV provisions:
- DMV must capture and preserve digital images and signatures for issuance of operator’s licenses and state ID cards; images may be retrieved only by the DMV for renewals/replacements except as specified.
- The DMV may release images/signatures only under enumerated exceptions (law enforcement/driver‑licensing agencies, Secretary of State for voter ID/registration, and to the Nebraska State Patrol for posting on its Missing Persons Clearinghouse under an agreement).
- The DMV and Nebraska State Patrol may enter agreements governing release, use, protection, storage, retention, and the Patrol must apply security protocols and remove images within three business days after a subject is located.
- DMV must develop the Secretary of State release process and may adopt rules; unauthorized disclosure by DMV personnel is a Class I misdemeanor.
No funding, appropriation, or budget changes are included.

Summary: LB123 amends enforcement of budget, audit, and property-tax filing requirements. LB123 amends enforcement of budget, audit, and property-tax filing requirements. The Auditor of Public Accounts (APA) must prepare budget documents, calculate restricted funds authority, and notify a governmental unit and the State Treasurer of noncompliance. The State Treasurer is directed to suspend or withhold state aid to noncompliant political subdivisions or municipalities until compliance. Suspended funds are held for six months; if noncompliance continues they are forfeited and redistributed to other eligible recipients in the county or returned to the Highway Allocation Fund (or to the General Fund for homestead-exemption reimbursements). If noncompliance persists for 12 months after APA notice, the subdivision becomes ineligible for future state-aid distributions until compliance. The bill also updates audit-filing enforcement for cities and villages and repeals the original cited statutes (including section 13-3407).

- Agencies mentioned: Auditor of Public Accounts and the State Treasurer.
- Added provisions: The Auditor notifies the State Treasurer of a governmental unit's delinquency and later of compliance; state aid is forfeited until the Auditor reports compliance to the State Treasurer.
- Funding effects: Forfeited state aid remains forfeited and will be redistributed per the bill; if there is no eligible recipient the funds return to the Highway Allocation Fund.
- Penalties: Any political subdivision failing to comply within 12 months of the Auditor's notice is ineligible for future state aid distributions (cities/villages losing entitlement under sections 39-2511–39-2520); eligibility is restored upon compliance.

LB124 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §28-394 (Homicide of the Unborn Child Act) to modify penalties for motor vehicle homicide of an unborn child. It (1) retains a default Class I misdemeanor for unintentional vehicular deaths of an unborn child but (2) elevates offenses to felonies when committed in violation of specified motor-vehicle statutes: violations of §60-6,213 or §60-6,214 become Class IIIA felonies; violations of §60-6,196 or §60-6,197.06 become Class IIA felonies, and become Class II felonies if the defendant has a prior §60-6,196-related conviction. As part of conviction, the court must impose a driving prohibition and revoke the operator’s license for 60 days up to 15 years (revocation not concurrent with any jail term). The offense is treated as separate from other related offenses. No funding or appropriations are included.

LB126 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §10-126 governing redemption of local government bonds. It clarifies that most municipal bonds are callable at the issuer’s option after five years, but exempts bonds of public power districts, public power and irrigation districts, metropolitan utilities districts, cities of metropolitan and primary class, housing authorities, certain large city/village revenue issues, large school-district issues, bonds sold by counties via competitive sale (per §10-145), and bonds issued by the Board of Regents of the University of Nebraska and the Board of Trustees of the Nebraska State Colleges. Issuers may pay a call premium up to 4% for single issues ≥ $500,000 (2% for districts under Chapters 31 or 39). Bonds lacking special prepayment procedures may be called by governing-body resolution/ordinance, potentially conditioned on issuance of refunding bonds; calls require deposit with the paying agent to be effective. The bill repeals the original section. No funding or appropriation changes.

LB127 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §29-1208 to create a statutory damages remedy for defendants whose criminal charges are dismissed, who are found not guilty, granted absolute discharge, or whose convictions are overturned. It defines “prosecutor” to include the Attorney General, deputy and assistant attorneys general, county and deputy county attorneys, city attorneys, and any other person with prosecutorial authority. The trial court must hold a hearing to award reasonable attorney fees and litigation expenses and actual damages (including lost wages). Relief is barred if the defendant is convicted of a separate, nonvacated offense arising from substantially the same misconduct; defendants may waive damages by agreement with a prosecutor. No funding or appropriation changes are included. The original §29-1208 is repealed.
Additions: Adds a wrongful-prosecution damages remedy and defines "prosecutor" to include the Attorney General, deputy/assistant attorneys general, county and deputy county attorneys, city attorneys, and any person with authority to prosecute. Adds a wrongful-prosecution damages remedy and defines "prosecutor" to include the Attorney General, deputy/assistant attorneys general, county and deputy county attorneys, city attorneys, and any person with authority to prosecute. It requires the trial court, after certain dismissals or acquittals, to hold a hearing and award reasonable attorney fees and litigation expenses and actual damages (e.g., lost wages). Relief is barred if the defendant is convicted of another substantially similar offense that remains valid; defendants may waive damages in agreements with prosecutors. No specific appropriations, budget allocations, or new funding streams are set forth (though awards could create fiscal exposure for government entities).

It creates no statute-of-limitations for suits against the individual who directly caused the injury when the offense occurred on or after August 24, 2017 (or earlier if not previously time barred), and for other persons or entities when the offense occurs on or after the bill's effective date (or earlier if not previously time barred). Criminal prosecution is not required to pursue a civil action. No specific state agencies or departments are named, and the bill contains no funding, appropriation, or budgetary changes.

LB130 amends section 77‑4602 to revise reporting and transfer rules for General Fund net receipts. The Tax Commissioner must, within 15 days after each month and fiscal year end, publish comparisons of actual General Fund net receipts to (a) the most recent Nebraska Economic Forecasting Advisory Board forecast and (b) the prior fiscal year. After each fiscal year the Tax Commissioner computes (i) actual minus certified estimated net receipts and (ii) 50% of actual net receipts times the difference between the year’s growth rate and the 20‑year average growth (excluding the lowest year). If (i) is positive, the Commissioner certifies the larger amount to the Director of Administrative Services; the State Treasurer transfers that certified sum from the General Fund to the Cash Reserve Fund (partial immediate transfer with remainder by the following fiscal year). Transfers are limited so the Cash Reserve Fund does not exceed 16% of budgeted General Fund expenditures, subject to legislative override for specified needs. The bill repeals the original section and takes effect immediately.
Additions: Within 15 days after each fiscal year ends the Tax Commissioner must calculate: (i) actual General Fund net receipts minus the certified estimate for that year, and (ii) 50% of (actual receipts × the difference between that year’s growth rate and the 20‑year average growth rate, excluding the lowest… 
Within 15 days after each fiscal year ends the Tax Commissioner must calculate: (i) actual General Fund net receipts minus the certified estimate for that year, and (ii) 50% of (actual receipts × the difference between that year’s growth rate and the 20‑year average growth rate, excluding the lowest year). If (i) is positive, the Tax Commissioner certifies the larger of the two figures to the Director of Administrative Services. Upon that director’s certification, the State Treasurer transfers the certified amount from the General Fund to the Cash Reserve Fund — an amount equal to (i) immediately and any remainder by the end of the next fiscal year. Transfers are reduced to prevent the Cash Reserve Fund balance from exceeding 16% of budgeted General Fund expenditures (excluding reappropriations/encumbrances), though the Legislature may authorize exceeding 16% for specified needs.

It creates a Department of Revenue Miscellaneous Receipts Fund (for receipts under specified tax sections) to defray publication and administrative costs; the fund may be invested by the state investment officer and transfers to the General Fund may occur at the Legislature's direction. The State Treasurer and the Accounting Administrator of the Department of Administrative Services must designate required state fund types for the Nebraska educational savings plan trust; the trust operates without General Fund appropriations, its Administrative Fund expenditures require legislative appropriation, and the fee-funded Expense Fund must transfer a pro rata share to the State Investment Officer’s Cash Fund with annual reporting to DAS’s budget division and the Legislative Fiscal Analyst. The Department of Health and Human Services must annually transmit child/guardian identifying information to the State Treasurer for Meadowlark Program administration; related costs are payable from the Education Savings Plan Expense Fund.

- Educational savings plan trust: no General Fund support; Administrative Fund expenditures subject to appropriation; Expense Fund required to transfer investment-management shares and cover DHHS data-transfer costs.

LB135 standardizes election procedures for school-district and related local fiscal questions and reallocates certain administrative responsibilities among election officials and state fiscal offices.

Key agencies and changes
- Election commissioners / county clerks: must conduct school bond, levy, and budget-exceeding elections under the uniform procedures of §32-559(3); prepare ballots, provide early-voting ballots, count ballots, certify results, and may bill school districts directly for special-election costs. Timing and notice requirements are clarified (e.g., ballots/notice windows).
- School boards / political subdivisions: must file orders/resolutions with the appropriate election commissioner or county clerk; joint entities (and joint public agencies that include school districts or ESUs) cannot issue bonds without voter approval at elections held per §32-559(3); joint entities must give at least 50 days’ notice for such elections.
- County boards / county clerks / election commissioners: retain authority to place levy-exceeding questions on ballots and implement levy changes consistent with election results.
- Property Tax Administrator: receives reports of levy-allocation amounts for joint public agencies.
- Auditor of Public Accounts: receives records when resident meetings approve one-year budget-growth exceptions.

Budget/funding effects
- Clarifies transfer and calculation rules for restricted funds and allowable growth in governmental budgets (§13-519).
- Political subdivisions remain responsible for election costs; allocation and minimum charges are specified; school districts can be billed directly for special elections. No new appropriations are made.

- Requires school board elections to comply with subsection (3) of §32-559 and sets filing deadlines for ballot certification (March 1 for statewide primary, Sept. 1 for statewide general, eighth Friday before a political‑subdivision general).
- Assigns administration and ballot counting to the election commissioner or county clerk, assisted by two disinterested persons; receiving boards deliver ballots to that official for counting.
- Requires 30‑day first‑class mail notice, publication of a sample ballot 7–15 days before the election, early‑voting ballots available 21 days prior, and cross‑county certification/transfer of registration lists on request.
- Two appointed counters must be paid at least the minimum hourly rate under §48‑1203.
No new appropriations or other funding changes are specified.

Summary: LB138 directs the department to establish a fee‑for‑service pharmacy dispensing fee of $10.38 per prescription for independent pharmacies beginning in FY2024‑25, contingent on implementation of contractual agreements with Medicaid managed care organizations and federal Medicaid state plan approval. LB138 directs the department to establish a fee‑for‑service pharmacy dispensing fee of $10.38 per prescription for independent pharmacies beginning in FY2024‑25, contingent on implementation of contractual agreements with Medicaid managed care organizations and federal Medicaid state plan approval. The department must determine the actual dispensing fee via a cost‑of‑dispensing survey of participating independent pharmacies every two years and amend all Medicaid managed care organization contracts to authorize a managed‑care dispensing fee consistent with the fee‑for‑service rate. Survey submissions that identify individual pharmacy costs are confidential. The department must electronically report recommendations for interim fee adjustments to the Clerk of the Legislature by December 15, 2024. Independent pharmacies are those owning six or fewer locations. The bill contains no separate appropriation or explicit budget allocation.

LB139 amends enforcement and registration provisions under Nebraska's Real Property Appraiser Act and Appraisal Management Company (AMC) Registration Act. Key agency actions and requirements:

- The Real Property Appraiser Board may investigate alleged violations, contract for technical assistance, enter contingent dismissal agreements with remedial measures (for credential holders or AMCs), and report disciplinary actions to federal authorities as required by Title XI. A successfully completed contingent dismissal is not disciplinary action.  
- AMCs must have owners (>10%) submit fingerprint cards/electronic prints for national criminal history checks (Nebraska State Patrol and FBI). The board is directed to pay the Nebraska State Patrol for those fingerprint-based checks.  
- The board may issue cease-and-desist orders, seek enforcement through the Attorney General, and must report AMC violations/discipline to the Appraisal Subcommittee per Title XI/AMC rule.

The bill requires the Director of Agriculture to administer a grant program from the Noxious Weed and Invasive Plant Species Assistance Fund to assist local control authorities and weed-management entities in implementing noxious weed control programs. The Director will accept applications, consult the advisory committee, and award grants for research, demonstrations, response, monitoring, education, and related activities. The Department of Agriculture may adopt rules and regulations to implement the section, and the Director may annually apply to the Natural Resources Conservation Service (USDA) for conservation funding. Beginning in FY2025-26 the Legislature intends to appropriate $6,000,000 annually for vegetation management in stream banks/floodplains to improve streamflow; grants are limited to specified local entities with priority to interstate-decree river basins.

LB148 requires applicants for initial dental and related professional licenses to submit fingerprints for national FBI criminal-history checks. The Nebraska State Patrol forwards fingerprints to the FBI and must report results to "the department," defined for FBI interpretation as the Division of Public Health of the Department of Health and Human Services. The bill authorizes the department to receive those reports, adopt rules concerning associated costs, and—upon board recommendation—issue licenses. No appropriations, budget allocations, or other funding changes for the Department of Health and Human Services are contained in the bill.

The added language adopts the Dentist and Dental Hygienist Compact, creating Compact Privileges for interstate practice and a multi‑state Commission to oversee licensure data sharing, adverse‑action reporting, rulemaking, investigations, and enforcement. It requires Participating State licensing authorities to submit licensure, disciplinary, and investigative information to a shared data system and to enforce adverse actions and alternative‑program restrictions. Although the Compact authorizes the Commission to establish a budget, levy assessments, charge fees, accept grants/donations, and hire staff, the text contains no direct appropriation, funding directive, or specific budget allocation for Nebraska's Department of Health and Human Services. DHHS (if it serves as the State Licensing Authority) would have operational/reporting obligations and potential exposure to assessments or fee collection but no explicit new state funding in the bill.

LB149 amends student-discipline statutes (sections 79-263, 79-265, 79-267), repeals the original sections and outright repeals section 79-265.01. It removes the prohibition on suspending students in pre‑kindergarten through second grade and clarifies short‑term suspension procedures (principal may suspend up to five school days with required notice, explanation, and parent conference efforts). It retains the one‑year expulsion policy for knowingly possessing a firearm and continues the requirement that each school district annually file an assurance and details of such expulsions with the Nebraska Department of Education. Government entities referenced include school districts, superintendents, school boards/boards of education, principals, and the State Department of Education. No funding or appropriation changes are included.

The bill repeatedly cites the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA). Separately, the Legislature states its intent to appropriate General Fund money to implement the Hunger‑Free Schools Act.

No state Department of Agriculture responsibilities, duties, or funding changes are created. The bill only cites the federal United States Department of Agriculture as the source of federal program definitions and reimbursement rates. The Hunger‑Free Schools Program is administered by the State Department of Education, which the bill intends to fund from the General Fund to reimburse schools. Reimbursement formulas are specified (differences between federal free and fully‑paid rates for fully paid meals; for non‑CEP schools, 30¢ per reduced‑price breakfast and 40¢ per reduced‑price lunch plus the free-vs-fully‑paid differences). In short: no direct effect on the state Department of Agriculture; funding/appropriation actions are directed to the State Department of Education.

Summary: LB150 centralizes parole functions in the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), eliminating the Division of Parole Supervision and transferring related duties to the DCS Director. LB150 centralizes parole functions in the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), eliminating the Division of Parole Supervision and transferring related duties to the DCS Director. DCS assumes expanded responsibilities for incarceration (sentences >1 year), parole administration and records, validated risk-and-needs assessments (initial and semiannual), performance metrics, staff training, sanction/reward matrices, a technical‑violation residential pilot, lifetime supervision procedures, and development/oversight of community correctional, work‑release and reentry centers (including contracting and use of designated legislative funds). DCS will collect parole programming fees credited to a new Parole Program Cash Fund; the Legislature intends a $1,000,000 General Fund appropriation to implement the Community Work Release and Reentry Centers Act. DCS must certify overcrowding emergencies (140% capacity) and expedite releases; its Director joins the Reentry Continuity Advisory Board. DHHS gains data access for treatment evaluation, subpoena access for licensing investigations, authority on paternity genetic testing, and firearm‑disability notification duties. The Department of Banking and Finance must collect/post in‑state garnishment agents and is immune from liability. The Department of Revenue is excluded from the law‑enforcement definition; Transportation may require anti‑discrimination assurance for directional sign eligibility.
Additions: - Department of Banking and Finance: Adds clarifying garnishment service rules for corporate entities (excludes certain financial institutions). Service may be by section 25-509.01 or mutual agreement; if not served on the registered agent a copy must be sent to the agent’s location unless requested… 
- Department of Banking and Finance: Adds clarifying garnishment service rules for corporate entities (excludes certain financial institutions). Service may be by section 25-509.01 or mutual agreement; if not served on the registered agent a copy must be sent to the agent’s location unless requested otherwise; proof of that mailing is not required to continue garnishment.

- Department of Correctional Services: Allows jails or DOC facilities to host expanded mental‑health beds under the new Regional Mental Health Expansion Pilot Program; permits mental‑health board hearings by videoconference from DOC facilities; includes exclusions for convicted sex offenders. No direct appropriation to DOC is specified.

- Department of Health and Human Services: Pilot promotes expanded regional mental‑health beds and cooperation; the Nebraska Commission on Law Enforcement will administer grants and seek federal funding for collaborative emergency response. DHHS is implicated in mental‑health board/hearing changes but receives no explicit funding in the text.

- Department of Revenue: No substantive changes affecting the department appear in the added text.

- Department of Transportation: Adds criminal‑statute definitions for “tamper” and “rail infrastructure” (affecting rail assets); DOT not directly addressed and no funding changes.

Summary: The bill assigns the Department of Revenue responsibility to implement the First‑Time Homebuyers Savings Account Act. Duties include adopting rules and regulations; creating and making available required forms (account designation, beneficiary designation, annual report specifying transactions and supporting documentation, and a transaction report for withdrawals); and receiving those reports and any IRS Form 1099s with the taxpayer's Nebraska re… 
The bill assigns the Department of Revenue responsibility to implement the First‑Time Homebuyers Savings Account Act. Duties include adopting rules and regulations; creating and making available required forms (account designation, beneficiary designation, annual report specifying transactions and supporting documentation, and a transaction report for withdrawals); and receiving those reports and any IRS Form 1099s with the taxpayer's Nebraska return. The Department of Revenue is directed to collect a 10% penalty on certain nonqualified withdrawals and remit penalties to the State Treasurer per the Nebraska Constitution. The act becomes operative January 1, 2026. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department of Revenue are provided in the bill.
Additions: Highlights affecting the Department of Revenue: - Required to adopt rules and promulgate regulations to implement the First‑Time Homebuyers Savings Account Act. - Must create and provide multiple forms: account‑designation, beneficiary‑designation, annual report (transaction list and required suppor… 
Highlights affecting the Department of Revenue:
- Required to adopt rules and promulgate regulations to implement the First‑Time Homebuyers Savings Account Act.
- Must create and provide multiple forms: account‑designation, beneficiary‑designation, annual report (transaction list and required supporting documentation), and transaction report (eligible home costs applied and remaining balance).
- Annual and transaction reports must be submitted to the department with the taxpayer's Nebraska income tax return; account designation/beneficiary forms must be filed by the return due date (per §77‑2768).
- Responsible for collecting a 10% penalty on certain nonqualified withdrawals and remitting those receipts to the State Treasurer per constitutional distribution rules.
- No explicit new appropriations, funding, or budget allocations for the Department are included in the added text.

Summary: LB152 amends the Property Tax Credit Act (section 77-4212). LB152 amends the Property Tax Credit Act (section 77-4212). It sets minimum statewide property tax relief amounts: $430 million (tax year 2025), $445 million (2026), $460 million (2027), and $475 million (2028). For tax year 2029 the minimum equals the prior year’s minimum plus a percentage increase equal to the percentage increase, if any, in total assessed value of all real property in the state as determined by the Department of Revenue, plus an additional $75 million. For tax year 2030 and thereafter the minimum equals the prior year’s minimum plus the percentage increase in total assessed value as determined by the Department of Revenue.
Additions: Creates a new statewide homestead exemption: beginning January 1, 2026, the first $100,000 of a homestead's actual value is exempt from taxation. It confirms existing exemptions in sections 77-3506, 77-3507, and 77-3508 remain in addition to this new exemption. Legislative findings state the exempti… 
Creates a new statewide homestead exemption: beginning January 1, 2026, the first $100,000 of a homestead's actual value is exempt from taxation. It confirms existing exemptions in sections 77-3506, 77-3507, and 77-3508 remain in addition to this new exemption. Legislative findings state the exemption is authorized by the Nebraska Constitution and intended to expand homestead relief.

Implications for Department of Revenue: the Department will need to implement and administer the new $100,000 exemption in property tax assessment processes and related guidance. The text contains no explicit funding, appropriation, or budget allocation for the Department.

Summary: LB153 requires the Department of Health and Human Services to: seek federal approval to extend Medicaid postpartum coverage from 60 days to at least six months (subsection 6); provide electric personal-use breast pumps and at least ten lactation consultation visits by Jan 1, 2025 (subsection 8); provide coverage and reimburse providers for necessary translation and interpretation services by Jan 1, 2024 (subsection 9); submit, by Oct 1, 2025, a s… 
LB153 requires the Department of Health and Human Services to: seek federal approval to extend Medicaid postpartum coverage from 60 days to at least six months (subsection 6); provide electric personal-use breast pumps and at least ten lactation consultation visits by Jan 1, 2025 (subsection 8); provide coverage and reimburse providers for necessary translation and interpretation services by Jan 1, 2024 (subsection 9); submit, by Oct 1, 2025, a state plan amendment or waiver to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to implement at least six months of postpartum coverage through the Children's Health Insurance Program (subsection 10). The bill designates the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund to finance the CHIP postpartum coverage and explicitly adds CHIP postpartum coverage to the fund’s allowable uses; investment earnings in the fund are credited to the General Fund beginning Oct. 1, 2024.

The Department of Health and Human Services must, by October 1, 2025, seek CMS approval via a CHIP state plan amendment to obtain federal matching funds to provide at least six months of postpartum coverage for mothers whose child is enrolled under the unborn child option. Covered services must match the comprehensive postpartum services provided under Medicaid; the department may instead pursue a 12‑month coverage SPA. The Legislature expresses intent to fund these services from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund (see §68‑996). No specific dollar amounts or new appropriations are specified.

LB154 amends the Hearing Instrument Specialists Practice Act and shifts administrative responsibilities to the state credentialing apparatus. The Department (per the Uniform Credentialing Act) and the Hearing Instrument Specialists board jointly: define licensure standards and exams; issue and renew licenses and temporary training permits; require annual employer filings listing licensed specialists; set record-retention (seven years); and may waive exam components. The board’s composition is specified (three licensed hearing instrument specialists, one otolaryngologist, one audiologist, plus one public member). The Board of Medicine and Surgery must be consulted for rules on cerumen-removal training courses. The State Department of Education is retained in an existing exemption. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds definitions and regulatory duties involving the state "department" and the licensing "board." Key agency actions: organizations must file annually with the department (lists of licensed hearing instrument specialists and statements of compliance on department forms); the department, with board… 
Adds definitions and regulatory duties involving the state "department" and the licensing "board." Key agency actions: organizations must file annually with the department (lists of licensed hearing instrument specialists and statements of compliance on department forms); the department, with board recommendation, may evaluate foreign programs, waive exam components, determine exam eligibility, and accept receipts as verification. The board sets exam structure, practical/competency standards, retake rules, and may adopt cerumen‑removal course requirements only after consulting the Board of Medicine and Surgery. The bill references federal rule 21 C.F.R. 801.109 for device ordering. It also requires seven‑year record retention and professional liability insurance for cerumen removal. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are added.

Summary: LB155 amends Nebraska statutes on justification for use of force (sections 28-1406, 28-1409, 28-1410). It defines “public officer” as any elected or appointed officer or employee of the State of Nebraska or its political subdivisions (excluding duly authorized law enforcement officers) and excludes law enforcement officers from the term “actor.” The bill clarifies that public officers (and persons assisting them or making arrests) are not require… 
LB155 amends Nebraska statutes on justification for use of force (sections 28-1406, 28-1409, 28-1410). It defines “public officer” as any elected or appointed officer or employee of the State of Nebraska or its political subdivisions (excluding duly authorized law enforcement officers) and excludes law enforcement officers from the term “actor.” The bill clarifies that public officers (and persons assisting them or making arrests) are not required to desist from performing duties due to resistance, and expressly provides there is no duty to retreat before using deadly force when lawfully present in a motor vehicle. No agencies, departments, or programs receive funding changes or appropriations in this bill.

Also clarifies that an actor lawfully present in a motor vehicle is not required to retreat from that vehicle unless the actor was the initial ag… 
Adds an exclusion for "any duly authorized law enforcement officer of the State of Nebraska or its political subdivisions" from the definition of "actor." Also clarifies that an actor lawfully present in a motor vehicle is not required to retreat from that vehicle unless the actor was the initial aggressor. No other government agencies or departments are referenced, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes.

LB156 amends section 81-8,219 to carve out that, in adoption or placement cases, the State Tort Claims Act applies to claims alleging misrepresentation or deceit by the Department of Health and Human Services. The bill contains no appropriations or funding changes.

LB157 designates "Department" as the Department of Revenue and creates the Child Tax Credit Act. The Department of Revenue is directed to: adjust, beginning in 2027, the credit amounts, thresholds, and reduction increments for inflation using the same percentage as individual income tax bracket adjustments; submit an annual report to the Legislature on Child Tax Credit usage each July 15 beginning 2027; and adopt rules and regulations to implement the Act. Separately, the Department of Revenue is authorized to recapture a separate residence-purchase tax credit if the taxpayer disposes of or stops using the residence as primary within five years. No appropriations, funding increases, or budget allocations for the Department are included.

Defines "Department" as the Department of Revenue and assigns the department these duties for the new Child Tax Credit Act: administer the refundable child tax credit (effective for tax years beginning on or after Jan 1, 2026); beginning 2027, annually inflation‑adjust credit amount, phase‑out thresholds, and reduction increments using the same percentage that adjusts individual income tax brackets; submit an annual usage report to the Legislature by July 15; and adopt rules and regulations to implement the Act. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department are included in the added text.

LB158 requires health carriers and pharmacy benefit managers to include amounts paid by a health benefit plan enrollee (or paid on the enrollee’s behalf) when calculating the enrollee’s contribution toward any out‑of‑pocket maximum or other cost‑sharing requirement for plans entered, amended, extended, or renewed on or after January 1, 2026. The bill references Nebraska statutory definitions for "health carrier" (see §44‑1303) and "pharmacy benefit manager" (see §44‑4603) and defers to federal tax law: the rule is limited where application would render a health savings account ineligible under Internal Revenue Code §223, in which case counting applies only after the IRC §223 minimum deductible is met (preventive care is counted regardless). No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB160 (Introduced by Riepe; referred to the Health and Human Services Committee) amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §71-216.01 to revise barber licensure examination retake and coursework requirements administered by the board (the licensing board referenced in the statute). Key changes: an applicant may retake the barber exam up to two additional times without further schooling; after a third failure, the applicant must complete a 500-hour course in a school of barbering (maximum ten hours per day) before further examination. After 250 hours, the board may approve a proficiency demonstration to waive the remaining hours; if the applicant then fails, the remaining 250 hours must be completed before a fifth exam attempt. The bill repeals the original section. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds licensing exam retake and training requirements administered by the board (the licensing/board of barbering). Adds licensing exam retake and training requirements administered by the board (the licensing/board of barbering). An applicant may retake the barber exam up to two additional times without further schooling; failing a third time triggers a required 500‑hour remedial course at a school of barbering (max 10 hours per day). After 250 hours the board may allow a proficiency demonstration to waive the remaining hours; if the applicant fails the exam after that waiver attempt, they must finish the remaining 250 hours before a fifth exam attempt. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB162 (Child Care Safety and Security Act) establishes a Child Care Safety and Security Fund administered by the State Department of Education. The fund consists of money transferred by the Legislature and is investable by the state investment officer under existing state investment law. Subject to available appropriations, the department competitively awards grants to educational service units (ESUs) to fund designees—public school districts, cities/villages, local public health departments, law enforcement, early childhood support agencies, or local emergency management agencies—via memoranda of understanding. Grants support emergency response notification systems, safety/reunification materials, and training; funding to a designee for each listed function is capped at $1,000 per year. ESUs must submit applications and approved security/reunification plans. The State Board of Education may adopt rules. The department must file an annual electronic report to the Clerk of the Legislature.
Additions: Creates the Child Care Safety and Security Fund, to be administered by the Nebraska State Department of Education (SDE) and funded by transfers from the Legislature; fund assets may be invested by the state investment officer under existing state investment laws. Creates the Child Care Safety and Security Fund, to be administered by the Nebraska State Department of Education (SDE) and funded by transfers from the Legislature; fund assets may be invested by the state investment officer under existing state investment laws. SDE, subject to available appropriations, will competitively award grants to educational service units (ESUs) on behalf of designees (public school districts, cities/villages, local public health departments, law enforcement, early childhood support agencies, or local emergency management agencies) for emergency notification systems, training, and reunification materials. Grants to designees for administering notification systems, distributing materials, and providing training are each capped at $1,000 per year. SDE must file an annual electronic report to the Clerk of the Legislature; the State Board of Education may adopt implementing rules.

LB166 amends state public‑records and election filing statutes. County assessors, registers of deeds, and county treasurers must withhold residential addresses of law‑enforcement officers, Nebraska National Guard members, and judges who apply; the county assessor administers the application, notifies the register of deeds and county treasurer, and applications must be renewed every five years. LB168 enacts the "340B Contract Pharmacy Protection Act." It authorizes the Nebraska Attorney General or any county attorney to bring state actions (including injunctions) to enforce prohibitions on manufacturers, their agents/affiliates, or third‑party logistics providers from: (1) denying or restricting acquisition or delivery of 340B‑priced drugs to locations authorized by 340B entities (as defined by 42 U.S.C. 256b); and (2) conditioning such access on submission of non‑federally required data. The bill includes a severability clause, clarifies it must not conflict with federal law, contains an emergency clause making it effective on enactment, and contains no appropriations or budget changes.
Additions: Creates the "340B Contract Pharmacy Protection Act," defining "340B drug," "340B entity" (per 42 U.S.C. 256b as of Jan 1, 2025), and "Manufacturer" (per Neb. Rev. Stat. §71-7438). Creates the "340B Contract Pharmacy Protection Act," defining "340B drug," "340B entity" (per 42 U.S.C. 256b as of Jan 1, 2025), and "Manufacturer" (per Neb. Rev. Stat. §71-7438). Prohibits manufacturers, their agents/affiliates, and third‑party logistics providers from denying, restricting, or conditioning delivery or acquisition of 340B drugs to locations authorized by 340B entities, and from requiring non‑federally‑mandated data as a condition of access. Enforcement: the Nebraska Attorney General or any county attorney may sue in the name of the State for injunctions or other relief. Includes a savings clause deferring to compatible federal or other state law. No funding, appropriations, or budget changes included.

Summary: LB171 amends Nebraska income tax law. LB171 amends Nebraska income tax law. Key agencies/actions:
- Tax Commissioner (Nebraska Department of Revenue functions): continues to adjust individual tax brackets for inflation, prescribe and publish updated tax rate schedules, prepare tax tables, and may require taxpayer use of tables. Adjustments reference the Consumer Price Index published by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics and earlier Internal Revenue Code methodology for limited years.
- Legislature: enacts rate changes described below.

Tax changes:
- Individual: the third bracket is 5.01% through 2025 and drops to 4.99% for taxable years beginning on/after Jan. 1, 2026; the top (fourth) bracket phases down and becomes 4.99% on/after Jan. 1, 2026.

The bill directs reporting and investigatory roles for DHHS and new prosecutorial authority for the Attorney General’s Child Protection Division: allegations of sexual assault involving victims under 18 must be reported to the Department of Health and Human Services; criminal‑justice agencies may share victim identity and identifying information with DHHS for child abuse/neglect investigations; and the AG’s Child Protection Division may, on written request from DHHS (or others), investigate or initiate prosecution of crimes against children.

For the Department of Correctional Services, the bill requires DCS to order mental‑health evaluations to assess “dangerous sex offender” status for specified convictions. Incarcerated persons who refuse or fail sex‑offender treatment offered by DCS or DHHS are subject to evaluation, except when noncompletion is due to time constraints or lack of programming; evaluations must be ordered ≥180 days before release with written findings by 150 days prior.

No explicit appropriations, funding changes, or budget allocations for DHHS or DCS are included.

LB174 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §25-1558 to create a separate, lower garnishment limit for medical debt sought by medical debt buyers or medical creditors: garnishment may not exceed the lesser of 10% of disposable earnings, the amount by which disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum wage, or (if the creditor alleges specific facts in a sworn affidavit that the debtor is not a head of household) 20%. The bill adds definitions for health care services, medical debt, medical debt buyer, and medical creditor, voids wage assignments beyond these exemptions, and prohibits courts from issuing garnishments that violate the section. The Commissioner of Labor is authorized to promulgate rules converting the statutory weekly threshold for other pay periods. No funding or appropriations are included.

Adds caps and definitions for medical-debt garnishment and actors. Garnishment: for any workweek, the amount taken for medical debt may not exceed the lesser of (a) 10% of disposable earnings; (b) the amount by which disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum hourly wage (29 U.S.C. 206(a)(1)); or (c) 20% of disposable earnings if the individual is not a head of family, established by sworn affidavit from the judgment creditor. Defines “health care services,” “medical debt,” “medical debt buyer” (entities that purchase debts for collection), and “medical creditor” (providers or prior holders of such debts). No government agencies or departments are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

LB175 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §74-1335 to allow interested landowners to file written complaints with the Department of Transportation alleging that a railroad crossing (including crossings involving a railroad's successor in interest) is inadequate or unsafe. The Department is authorized to investigate, hold hearings, and issue orders; it may require overhead, underground, or grade-separated crossings, wing fences at underground crossings, or relocation of existing crossings. For special crossings costing more than $1,500, the landowner must pay one-half of the portion of expenses exceeding $1,500. The bill repeals the original section.

LB176 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §86-1304 (Nebraska Broadband Bridge Act). It continues to vest grant administration in "the commission" (grant deadlines, speed‑test requirements, and enforcement) and requires applications from political subdivisions or Indian tribes to be public–private partnerships with a provider. New application requirements mandate a resolution of project support adopted by each county, city, and village in the project area that includes a project map, permit acknowledgement, and timeline. Matching funds remain required (50% outside high‑cost areas; 25% inside; federal funds excluded from the match). Grants must be completed in 18 months or face graduated repayment. Applicants using equipment on the FCC Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau "Covered List" are ineligible. No new appropriations or statewide budget reallocations are included.
Additions: Adds a requirement that applicants include a resolution of project support adopted by each county, city, and village where the project will be located. Adds a requirement that applicants include a resolution of project support adopted by each county, city, and village where the project will be located. Each resolution must at minimum include: (a) a map of the proposed project area; (b) an acknowledgement that the applicant will apply for appropriate permits; and (c) a proposed project timeline. No specific state or federal agencies or departments are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

Summary: LB178 directs the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission (commission) to establish mandatory server alcohol training, approve programs, certify individuals, and maintain certification lists. LB178 directs the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission (commission) to establish mandatory server alcohol training, approve programs, certify individuals, and maintain certification lists. Approved programs must issue completion certificates and report participants to the commission. The commission may charge enrollment fees (up to $30) and certification fees (up to $20); all fees are collected, remitted to the State Treasurer, and credited to the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission Rule and Regulation Cash Fund. The fund’s purposes are expanded to cover administrative costs (including salaries/benefits), electronic regulatory transactions, industry education, enforcement training, regulatory equipment, and administering the new training requirements. Funds may be transferred to the General Fund at the Legislature’s direction and invested by the state investment officer under existing state investment statutes. Retail license noncompliance may lead to suspension, cancellation, or revocation. Effective Jan 1, 2026.
Additions: Requires the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission to create and administer a mandatory server alcohol training and certification program (see section 6 and section 53-117.03). The commission may charge an enrollment fee up to $30; fees are collected by the commission and remitted to the State Treasure… 
Requires the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission to create and administer a mandatory server alcohol training and certification program (see section 6 and section 53-117.03). The commission may charge an enrollment fee up to $30; fees are collected by the commission and remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Nebraska Liquor Control Commission Rule and Regulation Cash Fund. Beginning January 1, 2026, retail licensees may only employ persons involved in alcohol sale/service, security, or age verification who hold the commission‑approved certification (or obtain it within 90 days of hire). Licensees must keep employee certificates (or proof of <90 days employment) on the premises. The commission may suspend, cancel, or revoke licenses for noncompliance.

LB179 amends statutes governing municipal police and firefighters.

- Cities of the first class / Police Officers Retirement System: raises required police officer employee contributions from 7% to 9% of salary effective October 1, 2025. Cities continue to "pick up" those contributions and treat them as employer contributions for federal tax purposes; contributions are credited to employee accounts and the Police Officers Retirement System Fund.

- Cities / Firefighters Retirement Act: requires the retirement system (and its retirement committee) to permit optional benefit forms allowing retiring firefighters (for retirements on or after Jan 1, 1997) to elect a single lump-sum payment or one or more partial payments. The retirement committee and city council retain roles in selecting/prescribing annuity comparisons and lump-sum determinations.

- Funding: if a firefighter's retirement value cannot purchase the statutory minimum pension, the city must use funds from the retirement system's unallocated employer account to provide the required benefit.

- Operative date: firefighter option and repeal provisions effective Oct 1, 2025.
Additions: Adds two provisions: (1) effective October 1, 2025, each police officer must contribute 9% of salary to the retirement system; and (2) permits retiring firefighters to elect to receive their retirement value as a single lump sum or as one or more partial payments in amounts and frequency they choose… 
Adds two provisions: (1) effective October 1, 2025, each police officer must contribute 9% of salary to the retirement system; and (2) permits retiring firefighters to elect to receive their retirement value as a single lump sum or as one or more partial payments in amounts and frequency they choose. No specific state agency beyond the retirement system is named and no new funding or appropriations are included.

LB17 amends the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act to restrict landlord fees, require disclosure of total rent and itemized mandatory/optional fees, and mandate provision of any consumer report obtained. It prescribes permissible fees (rent, security deposit, NSF fee limited to landlord’s cost, late fee up to 5% or $50, and application fee limited to actual cost of a consumer report) and sets rules for collection, retention, and equality of application fees. The bill requires landlords to identify consumer reporting agencies used and inform tenants of their dispute rights. Enforcement is through Nebraska’s Consumer Protection Act (section 59-1602) and may be pursued by an aggrieved person or the Nebraska Attorney General. Violations can incur civil penalties up to $300 per violation, plus court costs and reasonable attorney fees. No funding, appropriations, or budget changes are included.

The added language regulates landlord fees: only rent, a security deposit (per §76-1416), returned-payment fees (limited to landlord cost), limited late fees, and application fees no greater than the actual cost of obtaining a consumer report. It requires disclosure and handling rules for application fees, delivery of any consumer/tenant screening reports to applicants, and notices identifying the consumer/consumer reporting agencies and tenants’ dispute rights. It references the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act and state criminal-history disclosure laws. Optional feeed services require written informed consent and opt-out rights; total rent and itemized mandatory/optional fees must be disclosed before application. Enforcement is through the Consumer Protection Act and may be brought by an aggrieved person or the Attorney General; knowing violations can incur up to $300 per violation plus costs and attorney fees. No funding, appropriations, or budget changes are included.
