LB181 directs the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to expand the Young Adult Bridge to Independence program to cover young adults not lawfully present in the U.S. DHHS must: (1) submit a Medicaid state plan amendment to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) by October 1, 2025 to provide Title XIX/XXI medical assistance to such participants; (2) seek federal Title IV‑E funding under 42 U.S.C. §§672–673 (including earlier required submissions to obtain IV‑E for newly eligible youth); and (3) adopt implementing rules by October 1, 2025. The bill directs DHHS to pursue other coverage options if federal eligibility is unavailable, including payment from the State General Fund.

Requires the state "department" to provide medical care for young adults in the Bridge to Independence program under federal Medicaid (Title XIX) or CHIP (Title XXI) where they qualify. - Fiscal allocations: On or before Nov. 1 each year, any Unclaimed Property Trust Fund balance exceeding $1,000,000 is distributed to the Permanent School Fund. Funds may be invested by the state investment officer under existing state investment laws.

Summary: LB184 prohibits sale or distribution of nitrous oxide in tobacco specialty stores and by licensed sellers (including delivery sales), and bans sale of devices specifically designed to inhale nitrous oxide for recreational use. Violations carry criminal penalties (Class III up to Class I misdemeanors depending on offense and repetition), authorize seizure, forfeiture, and destruction of products with costs borne by the violator, and allow court-or… 
LB184 prohibits sale or distribution of nitrous oxide in tobacco specialty stores and by licensed sellers (including delivery sales), and bans sale of devices specifically designed to inhale nitrous oxide for recreational use. Violations carry criminal penalties (Class III up to Class I misdemeanors depending on offense and repetition), authorize seizure, forfeiture, and destruction of products with costs borne by the violator, and allow court-ordered revocation and forfeiture of tobacco licenses with one- and five-year reissuance bars. The cigarette tax division of the Nebraska Tax Commissioner may revoke or suspend licenses under the referenced tobacco statutes for violations and treats contraband cigarettes as subject to seizure and destruction. No appropriations, funding, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds prohibitions on selling, distributing, or furnishing objects containing nitrous oxide: tobacco specialty stores (licensees under sections 28-1420–28-1429) may not sell or allow removal of such items; delivery sales to consumers are barred; and items designed for recreational inhalation are bann… 
Adds prohibitions on selling, distributing, or furnishing objects containing nitrous oxide: tobacco specialty stores (licensees under sections 28-1420–28-1429) may not sell or allow removal of such items; delivery sales to consumers are barred; and items designed for recreational inhalation are banned. Penalties escalate from Class III to Class I/II misdemeanors for repeat offenses, courts may revoke/forfeit tobacco specialty store licenses, and common carriers who knowingly transport violative items face Class I misdemeanors. Violations also constitute deceptive trade practices under the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act. All violative products are subject to seizure, forfeiture, and destruction at the violator’s expense. Exceptions: shipments to a federal foreign‑trade zone (19 U.S.C. 81a et seq.) and government employees acting in official duties. No changes to funding or appropriations are included.

Local governing bodies (cities, villages, counties) may designate or revoke entertainment districts and must file actions with the Commission (Nebraska Liquor Control Commission). The Commission receives and processes entertainment-district license applications, is notified of filings, and may act on appeals and license enforcement. Clerks of local governing bodies collect a new additional $300 annual entertainment-district license fee payable in the same manner as existing license fees; local governing bodies may also impose an occupation tax on entertainment-district businesses. Entertainment-district licenses are issued and renewed on the same schedule as the holder’s underlying retail, craft brewery, microdistillery, or manufacturer license. Violations may prompt suspension, cancellation, or revocation; an emergency clause is declared.

Bill LB18 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §86-1236 (Small Wireless Facilities Deployment Act). It clarifies duties and limitations for "authorities" (local permitting entities) and requirements for wireless providers: authorities may not grant exclusive right-of-way use and may only assess nondiscriminatory fees consistent with §86-1239 or choose to waive fees. The bill sets nondiscriminatory height limits for new/modified utility poles and small wireless facilities, allows authorities to approve exceptions, permits replacement of decorative poles to match existing aesthetics, and authorizes objective design/concealment measures in historic districts (subject to 47 C.F.R. 1.1307(a)(4) exceptions). Authorities may require and charge for restoration of right-of-way damage, including emergency repairs, and must verify ADA compliance (Americans with Disabilities Act) and absence of travel, safety, or utility-use obstructions before permitting installations. The original section is repealed. No funding or appropriation changes.

Requires the responsible authority (the permitting authority for right-of-way work) to, before installing or modifying any utility pole, verify: (1) compliance with the federal Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 and its implementing federal regulations as of Jan 1, 2025; (2) that the pole will not obstruct or hinder ordinary travel or public safety in the right-of-way; and (3) that it will not obstruct another utility’s legal use or impede safe operation or service. If any criterion is not met, the authority must deny permission. No specific agencies beyond the federal ADA/regulations are named and no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are added.

The bill amends duties of the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) regarding SNAP. DHHS must apply for and use all federal SNAP options, seek to maximize federal funding and minimize General Fund use, employ necessary staff, and submit an annual report to the Legislature on options, actions, caseload, and costs. DHHS must develop a state outreach plan that meets Food and Nutrition Service (U.S. Department of Agriculture) criteria, may accept gifts/grants/donations, partner with counties/nonprofits, submit the plan to FNS and request federal matching funds, and may be exempt from implementation if private/federal funds are insufficient. Original section repealed.

LB193 revises Neb. Rev. Stat. §81-836 to define membership and operations of the Committee on Pacific Conflict. Voting members are the Director of State Homeland Security (chair; appointment per §81-830), the Director of Administrative Services, the state investment officer, the Adjutant General, and three Governor-appointed subject-matter experts (including at least one critical‑infrastructure operator). Five legislative members appointed by the Executive Board of the Legislative Council serve as nonvoting members. The committee may establish advisory boards, consult federal and other state authorities and research institutions, and conduct secure briefings with critical‑infrastructure providers. Meetings are exempt from the Open Meetings Act and committee records are not public. The Governor must annually publish a state threat assessment (including nonconfidential Committee findings) before the Governor’s annual legislative address; the committee may also produce a confidential report stored in a Governor‑designated secure location. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB198 amends Nebraska’s Pharmacy Benefit Manager Licensure and Regulation Act and governs pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), health carriers/health benefit plans, plan sponsors, pharmacy services administrative organizations, specialty and retail pharmacies, and network pharmacists. Major actions: require PBM inclusion of accredited specialty pharmacies and limit audit/reporting frequency; establish delivery, documentation, and appeal processes for clinician‑administered drugs and prohibit penalizing providers who decline PBM‑sourced drugs; bar PBMs/carriers from mail‑order exclusivity, involuntary prescription transfers, and financial incentives favoring PBM affiliate pharmacies (with narrow maintenance‑drug exceptions); permit network pharmacies to refuse to fill if paid below acquisition cost without retaliation; and phase out spread pricing in PBM‑plan contracts (no new contracts with spread pricing after Jan 1, 2026; banned by Jan 1, 2029). Adds definitions and regulatory limits on pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), health carriers, health benefit plans, plan sponsors, specialty and retail pharmacies, and providers. Key provisions require PBMs to: treat unaffiliated specialty pharmacies no more stringently than affiliates; limit reporting to quarterly unless necessary; comply with federal Drug Supply Chain Security Act track‑and‑trace requirements and provide data on request; meet delivery timing/signature rules for clinician‑administered drugs; establish appeal/exception processes; and refrain from forcing patient pickup, penalizing providers, or using exclusive mail‑order steering except narrow opt‑outs. Permits pharmacies to decline under‑cost dispensing without retaliation. bans spread pricing in new PBM–plan contracts after Jan 1, 2026 (with limited grandfathering) and fully bans it Jan 1, 2029. Adds a mandatory disclosure regime for nonrecourse civil litigation funding. Consumers or their attorneys must, without awaiting discovery, deliver copies of such funding contracts to: (a) other parties/their attorneys; (b) any court, agency, or tribunal where the claim is pending (expressly covering administrative proceedings); and (c) any known person — including insurers with preexisting indemnity/defense obligations (the insurer disclosure duty applies even before a case or administrative proceeding is filed). The duty is continuing: new or amended contracts must be disclosed within 30 days. Litigation funding contracts and all participants are expressly discoverable. No changes to government funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB19 amends numerous statutes governing cities of the metropolitan class to move nomination and election timing to the statewide primary and general elections beginning in 2028, harmonizing references across election, initiative, franchise, bond, and bridge acquisition provisions. Key government actors affected: city councils, mayors, city clerks, county clerks or election commissioners (authorized to verify petitions and canvass votes), official canvassing authorities, and municipal printers/newspapers for publication. Terms of office will commence on the fourth Monday after the statewide general; officers elected in May 2025 serve until the fourth Monday after the 2028 statewide general and may run in 2028. The bill does not create new appropriations. Existing municipal bond authorities remain: park bonds ($100,000/year without elector vote), bridge revenue bonds (statutory $2 million threshold), and additional repair bonds up to 15% of purchase price.

Adds that, notwithstanding local charters, beginning with the 2028 statewide primary and every four years thereafter, candidates for elective offices in a "city of the metropolitan class" must be nominated at the statewide primary and elected at the statewide general; terms begin the fourth Monday after the election. Provides a transition: officers whose term began the fourth Monday after the May 2025 general election will serve until the fourth Monday after the 2028 statewide general and may run for reelection in 2028. States each metropolitan-class city shall elect seven city council members as provided in section 32-536. No state agencies or departments are specifically named, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes.

LB204 (Biometric Autonomy Liberty Law) designates the State of Nebraska, state and local governmental agencies, political subdivisions, Nebraska courts, and the Legislative Council as "public entities" subject to the bill. The State Department of Education sets the seventh‑grade lexile standard for required consent language. The Department of Motor Vehicles is expressly exempted for facial‑recognition fraud detection. Emergency medical care under the Emergency Medical Services Practice Act and HIPAA‑covered health information are excluded. Law enforcement agencies may use or receive biometric data for legitimate purposes; processors may disclose when cooperating with law enforcement. The Attorney General may subpoena, seek injunctive relief, and bring civil actions (with a 60‑day cure period) under the Consumer Protection Act. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are specified. Operative date: January 1, 2026.

LB205 restricts admissible evidence and awards for medical damages in Nebraska civil actions and imposes a $1,000,000 cap on noneconomic damages against commercial motor vehicle carriers. It directs courts to admit only specified measures of past and future medical costs: actual amounts paid; insurer-allowed amounts plus the claimant’s share when private coverage exists; or, for uninsured or Medicare/Medicaid patients, 120% of the applicable Medicare reimbursement rate or 170% of the state Medicaid rate. Claimants must disclose health coverage status and any letters of protection; transfers of accounts receivable to factoring companies and purchase amounts must be disclosed. For commercial motor vehicle cases (as defined at §60‑316), juries or judges must first find noneconomic damages then the court must reduce awards to the $1,000,000 limit. No funding or appropriations are included.
Additions: Adds rules limiting admissible evidence and recoverable medical damages in personal-injury/wrongful-death cases: defines "letter of protection"; limits past unpaid charges to amounts actually paid, insurer obligations, or (if uninsured or on Medicare/Medicaid) 120% of the Medicare reimbursement rate… 
Adds rules limiting admissible evidence and recoverable medical damages in personal-injury/wrongful-death cases: defines "letter of protection"; limits past unpaid charges to amounts actually paid, insurer obligations, or (if uninsured or on Medicare/Medicaid) 120% of the Medicare reimbursement rate or 170% of the applicable state Medicaid rate; requires disclosure if medical receivables were sold, of the purchaser and purchase price, and disclosure of the claimant's health coverage and any letter-of-protection referrals (including attorney referrals). Establishes a $1 million cap on noneconomic damages for claims involving commercial motor vehicles requiring a CDL, with juries/courts instructed to first find full damages then reduce awards to the cap. Government programs referenced: Medicare and Medicaid (including state Medicaid rates). No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are changed.

LB211 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §13-3403 (Property Tax Growth Limitation Act) for fiscal years beginning July 1, 2025. It retains the preliminary property tax request authority for political subdivisions as the amount levied by the county board of equalization in the prior year less exceptions under §13-3404, then modifies allowable increases. If public safety (per §13-320) is ≥20% of a subdivision’s property-tax-funded budget, increases equal growth percentage plus the greater of zero or the inflation percentage. If public safety is <20%, the inflation component is floored at 2% (greater of 2% or inflation). The bill repeals the original §13-3403 and takes effect immediately upon passage due to an emergency clause.
Additions: Adds a formula letting political subdivisions (local governments) increase their property tax request authority based on prior-year levies (minus exceptions under §13-3404(1)&(2)). Adds a formula letting political subdivisions (local governments) increase their property tax request authority based on prior-year levies (minus exceptions under §13-3404(1)&(2)). Two components apply in both cases: (i) prior-year tax base × growth percentage; and (ii) prior-year tax base × inflation percentage with different floors. If public safety services (as defined in §13-320) are ≥20% of the property tax‑funded budget, the inflation component uses the greater of zero or the inflation rate. If public safety is <20%, the inflation component uses the greater of two percent or the inflation rate. This amends how much localities may raise property-tax revenue; it is not a direct state appropriation.

Summary: LB216 centralizes district‑court clerical functions under the Nebraska Supreme Court. LB216 centralizes district‑court clerical functions under the Nebraska Supreme Court. Beginning January 7, 2027, elected clerks of the district court and their employees convert to state employment under the Supreme Court; the State (with funds appropriated to the Supreme Court) will pay their salaries, benefits, and expenses. The State Court Administrator receives court books/files (county‑owned equipment remains with counties). Counties must transfer and partially reimburse the State for accrued sick and vacation leave per specified formulas. Retirement treatment is addressed (transition to State Employees Retirement System or preservation of county retirement benefits with proportional cost‑sharing). The Supreme Court will fund certain district and separate juvenile court IT and communications costs. Federal reimbursements for child‑support administration will be credited to the State Treasurer for Agency 5 – Supreme Court. Oaths filed with the Secretary of State; emergency effective date.
Additions: Adds that, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, elected clerks of district courts and their employees become state employees under the Nebraska Supreme Court. The State (with funds appropriated to the Supreme Court/Agency 5) will directly pay salaries, benefits, and expenses; the Supreme Court controls new clerk… 
Adds that, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, elected clerks of district courts and their employees become state employees under the Nebraska Supreme Court. The State (with funds appropriated to the Supreme Court/Agency 5) will directly pay salaries, benefits, and expenses; the Supreme Court controls new clerk positions and non‑county‑consistent pay/benefit changes. Counties must provide accrual value data to the Supreme Court. Asset/records rules: county keeps furniture/equipment; books/files/records transfer to the State Court Administrator. Leave and retirement funding: counties reimburse the State for portions of transferred sick leave (25% up to 1,440 hours) and reimburse 100% of transferred vacation leave value (up to 280 hours); excess leave reimbursements go to employees per provisions. Retirement transfer costs are shared proportionately between county and state. Transferred staff may join Nebraska State Insurance Program (no waiting period). Federal reimbursements for child‑support processing are credited to the State Treasurer for Agency 5 – Supreme Court. Oaths filed with Secretary of State.

- Provide annual suicide-awareness training for DHHS child-welfare staff who provide direct services or interact with children/families, delivered within existing department training programs and completed before independent contact.

- Establish standardized suicide-awareness training requirements for employees of child‑placing agencies and may approve agency curricula that meet the DHHS baseline.

Training must incorporate evidence-based practices (early warning signs, appropriate responses, trauma-informed care). Operative October 1, 2025. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are specified.

All DHHS child‑welfare staff who provide or directly interact with children/families (and other personnel designated by the Division of Children and Family Services) must receive annual training and complete it before any independent contact with youth/families. LB21 adopts the Uniform Unlawful Restrictions in Land Records Act, authorizing property owners to record amendments removing unlawful restrictions from deeds or other title documents. Amendments must identify the owner, the affected real property, and the original document; include a specified conspicuous statement; be executed and acknowledged according to requirements for recordation; and be recorded in the land records of each county where the original document is recorded (i.e., county recorders/registrars of deeds). Summary: LB222 amends Nebraska Rules of the Road enforcement authorities and officer duties. LB222 amends Nebraska Rules of the Road enforcement authorities and officer duties. It explicitly ties powers to enforce motor-vehicle laws to the Superintendent of Law Enforcement and Public Safety and officers of the Nebraska State Patrol (with carrier enforcement officers excepted), and harmonizes §60-683 and §81-2005. New Sections 3–4 restrict other peace officers’ authority to stop or detain vehicle operators (prohibiting stops for nonmoving violations, most DWLS/DWLR stops, and many misdemeanor warrants) and limit equipment-failure stops to situations posing an “immediate, serious threat.” Officers must log/notify dispatch of the stop reason, inform operators, and may not request consent searches in those stops. Vehicle searches generally require a warrant or written consent on a specified bilingual form (with interpreter access); evidence obtained in violation is inadmissible. The bill repeals original sections and takes effect immediately. No funding, appropriations, or budget changes are included.
Additions: Adds officer conduct and search rules governing "peace officers" and requires pre-stop notification to police dispatch. Key agency-related points: - Peace officers may not stop or detain drivers for listed nonmoving violations, certain suspended-license cases, or most misdemeanor warrants, except sp… 
Adds officer conduct and search rules governing "peace officers" and requires pre-stop notification to police dispatch. Key agency-related points:
- Peace officers may not stop or detain drivers for listed nonmoving violations, certain suspended-license cases, or most misdemeanor warrants, except specified offenses.
- Equipment-failure stops allowed only if defect relates to the vehicle and poses an objectively reasonable, immediate, serious safety threat; officer must digitally log or notify dispatch of the primary reason and threat before initiating the stop.
- On contact, officers must state the reason, may not request a consent search under section 4, and may only question about other crimes if plain-view evidence creates reasonable suspicion.
- Vehicle searches require a warrant or written consent from the "authorized person" (operator) using a mandated consent form (English and Spanish, oral explanation, right to counsel, ability to refuse or revoke, interpreter services as needed).
- Evidence obtained in violation is inadmissible.
No agencies are newly created and no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB223 amends the Nebraska Fair Housing Act to add "lawful source of income" and compliance with public assistance or housing-assistance program requirements as protected categories. Administration and enforcement remain with the Nebraska Equal Opportunity Commission (the commission), with the State Fire Marshal responsible for accessibility standards and county attorneys authorized to enforce the Act (with the commission notified of county complaints). The bill defines lawful source of income (including Social Security, child support, foster-care subsidies, alimony, veterans benefits, and public housing vouchers). It expands the commission’s investigative, conciliation, subpoena, hearing, and publication powers; requires electronic annual reporting to the Legislature and public data collection that includes lawful source of income; authorizes cooperative agreements with HUD and testing organizations while prohibiting testing-payments tied to conciliations/settlements. No appropriations or budget changes are included.
Additions: Adds a definition of "lawful source of income" to include social security, child support, foster care subsidies, alimony, veterans benefits, and any form of federal, state, or local public general assistance or housing assistance (whether paid to renters or landlords), explicitly citing vouchers und… 
Adds a definition of "lawful source of income" to include social security, child support, foster care subsidies, alimony, veterans benefits, and any form of federal, state, or local public general assistance or housing assistance (whether paid to renters or landlords), explicitly citing vouchers under 42 U.S.C. 1437f. Also clarifies the Nebraska Fair Housing Act does not prohibit otherwise nondiscriminatory actions intended to benefit recipients of public assistance (e.g., housing limited to such recipients or favorable loan/lease/mortgage terms for them). Agencies/departments referenced: federal, state, and local public assistance and housing assistance programs and federal low‑income housing assistance under 42 U.S.C. 1437f (federal housing voucher program). LB224 requires the State of Nebraska to provide paid maternity leave to state employees. Key provisions: full‑time state employees receive 12 weeks paid leave to bond with a child; part‑time employees receive a prorated amount. Leave may not begin before birth or after six months, cannot be used intermittently except by mutual written agreement or for child medical necessity, and runs concurrently with the federal Family and Medical Leave Act. The state may not charge this leave against sick, vacation, compensatory, or other leave, and must restore employees to their prior or equivalent positions. Retaliatory actions against employees using leave are prohibited. No specific funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Adds a paid maternity leave entitlement for state employees: 12 weeks for full‑time staff (pro rata for part‑time). Key rules: leave begins no earlier than the birth and must be used within six months; generally not intermittent unless by mutual written agreement or medical certification; runs concurrently with the federal Family and Medical Leave Act. Employees must give 30 days' notice when possible. The state may not charge the leave against sick, vacation, comp, or other leave, and unused maternity leave is not paid out at termination. LB225 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §60-168 governing duplicate motor vehicle certificates of title. It specifies that applications must be on a form prescribed by the department and may be submitted to the department or any county treasurer. The county treasurer, with department approval, or the department itself may issue duplicates. If title records were destroyed under §60-152, the county treasurer may issue a duplicate on such proof as the treasurer deems sufficient. Applicants lacking proof of ownership may apply directly to the department, which may authorize a county treasurer to issue a duplicate if evidence is satisfactory. Duplicates show only unreleased liens; the fee remains as prescribed in §60-156. The bill repeals the original §60-168. No new appropriations or funding changes are included.

The bill amends the Security, Privacy, and Dissemination of Criminal History Information Act to create a private cause of action against state agencies, political subdivisions, and their officers/employees for violations, waiving sovereign immunity for such suits. Remedies include actual damages, equitable relief, and mandamus; actions are excluded from the State Tort Claims Act and Political Subdivisions Tort Claims Act. Limitations: generally four years after accrual, with a special January 1, 2029 deadline for certain claims accrued on or after January 1, 2015. The Attorney General may be asked by the commission to bring suit. No funding or appropriation changes.

Adds procedures allowing persons convicted or adjudicated for certain concealed-weapon offenses to move to set aside the conviction and then seek sealing of criminal history records in the county, district, or juvenile court that entered the conviction. Creates private liability for a state agency, political subdivision, or their officers/employees who violate rules under the Security, Privacy, and Dissemination of Criminal History Information Act, and expressly permits plaintiffs to join the state, its agencies, or subdivisions as defendants (waiving sovereign immunity). Actions under the provision are excluded from the State Tort Claims Act and the Political Subdivisions Tort Claims Act and are subject to specified limitations periods (generally four years, with a special Jan 1, 2029 deadline for certain older claims). - In evaluating such authorizations, the Public Service Commission must consult with the Director of Medicaid and Long-Term Care (or designee) of DHHS's Division of Medicaid and Long-Term Care.
- Transportation network companies or participating drivers may not transport persons under DHHS contracts without specific commission authorization; the commission must grant authorization unless a protestant proves existing carriers meet the need or the applicant would impair existing carriers.
- No appropriations, funding, or budget changes are included.

LB229 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §48-604 (Employment Security Law) to specify that services by a "marketplace network contractor" for a "marketplace network platform" are not employment—subject to written contractor designation and operational criteria—and defines those terms. Relevant government entities referenced: the statute’s "commissioner" (administrative authority under the Employment Security Law), the U.S. Secretary of Labor and the Federal Unemployment Tax Act (federal tax coverage/credit considerations), Congress, federal agencies (for work-training/program exceptions), the Public Service Commission and the Division of Motor Carrier Services (motor carrier/lessor rules), and references to the Internal Revenue Code. Adds a new carve-out and definitions for "marketplace network contractor" and "marketplace network platform." A contractor qualifies if a written agreement labels them an independent contractor, the platform cannot set mandatory hours, cannot bar outside work except while on-platform, and cannot fire the contractor for declining a specific request. LB22 designates the Department of Health and Human Services (department) as responsible for the new Family Home Visitation Act, requiring the department to fund only evidence-based home‑visitation programs, permit use of funds for workforce and certification, adopt rules, and submit electronic reports (by Feb 15, 2026–2028) including amounts expended. The department must submit CMS state plan amendments/waivers for: evidence‑based nurse home‑visiting targeted case management (by Oct 1, 2025) — with legislative intent that these services be funded from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund and not the General Fund — and other coverage changes (postpartum extension, medical respite designation, breast pumps, lactation services, translation/interpretation). The Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund is amended to explicitly allow spending for evidence‑based nurse home‑visiting services and related specified programs; specific appropriation intents include a $600,000 cap for CGM implementation and a 145% rate increase for lactation consultation.

The added provisions designate the Department of Health and Human Services as responsible for the Family Home Visitation Act and require the department to fund only evidence‑based, periodic home‑visitation programs meeting specified staffing, model, quality, and outcome criteria. DHHS may adopt rules, may use program funds for workforce development and certification, and must publish electronic reports (due Feb 15, 2026, and again through Feb 15, 2028) detailing program types, outcomes, families served, expenditures, models, eligibility, and more. By Oct 1, 2025 DHHS must seek CMS approval via a state‑plan amendment to obtain federal matching funds for targeted case management delivering evidence‑based nurse home visits to postpartum mothers and Medicaid‑enrolled children up to six months. The Legislature intends funding to come from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund (section 68‑996), not the General Fund. No direct new General Fund appropriation is specified.

Summary: The bill assigns primary administrative authority over the Kratom Consumer Protection Act to the Department of Revenue, empowering the Department to register processors, adopt rules, require product testing (including by a Department‑selected laboratory), impose civil penalties (first offense up to $1,000; second up to $5,000; third/subsequent $5,000–$20,000 plus a three‑year processor sales ban), and allow affected parties a hearing before the T… 
The bill assigns primary administrative authority over the Kratom Consumer Protection Act to the Department of Revenue, empowering the Department to register processors, adopt rules, require product testing (including by a Department‑selected laboratory), impose civil penalties (first offense up to $1,000; second up to $5,000; third/subsequent $5,000–$20,000 plus a three‑year processor sales ban), and allow affected parties a hearing before the Tax Commissioner. It also preserves the Department’s tax‑amnesty administration and annual reporting duties (forms/procedures, personnel, technology, revenue). The bill creates a Department of Revenue Enforcement Fund, specifying allocations: at least 80% of amnesty proceeds to the General Fund, 10% (capped at $500,000) to the Enforcement Fund (excess to General Fund); initial Enforcement Fund proceeds are appropriated to the Department to hire enforcement personnel. Thereafter 20% (up to $750,000) of revenue generated by those hires and 10% of §77‑367 contract revenues are deposited to the Fund; transfers are authorized and Fund investment earnings are directed to the General Fund beginning Oct. 1, 2024.
Additions: Key additions involving the Department of Revenue (the "department"): - "Department" is defined as the Department of Revenue. - Enforcement powers: on evidence a product may be adulterated, the department may require independent third‑party testing by a laboratory of its choosing. The department… 
Key additions involving the Department of Revenue (the "department"):

- "Department" is defined as the Department of Revenue.  
- Enforcement powers: on evidence a product may be adulterated, the department may require independent third‑party testing by a laboratory of its choosing. The department may adopt rules to implement the Act.  
- Penalties imposed by the department on processors/retailers: first violation up to $1,000; second up to $5,000; third and subsequent violations $5,000–$20,000 and, for processors, a three‑year ban on selling their kratom products in Nebraska. A clean four‑year period resets status to "first violation."  
- Due process: determinations require notice and a hearing before the Tax Commissioner if requested.  
- Forfeiture: conviction or materially false application statements can forfeit registration and monies paid.  
- Funding: registration/registration‑fee monies shall be used by the Department of Revenue to defray administration costs of the Act.

Substantive provisions impose duties on insurers: insurers must provide any known assignee with at least 30 days' notice of pending lapse/termination of life insurance policies assigned as security for indebtedness; assignees may request electronic notice (effective within 10 business days), and insurers may charge up to $2.50 per notice. For Nebraska-resident senior-citizen insureds (65+), insurers must allow designation of one third-party to receive notices of cancellation, nonrenewal, and conditional renewal (designation/termination procedures and annual notice to seniors specified).

Adds consumer-protection requirements for life insurers (Nebraska references): 
- For life policies assigned as collateral, insurers must notify any known assignee at least 30 days before lapse/termination; electronic notice is allowed and insurers may charge up to $2.50 per notice. Assignees must request such notices in writing (certified mail or electronically) before default; requests take effect within 10 business days. Assignees must mail a release upon termination of their assignment. Excludes nonrenewal and does not alter assignees’ contractual rights.  
- For individual life policies on Nebraska senior citizens (age 65+), insurers must allow the insured to designate one third-party to receive cancellation, nonrenewal, and conditional renewal notices (written designation via certified mail or electronically; effective in 10 business days). Designees may terminate; receiving notices does not create liability. Insurers must annually inform seniors of this option unless a designation exists.

No government agencies or budget/appropriation changes are mentioned.

LB234 (Conrad) amends the Urban Redevelopment Act by redefining "economic redevelopment area" in section 77-6906. LB235 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §76-1446 (Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act). It (1) sets trials for possession at not less than 10 nor more than 14 days after issuance of the summons unless the court grants additional time, and requires the action be tried by the court (no jury); (2) requires the court, if it awards restitution, to issue a writ directing the constable or sheriff to restore possession on a date not less than 10 days after issuance, but permits earlier execution only upon (a) a showing that the defendant poses a true and imminent threat to the safety of other tenants, the landlord, or the landlord’s employees/agents, or (b) the parties’ informed, express agreement; and (3) requires compliance with the Disposition of Personal Property Landlord and Tenant Act and §76-1414(5) for removal of remaining personal property. LB236 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §13-910 (Political Subdivisions Tort Claims Act). It preserves broad immunities for political subdivisions, their governing bodies, employees, and law enforcement, while creating a narrow exception that allows tort claims for child abuse or sexual assault of a child when the harm is a proximate result of a political subdivision’s or employee’s failure to exercise reasonable care to (a) control a person in its charge or (b) protect a person in its care, custody, or control from a non-employee actor. It also retains existing provisions referencing motor vehicle and boat title issuance (including electronic dealer services under §60-1507), the Nebraska Workers' Compensation Act, quarantine and inspection exceptions, and recreational-activity rules. No new agencies or departments are created and the bill contains no funding, appropriation, or budgetary changes. The original section is repealed.

LB237 authorizes counties to conduct elections by mail after the county election commissioner or county clerk submits a written plan to and receives approval from the Secretary of State. Approved counties must follow the mail‑ballot procedures in sections 32‑953 to 32‑959, with ballot receipt deadlines aligned to subsection (2) of section 32‑908. LB238 amends the Foster Care Review Act. It directs the executive director of "the office" to select local foster care review board members (4–10 per board) from applicants, requires demographic representation, and prohibits appointment of employees of the office, the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), residential child‑caring agencies, child‑placing agencies, or courts. The bill assigns and clarifies duties for the Department of Health and Human Services (the department). Key provisions: the department must administer Medicaid home-and-community-based services waivers and determine individual funding via an objective assessment it develops (to be published on the department's website and approved by the Governor’s developmental disability advisory board or stakeholder group). The assessment must be person-centered, include an independent mediated review administered outside the department, and cannot reduce a budget so as to remove a person from a setting. The department must provide or contract service coordination (individuals may choose the provider), create an expedited form for funding-priority-one requests with a five-calendar-day response, and maximize federal funding by requiring eligible residents to apply for Medicaid and other benefits. Annually by Sept. 15 the director must notify the Legislature’s Health and Human Services and Appropriations Committees of estimated unmet need and net additional resources required.
Additions: DHHS must publish the objective assessment formula on its website and submit it for approval to the Governor’s developmental disability advisory board or the required stakeholder group. The assessment cannot reduce an individual’s budget so as to remove them from a setting. Residential settings must… 
DHHS must publish the objective assessment formula on its website and submit it for approval to the Governor’s developmental disability advisory board or the required stakeholder group. The assessment cannot reduce an individual’s budget so as to remove them from a setting. Residential settings must be offered as options for persons in funding priorities 1, 2, 3, and 5, and may be offered for priorities 4 and 6 via the assessment. Redetermination requests must be completed within 30 days. The assessment must be person‑centered, reflect the individual support plan, and include an independent mediated review administered outside DHHS; the individual or legal representative selects the reviewing entity. DHHS must create an expedited form/process for priority‑1 consideration and respond within five calendar days. No funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes are specified.

LB240 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §18-2147 (Community Development Law). Key administrative changes: the Property Tax Administrator must prescribe the notice form and the redevelopment authority must send notice of a tax-division provision to the county assessor on or before July 1 of the effective year. The county assessor must notify the authority and owner of redevelopment project valuations; protests go to the county board of equalization (decision within 30 days; county clerk mails decision within 7 days); appeals may be filed with the Tax Equalization and Review Commission. The county treasurer is notified when authority debt is retired so taxes revert to public bodies. For metropolitan-class cities, the authority and city must prioritize affordable housing use of divided ad valorem tax funds (best efforts to allocate ≥30% annually to single-family housing and a qualified allocation plan). Failure to timely notify causes taxes to remain undivided. The bill takes effect immediately; no direct new appropriations are specified.

LB242 amends property-tax and municipal occupation tax administration and the School District Property Tax Relief Act.

Key agency impacts:
- County treasurers: must show, on tax statements, amounts funding public safety services and bond payments separately; may retain 1% of School District Property Tax Relief disbursements for costs and disburse remaining funds to mirror school tax receipts.
- County boards of equalization: prior-year levies (less certain exceptions) become the baseline for preliminary property tax request authority.
- Property Tax Administrator and State Treasurer: Property Tax Administrator certifies county disbursements, receives returned unused homestead credits, and credits the School District Property Tax Relief Credit Fund; Tax Commissioner prescribes reporting form.
- Municipalities: new or increased occupation taxes require annual public reporting of collections, uses, fund deposits, and termination dates.

Fiscal changes: specified statewide School District Property Tax Relief totals for tax years 2024–2029 (rising from $750M to $902M) and 3% annual increases thereafter; unused property tax authority carryforward capped at 5%; counties/cities/villages excluded from certain “governmental unit” definitions. The bill contains an emergency clause.
Additions: Adds that accumulated excess valuation as of July 1, 2025 must be included when calculating a governmental unit’s increase in excess valuation for redevelopment projects (first fiscal year beginning on/after July 1, 2025). Lists property‑tax exceptions/uses including amounts budgeted for substance‑a… 
Adds that accumulated excess valuation as of July 1, 2025 must be included when calculating a governmental unit’s increase in excess valuation for redevelopment projects (first fiscal year beginning on/after July 1, 2025). Lists property‑tax exceptions/uses including amounts budgeted for substance‑abuse prevention, behavioral health, opioid prevention, matching state and federal grants, and to replace revenue streams reduced or eliminated by legislation. Allows political subdivisions to convert unused restricted‑funds authority existing June 30, 2025 (per §13‑521) into unused property tax request authority for fiscal years beginning on/after July 1, 2025, capped at 5% of the political subdivision’s 2024 property tax levy. Provides that the county treasurer retains 1% for costs before disbursing remaining funds. References §§13‑3404 and 18‑2147.

LB244 (Sanders) amends the legislative findings in section 49-1402 of the Nebraska Political Accountability and Disclosure Act. The bill replaces the existing findings with numbered provisions emphasizing (1) increased public interest and need for accountability and disclosure in campaigns; (2) a compelling state interest in preventing corruption by fully disclosing campaign funding sources and uses; (3) the importance of independence and impartiality of public officials and employees; and (4) that conflicts between private interests and official duties undermine those ends and justify greater legal disclosure and guidance. The original section is repealed. No state agencies or departments are named, and the bill includes no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

LB246 amends the Nebraska Pure Food Act to add a definition for "cultivated-protein food product" (foods resembling animal tissue grown from manufacturing cells) and declares such products to be "adulterated." It bars manufacturing, importing, distributing, promoting, offering, or selling adulterated food and makes violations a separate deceptive trade practice. The bill links these changes to the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act by adding a specific cross-reference. The bill also references existing statutory adoptions of the Food Code and Current Good Manufacturing Practice standards (sections 81-2,257.01 and 81-2,259). No specific state agencies or departments are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

Adds a definition of “cultivated‑protein food product” as a food whose sensory attributes resemble animal tissue but is produced from manufacturing cells grown in vitro (including stem cells originally isolated from an agricultural food animal). Prohibits producing, importing, promoting, displaying for sale, or attempting to sell such cultivated‑protein products. States that any violation committed in the course of business also constitutes a deceptive trade practice and that this section does not alter liability under the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Also references violations of section 81‑2,282. No state agencies or departments are named, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes included.

LB247 amends statutes administered by the Department of Environment and Energy. Landfill/solid-waste disposal fees ($2.34 per specified unit) are paid quarterly to the department and remitted by the State Treasurer: 65% to the Integrated Solid Waste Management Cash Fund (for the department’s response to spills/environmental emergencies; regulation, investigation, remediation and monitoring; and CERCLA nonfederal cost-share, O&M for Superfund sites) and 35% to the Waste Reduction and Recycling Incentive Fund (grants to local governments and limited reimbursements to political subdivisions for roadside/dump-site cleanup). Disbursements to political subdivisions are capped at 5% of prior-year disposal-fee revenue. 

The Petroleum Release Remedial Action Cash Fund, administered by the department and credited by the State Treasurer, is clarified to fund specified remedial actions, third-party claims, State Fire Marshal fee collection, department expenses, State Claims Board approvals, and up to $1.5 million per fiscal year through June 30, 2025 for the department’s CERCLA cost-share/O&M obligations. Investment earnings are credited to the petroleum fund.

LB249 tasks the Nebraska Department of Education (referred to as "the department") with new and revised duties under the Tax Equity and Educational Opportunities Support Act. Beginning FY2025‑26 the department must calculate and pay “military impact funding” to districts that received federal impact aid under ESEA §7003 for federally connected active‑duty children, using a per‑pupil formula (per‑pupil federal impact aid vs. per‑pupil general fund tax levy). The bill (1) modifies what constitutes local system formula resources for certain years, (2) voids any state aid, budget authority, or reserve‑percentage certifications for FY2025‑26 completed before the act’s effective date, and (3) requires the department to certify district budget authority and applicable reserve percentages on or before June 15, 2025, and March 1 thereafter. The Legislative Appropriations Committee must include amounts necessary to fund those certified state aid figures in its budget recommendations. No specific dollar appropriations are set.
Additions: Creates a new ongoing state military-impact aid formula, effective for school fiscal year 2025‑26 and thereafter. The state department (state Dept. of Education implied) must determine and pay "military impact funding" to districts that received a federal ESEA §7003 basic support (impact aid) paymen… 
Creates a new ongoing state military-impact aid formula, effective for school fiscal year 2025‑26 and thereafter. The state department (state Dept. of Education implied) must determine and pay "military impact funding" to districts that received a federal ESEA §7003 basic support (impact aid) payment in the prior year and educate federally connected children of active‑duty parents. The bill ties payments to a formula: per‑pupil federal impact aid (prior year §7003 payment ÷ enrolled federally connected active‑duty pupils) and per‑pupil general fund tax levy (prior year local property tax receipts ÷ fall membership excluding those federally connected pupils). Military impact funding = (per‑pupil general fund tax levy − per‑pupil federal impact aid) × number of eligible pupils, floored at zero if negative. No specific appropriation or dollar amounts are provided.

LB24 amends two probation statutes. Courts (district/county/sentencing courts) must assess a $30 one-time administrative enrollment fee and monthly programming fees ($25 for standard probation, $35 for intensive supervision or participants in non‑probation programs using probation resources via interlocal agreement). Fees are paid to the clerk of the court and remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Probation Program Cash Fund; applicable costs may be covered by funds under §29‑2262.07. Courts may waive monthly fees if the offender was previously found indigent or, after hearing, if payment would be an undue hardship. Probation may be revoked for nonpayment except where the offender is financially unable and so found after hearing. For felony probationers, revocation for substance‑abuse or noncriminal violations may be instituted only after 90 days of cumulative custodial sanctions. Probation terms may be jointly extended by probationer and prosecutor pending resolution.
Additions: Adds that courts must waive, in whole or in part, the fees listed in subdivisions (2)(m) and (o) of §29‑2262 if the offender was previously found indigent in the same case or, after hearing, if payment would be an undue hardship due to limited income, employment/school status, or physical/mental han… 
Adds that courts must waive, in whole or in part, the fees listed in subdivisions (2)(m) and (o) of §29‑2262 if the offender was previously found indigent in the same case or, after hearing, if payment would be an undue hardship due to limited income, employment/school status, or physical/mental handicap. The waiver lasts only while the probationer or participant in a non‑probation program is unable to pay the monthly probation programming fee. Also permits the probation term to be extended, at the joint request of the probationer and the prosecutor, while a motion or information to revoke probation is pending (or until the statutory maximum probation period), provided the probationer has counsel or knowingly and voluntarily requests the extension in open court. Agencies referenced: courts, probation (probation departments/programs) and prosecutors. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are changed.

Summary: The bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services, when establishing and maintaining the Medicaid formulary and preferred drug list, to ensure no FDA‑approved non‑opioid pain medication is disadvantaged or discouraged relative to any opioid/narcotic for pain treatment. Impermissible disadvantaging includes (a) listing a non‑opioid as nonpreferred when an opioid is preferred and (b) imposing more restrictive utilization controls (e.g.,… 
The bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services, when establishing and maintaining the Medicaid formulary and preferred drug list, to ensure no FDA‑approved non‑opioid pain medication is disadvantaged or discouraged relative to any opioid/narcotic for pain treatment. Impermissible disadvantaging includes (a) listing a non‑opioid as nonpreferred when an opioid is preferred and (b) imposing more restrictive utilization controls (e.g., prior authorization, step therapy) on a non‑opioid than the least restrictive controls applied to an opioid. The provision does not prevent preferring one opioid over another or one non‑opioid over another. It applies immediately upon FDA approval and to drugs supplied under DHHS contracts with managed care organizations. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for DHHS are specified.
Additions: DHHS must ensure Medicaid formulary and preferred drug list treatment parity: no FDA‑approved non‑opioid pain drug may be disadvantaged versus opioids (e.g., labeled nonpreferred while an opioid is preferred or subject to more restrictive utilization controls such as prior authorization or step ther… 
DHHS must ensure Medicaid formulary and preferred drug list treatment parity: no FDA‑approved non‑opioid pain drug may be disadvantaged versus opioids (e.g., labeled nonpreferred while an opioid is preferred or subject to more restrictive utilization controls such as prior authorization or step therapy than the least restrictive opioid controls). Preferences may still be set among drugs within the same class. The requirement applies immediately upon FDA approval and to drugs provided under DHHS contracts with managed care organizations. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are mentioned.

Summary: LB256 adopts the Midwest Interstate Passenger Rail Compact and creates a multistate commission to coordinate and advocate for intercity and high‑speed passenger rail. LB256 adopts the Midwest Interstate Passenger Rail Compact and creates a multistate commission to coordinate and advocate for intercity and high‑speed passenger rail. Commission membership involves each Governor (or designee), two state legislators, and a private‑sector appointee; commissioners serve without commission compensation. The commission may hire staff, establish an office, assess dues, accept federal/state/local grants, gifts, and appropriations, and must submit budgets to the officer designated by each party state and report annually to member states’ Governors and legislatures. Financing of commission operations is by equal apportionment among compacting states when legislatures authorize appropriations; the commission may not issue debt. Nebraska is prohibited from participating in or appropriating funds for any compact rail project (including planning) unless authorized by a legislative bill. LB256 creates the Midwest Interstate Passenger Rail Compact Cash Fund to hold gifts, grants, bequests, or legislative transfers; investments managed by the state investment officer under Nebraska investment law.
Additions: Key additions limit Nebraska’s authority and create a dedicated fund. Nebraska may not participate in or appropriate funds for any Midwest Interstate Passenger Rail Compact project — including planning — unless the Legislature enacts a specific bill authorizing that project. A "Midwest Interstate Pa… 
Key additions limit Nebraska’s authority and create a dedicated fund. Nebraska may not participate in or appropriate funds for any Midwest Interstate Passenger Rail Compact project — including planning — unless the Legislature enacts a specific bill authorizing that project. A "Midwest Interstate Passenger Rail Compact Cash Fund" is created to hold gifts, grants, bequests (federal, state, public, or private) and any transfers by the Legislature. Fund proceeds are to be used for compact passenger-rail initiatives. The state investment officer will invest any available fund balances under the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and the Nebraska State Funds Investment Act. The text also contemplates receipts from federal government, party states, and state or local departments, agencies, or municipalities.

- Department may request State Fire Marshal fire-safety inspections, delegate environmental health inspections to local personnel, and rely on city/village/county inspections per statute.
- Nebraska State Patrol must transmit fingerprints to the FBI and report results to the department. The department may seek federal funds to offset fingerprinting costs and adopt implementing rules. No direct appropriations or new budget allocations are specified.

109-1-LB259_IntroReferralLegislature 109, Session 1 (2025)LB259_Intro_Copy.docxDOCX
Summary: LB259 creates the "Faithful Delegate to Federal Article V Convention Act." Key state bodies and officers referenced: - Nebraska Legislature: adopts delegate instructions, elects delegates/alternate delegates, determines unauthorized votes, fills vacancies, and receives oaths filed with the Secretary of State. - Committee on Committees: nominates one delegate and one alternate from each legislative caucus for legislative approval. - Article V Con… 
LB259 creates the "Faithful Delegate to Federal Article V Convention Act." Key state bodies and officers referenced:

- Nebraska Legislature: adopts delegate instructions, elects delegates/alternate delegates, determines unauthorized votes, fills vacancies, and receives oaths filed with the Secretary of State.
- Committee on Committees: nominates one delegate and one alternate from each legislative caucus for legislative approval.
- Article V Convention Committee: formed by elected delegates; chair and vice-chair elected by the Legislature.
- Executive Board of the Legislative Council and the Lieutenant Governor: serve as the advisory committee when the Legislature is not in session (chair of the executive board serves as advisory chair; Lt. Governor may cast tie-breaking votes); six affirmative advisory votes required to deem a vote unauthorized.
- Speaker of the Legislature: must notify convention presiding officer of disqualification.
- Secretary of State: receives filed oaths.
- References Nebraska Political Accountability and Disclosure Act and federal Senate/House offices regarding lobbyist gift prohibitions.

No new appropriations or changes to state funding are included; delegates receive no compensation but may be reimbursed under existing statutes (sections 81-1174 to 81-1177).
Additions: Creates an Article V Convention process centered in the Nebraska Legislature and its existing bodies. Key government actors named: the Legislature (which elects delegates, adopts instructions, and determines unauthorized votes); the Committee on Committees (nominates delegates/alternates); the Artic… 
Creates an Article V Convention process centered in the Nebraska Legislature and its existing bodies. Key government actors named: the Legislature (which elects delegates, adopts instructions, and determines unauthorized votes); the Committee on Committees (nominates delegates/alternates); the Article V Convention Committee (delegates/alternates compose it); the Executive Board of the Legislative Council and the Lieutenant Governor (serve as the advisory committee, chair by the executive board chair; Lt. Gov. breaks ties); the Speaker of the Legislature (must notify convention officers of disqualification); and the Secretary of State (files delegates’ oaths). References also include the Nebraska Political Accountability and Disclosure Act, state reimbursement statutes (sections 81-1174 to 81-1177), and federal officers (Secretary of the U.S. Senate, Clerk of the U.S. House). No new appropriations or budget allocations are made; delegates receive no compensation but may be reimbursed under existing expense rules.

LB266 prohibits local governments—defined as any city, village, county or any agency or subdivision thereof—from enacting or enforcing any ordinance (including resolutions, rules, or regulations) that would have the effect of imposing rent controls on private property. Exceptions: land‑use or inclusionary‑housing measures adopted to increase affordable housing, and voluntary contractual programs in which a private property owner agrees to rent restrictions. The prohibition applies notwithstanding home‑rule charters; any violating ordinance is null and void. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds a statewide prohibition preventing local governments (defined to include cities, villages, counties and their agencies/subdivisions) from enacting or enforcing any ordinance that would impose rent control on private property. "Ordinance" is broadly defined to include laws, resolutions, rules, o… 
Adds a statewide prohibition preventing local governments (defined to include cities, villages, counties and their agencies/subdivisions) from enacting or enforcing any ordinance that would impose rent control on private property. "Ordinance" is broadly defined to include laws, resolutions, rules, or regulations. Exceptions: ordinances adopted to increase affordable housing via land‑use or inclusionary housing requirements, and voluntary contractual programs in which property owners opt in to restrict rents. The provision overrides home rule charters and makes violating ordinances null and void. No agencies, budget changes, appropriations, or funding provisions are included.

Procedural duties for landlords: serve the required five‑day notice to the perpetrator, file suit for possession against only the perpetrator if they do not vacate, and—if judgment is entered—recover court costs and reasonable attorney’s fees, rekey/install new locks, and deny the perpetrator access unless escorted by law enforcement. Where the perpetrator is not a cotenant, landlords must change locks within 24 hours on tenant request; tenants may change locks if landlords fail to do so and must provide the landlord a key or code. Landlords acting in good faith are shielded from liability. No state agency appropriations or budget changes are included.
Additions: The additions reference courts and law enforcement but no specific agencies or budget changes. Protective or restraining orders (court-issued) or certified domestic-violence documentation permit a tenant to (a) remove a cotenant-perpetrator from the lease and trigger landlord eviction actions under… 
The additions reference courts and law enforcement but no specific agencies or budget changes. Protective or restraining orders (court-issued) or certified domestic-violence documentation permit a tenant to (a) remove a cotenant-perpetrator from the lease and trigger landlord eviction actions under section 76-1431 (with courts able to award court costs and reasonable attorney fees to the landlord if judgment is entered) and (b) require a landlord to rekey or replace locks within 24 hours when the perpetrator is not a cotenant. A law enforcement officer may be required to escort a perpetrator reclaiming property. Landlords are protected from liability for good-faith actions and may require tenants to pay actual, reasonable lock-change costs. No appropriations, funding, or departmental budget allocations are included.

LB272 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §77-3506 to expand homestead tax exemptions for veterans and surviving spouses. Beginning January 1, 2026, veterans with a service-connected disability rated at least 10% but less than 100% (and their qualifying surviving spouses) become eligible for a prorated exemption equal to the veteran’s VA disability percentage. The bill requires applicants to include certification from the United States Department of Veterans Affairs; applications remain annual for most categories, but VA certification need only be submitted every fifth year for applicable applicants. No state funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds two provisions: (1) for homesteads described in subdivision (2)(g), the tax-exempt amount is prorated — the exemption percentage equals the veteran’s VA disability percentage; and (2) effective January 1, 2026, expands eligibility to veterans discharged honorable or general (under honorable con… 
Adds two provisions: (1) for homesteads described in subdivision (2)(g), the tax-exempt amount is prorated — the exemption percentage equals the veteran’s VA disability percentage; and (2) effective January 1, 2026, expands eligibility to veterans discharged honorable or general (under honorable conditions) who receive 10%–99% service‑connected disability compensation from the United States Department of Veterans Affairs, and to their unremarried surviving spouses or spouses who remarried after age 57. No funding, appropriations, or other agencies are referenced.

LB274 amends the Child Care Licensing Act to (1) require applicants to provide written proof of liability insurance of at least $200,000 per occurrence before licensure and obligates licensees to maintain that coverage; inspectors must request and verify current proof at each unannounced inspection and the department will suspend a license if proof is not provided within three business days. (2) Clarify inspection and investigation authority: the department (licensing agency) may investigate, inspect, and delegate sanitation inspections to qualified local environmental health personnel; inspections may be conducted by city, village, or county per statute. (3) Allow the department to request fire‑safety inspections from the State Fire Marshal. (4) Require fingerprint‑based national criminal history checks processed by the Nebraska State Patrol and FBI; the department will seek federal funds to offset costs. No new appropriations are specified.

Adds requirements that licensees maintain required liability insurance while caring for children. At each unannounced inspection inspectors must request and verify current proof of insurance; if proof is missing or coverage lapsed the department must notify the licensee to provide proof within three business days and will suspend the license if not received. Licensure is reinstated when the department receives and verifies required proof (per section 71-1911.03). Also requires inspectors to request and verify proof of liability insurance at each investigation. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Summary: The bill amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §43-907 to impose duties on the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) for children under its charge: DHHS must take custody/control of children’s assets; screen each child for Social Security benefit eligibility within 60 days of entry and apply/appeal on the child's behalf; serve as representative payee when appropriate and manage/payments consistent with federal law (holding funds separate, conserving sp… 
The bill amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §43-907 to impose duties on the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) for children under its charge: DHHS must take custody/control of children’s assets; screen each child for Social Security benefit eligibility within 60 days of entry and apply/appeal on the child's behalf; serve as representative payee when appropriate and manage/payments consistent with federal law (holding funds separate, conserving specified minimum percentages by age, avoiding federal asset/resource limits, and using specified exempt accounts); provide accounting and written notices to children, guardians/attorneys, and the juvenile court (including itemized expenditures at review hearings); consult with beneficiaries 14+ every six months; assist with benefit continuation before discharge; create a public form and promulgate rules by October 1, 2026. DHHS must seek maximum federal Title IV‑E funding before using General Funds for implementation costs.
Additions: The added provisions require the Department of Health and Human Services to screen each child in its custody for Social Security benefit eligibility within 60 days, apply and appeal as needed, provide age‑appropriate written notices and accounting, and allow children (and certain representatives) ac… 
The added provisions require the Department of Health and Human Services to screen each child in its custody for Social Security benefit eligibility within 60 days, apply and appeal as needed, provide age‑appropriate written notices and accounting, and allow children (and certain representatives) access to records and requests to use/conserve funds. When the department is representative payee it must manage payments per federal law, hold funds separate (typically in a trust), use accounts that avoid exceeding federal asset limits (e.g., PASS, ABLE, IDAs, special‑needs trusts, dedicated back‑payment accounts), and conserve minimum percentages of benefits by age (14+: 20%; 16+: 30%; 17+: 40%; 18+: 50%). For beneficiaries 14+, the department must consult at least every six months and provide six‑month pre‑exit assistance and notice. By Oct. 1, 2026, DHHS must publish a form to request access. The department must seek federal Title IV‑E funding before using General Funds to implement these requirements. No specific appropriations are listed.

Summary: LB276 requires multiple executive and local agencies to implement new oversight, reporting, and public-disclosure duties: - Cities (metropolitan and primary) must create citizen police oversight boards by Jan 1, 2028; city councils appoint seven members. LB276 requires multiple executive and local agencies to implement new oversight, reporting, and public-disclosure duties:

- Cities (metropolitan and primary) must create citizen police oversight boards by Jan 1, 2028; city councils appoint seven members. Boards may subpoena, inspect police records, investigate complaints and officer-involved shootings, consult the Nebraska Commission on Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice and the Nebraska Police Standards Advisory Council, and publish reports to police departments, mayors, city councils, and county attorneys. Police departments must respond to recommendations; labor contracts cannot negate board authority.

- City attorneys, county attorneys, and the Attorney General must maintain and post Brady/Giglio lists online (updated monthly). The Nebraska Commission on Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice will adopt implementing rules by Sept 1, 2025.

- Chiefs/sheriffs/head administrators must file personnel changes with the training center within seven days, permanently retain misconduct records, and notify the Commission within 30 days of terminations/resignations for serious misconduct. The Commission must publish a public registry of decertified/convicted/misconduct findings and provide a challenge process.

- Judges/magistrates are barred from issuing no‑knock warrants. No appropriations or funding changes are specified.
Additions: Creates required citizen police oversight boards in all primary/metropolitan cities (by Jan 1, 2028). Boards (seven public members appointed by city council) may investigate complaints, discrimination/harassment, officer-involved shootings, and misconduct; inspect police records (including personnel… 
Creates required citizen police oversight boards in all primary/metropolitan cities (by Jan 1, 2028). Boards (seven public members appointed by city council) may investigate complaints, discrimination/harassment, officer-involved shootings, and misconduct; inspect police records (including personnel files); issue subpoenas; and consult standards from the Nebraska Commission on Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice and the Nebraska Police Standards Advisory Council. Boards must report findings to the city police department, mayor, city council, county attorney (for possible criminal conduct), and federal/state misconduct registries; reports and responses are public records and meetings fall under the Open Meetings Act. City/county attorneys and the Attorney General must maintain and post Brady/Giglio lists (updated monthly). The Nebraska Commission must promulgate implementing rules by Sept. 1, 2025. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are mentioned.

LB277 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §29-1401 to require district courts to impanel a grand jury when the county coroner or coroner’s physician certifies a death occurred while a person was being apprehended by or in the custody of law enforcement or detention personnel. The court must appoint a special prosecutor (minimum five years’ criminal/felony litigation experience) who will select a three-officer homicide-investigation team from outside the jurisdiction. Local law enforcement must secure scenes, preserve evidence, investigate until materials are transferred to the special prosecutor, and officers involved may not return to duty until grand jury proceedings conclude. A county attorney may present a certified natural-cause finding to a grand jury in lieu of appointing a special prosecutor. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

It also bars any law enforcement or detention personnel involved in a death from returning to duty until the grand jury completes its investigation. No executive agencies or departments (beyond courts, grand juries, and law enforcement/detention entities) are newly created or specified, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes included.

LB279 amends Nebraska motor vehicle registration law to require only one license plate to be displayed on registered motor vehicles or trailers. The bill directs the department to continue issuing one or two reflectorized plates and specifies that when two plates are issued only the rear plate must be displayed; when only one plate is issued it must be displayed on the rear (front for apportionable vehicles and truck‑tractors). The director must procure plate materials through competitive bids under the State Procurement Act. County treasurers will provide validation decals for single‑plate requests. The bill retains the existing additional annual nonrefundable $50 single‑plate fee (plus decal cost), collected by county treasurers and remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Highway Trust Fund.
Additions: Adds language changing the vehicle registration wording to require only one license plate ("only one license plate is required to") instead of "at least one license plate." No government agencies, departments, or funding/appropriations are referenced or affected.

Summary: Bill amends the Rural Health Systems and Professional Incentive Act and the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund statutes. It explicitly allows the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund to be used for Rural Health Act loan repayments and directs investment earnings (beginning Oct. 1, 2024) to the General Fund. It restates purposes (including creation of the Nebraska Rural Health Advisory Commission) and adds a dentist-specific loan-repayme… 
Bill amends the Rural Health Systems and Professional Incentive Act and the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund statutes. It explicitly allows the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund to be used for Rural Health Act loan repayments and directs investment earnings (beginning Oct. 1, 2024) to the General Fund. It restates purposes (including creation of the Nebraska Rural Health Advisory Commission) and adds a dentist-specific loan-repayment option administered by the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). Eligible dentists (less than five years in practice, no prior program aid) may contract directly with DHHS for up to $60,000 per year for five years (maximum $300,000 total), must meet Medicaid patient-share requirements, and face full repayment with 8% interest on breach. Agreements are exempt from the State Procurement Act. The Legislature intends to appropriate $1,500,000 from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund to DHHS for FY2025‑26 for these repayments.
Additions: Creates a DHHS‑administered loan repayment program for dentists who treat Medicaid patients, added to the Rural Health Systems and Professional Incentive Act. DHHS (the "department") may enter agreements exempt from the State Procurement Act; a commission will set required Medicaid patient threshold… 
Creates a DHHS‑administered loan repayment program for dentists who treat Medicaid patients, added to the Rural Health Systems and Professional Incentive Act. DHHS (the "department") may enter agreements exempt from the State Procurement Act; a commission will set required Medicaid patient thresholds and verify use of payments. Eligible dentists must have <5 years' practice and no prior program assistance, commit to five years' practice in Nebraska, and receive up to $60,000/year (maximum $300,000 per recipient) toward qualified educational debt. Breach triggers full repayment plus 8% simple interest; obligations cancel on death or total permanent disability. DHHS may only pay from specifically appropriated funds. The Legislature intends a $1.5 million appropriation from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund to DHHS for FY2025‑26 for these repayments.
