- Auditor of Public Accounts (APA): authorized to receive and review annual independent CPA audits (including internal control reports) filed by each authorized gaming operator (operator-paid) within six months of fiscal year end; to review for calculation errors or deficiencies affecting gross gaming revenue or gaming tax; to report findings to the Governor, Legislature, and the gaming commission; and to examine operators’ books, records, funds, and accounts as prescribed.
- State investment officer: investment earnings on the Racetrack Gaming Fund are credited to the General Fund beginning October 1, 2024.
Additions: Adds an annual audit requirement for each authorized gaming operator in Nebraska: operators must, at their own expense, hire an independent certified public accountant licensed in Nebraska to audit annual financial statements and report on internal controls covering all Nebraska operations. Audit re… 
Adds an annual audit requirement for each authorized gaming operator in Nebraska: operators must, at their own expense, hire an independent certified public accountant licensed in Nebraska to audit annual financial statements and report on internal controls covering all Nebraska operations. Audit reports must be submitted electronically to the Auditor of Public Accounts and the gaming commission within six months after year‑end (unless the Auditor grants a written extension). The Auditor of Public Accounts will review reports for mathematical errors, improper accounting, or deficiencies—especially those affecting gross gaming revenue or the annual gaming tax—and will report the review results electronically to the Governor, the Legislature, and the gaming commission. No new appropriations or budget allocations are specified.

LB281 consolidates and updates Nebraska nursing regulation. It removes a separate Board of Advanced Practice Registered Nurses and standardizes multiple statutory references to the Board of Nursing. The bill revises Board of Nursing composition and member qualifications (details for practical nurse, associate/diploma, baccalaureate educators, staff nurses, nursing service administrators, LPN members, and APRN members), prescribes APRN member term lengths effective January 1, 2026, and sets preferred APRN representation (CRNA, NP, CNS, CNM). The State Board of Health retains appointment responsibilities and representational directives. The board’s duties are clarified to include administering the Nurse Licensure Compact and authorize the department to report personal identifying information, including social security numbers, to the compact’s coordinated licensure information system. Sections 38-205, 38-206, and 38-2307 are repealed. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are made or changed.
Additions: Adds provisions, effective Jan. 1, 2026, governing advanced practice registered nurses serving on the board: initial staggered appointments of one three‑year, one four‑year and one five‑year term, with all subsequent appointments set at five years. Specifies preferred APRN representation on the boar… 
Adds provisions, effective Jan. 1, 2026, governing advanced practice registered nurses serving on the board: initial staggered appointments of one three‑year, one four‑year and one five‑year term, with all subsequent appointments set at five years. Specifies preferred APRN representation on the board: one certified registered nurse anesthetist, one nurse practitioner, one clinical nurse specialist and one certified nurse midwife; if that composition cannot be met, vacancies may be filled from the applicant pool. No state agency beyond "the board" is newly created or identified and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes.

LB285 prohibits the sale, marketing, or state tax certification of defined "flavored vapor products" (electronic nicotine delivery systems with flavors other than tobacco or menthol). It directs the Tax Commissioner not to issue certifications under the Tobacco Products Tax Act (§77-4011.01) for flavored vapor products. The cigarette tax division of the Tax Commissioner may revoke or suspend licenses or certifications for violations (§59-1523), and cigarettes acquired or imported in violation are contraband subject to seizure and destruction. Retail licensees under §§28-1420–28-1429 are barred from selling flavored vapor products; violations carry a Class III misdemeanor, license revocation/forfeiture, and specified reissuance suspension periods (five years for certain offenses, one year for others). No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds a definition of "flavored vapor product" as any electronic nicotine delivery system that (a) has a taste or smell other than tobacco or menthol distinguishable to consumers (examples listed), (b) is marketed as having such a taste/smell, or (c) is represented by the manufacturer or seller as ha… 
Adds a definition of "flavored vapor product" as any electronic nicotine delivery system that (a) has a taste or smell other than tobacco or menthol distinguishable to consumers (examples listed), (b) is marketed as having such a taste/smell, or (c) is represented by the manufacturer or seller as having such a taste/smell. It prohibits holders of licenses issued under sections 28-1420 to 28-1429 from marketing, advertising, selling, or causing sale of flavored vapor products. It also bars the Tax Commissioner from issuing certifications under section 77-4011.01 for flavored electronic nicotine delivery systems and forbids manufacturers from causing flavored ENDS to be sold at retail in the state. No funding or appropriation changes are included.

LB286 amends two economic development statutes, imposing application deadlines and procedural requirements. It directs the (department) director to accept Nebraska Innovation Hub (iHub) applications only through December 31, 2025, and bars new Nebraska Rural Projects Act applications after December 31, 2025 (complete applications filed by that date may still be approved and agreements executed). The bill requires $1,000 nonrefundable application fees for both programs; the director must remit iHub fees to the Innovation Hub Cash Fund and rural project fees to the Nebraska Rural Projects Fund via the State Treasurer. The department must establish weighted scoring, approval/designation guidelines, and annual reporting; iHubs report to the director and the Urban Affairs Committee, and the director must post reports and notify the Governor and Legislature. Original sections are repealed.
Additions: Adds a deadline extension: "The director shall accept applications filed under this section through December 31, 2025." No specific state agency or department is named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

LB287 amends the Nebraska Housing Agency Act (section 71-1572) to assign specific bed‑bug responsibilities to housing agencies for cities of the metropolitan class. The agency must visually inspect units before renting, may not show or lease units it knows or reasonably suspects are infested, and must disclose adjacent-unit infestations to prospective tenants. On complaint, the agency must acknowledge within five days, inspect or retain a pest control professional (a commercial applicator licensed under the Pesticide Act) within five days, remediate confirmed infestations within 14 days, inspect adjacent units within five days, provide advance notice before unit entry, notify affected tenants of determinations within five days, and retain complaint/remediation records for two years. The housing agency is made responsible for all investigation and remediation costs.
Additions: Adds duties for the "housing agency for a city of the metropolitan class," including mandated bed‑bug prevention and response actions. Key agency obligations: pre‑rental visual inspections and disclosure of adjacent unit treatments; refusal to show/rent units known or reasonably suspected to be infe… 
Adds duties for the "housing agency for a city of the metropolitan class," including mandated bed‑bug prevention and response actions. Key agency obligations: pre‑rental visual inspections and disclosure of adjacent unit treatments; refusal to show/rent units known or reasonably suspected to be infested; acknowledge complaints within 5 days; inspect or hire a licensed pest control professional within 5 days; remediate confirmed infestations within 14 days; inspect adjacent units within 5 days; provide tenant notice before entry and notice of pest professional determinations within 5 days; keep written complaint/control records for two years. Fiscal effect: the housing agency is expressly made responsible for all investigation and remediation costs (no specific appropriation provided).

Summary: The bill amends multiple affordable- and workforce-housing provisions involving the Department of Economic Development (DED). Key DED actions and fiscal provisions: - DED may not require new-construction or rental-conversion projects funded from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund to satisfy other department program application requirements (Sec. 10). - DED shall prioritize funding applications using available funds reduced by actual administrat… 
The bill amends multiple affordable- and workforce-housing provisions involving the Department of Economic Development (DED). Key DED actions and fiscal provisions:

- DED may not require new-construction or rental-conversion projects funded from the Affordable Housing Trust Fund to satisfy other department program application requirements (Sec. 10).  
- DED shall prioritize funding applications using available funds reduced by actual administrative costs, may contract for services, and may recapture unused or unspent awards (recaptured funds credit to the Trust Fund) (Secs. 11–12).  
- DED must include its administration budget, planned fund uses, and project-level summaries (including grant amounts requested) in its annual report (Sec. 12).  
- DED will administer the Middle Income Workforce Housing Investment Fund, create a subaccount for Economic Recovery Act parcel preparation, seek private funds, apply interest to grants, and return or transfer unexpended funds to the General Fund under specified timelines (Sec. 16).  
- Matching for workforce housing grants is reduced from 50% to 25% for awards on/after July 19, 2024; DED updates construction/value limits annually using the Producer Price Index (Secs. 15, 7).  

The Department of Labor is not referenced in the bill.
Additions: Department of Economic Development - New provisions govern Affordable Housing Trust Fund awards: the department may recoup funds if a recipient fails to complete agreed housing units (pro rata) and must credit recaptured amounts back to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund. - Recapture also applies to… 
Department of Economic Development
- New provisions govern Affordable Housing Trust Fund awards: the department may recoup funds if a recipient fails to complete agreed housing units (pro rata) and must credit recaptured amounts back to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund.
- Recapture also applies to homebuyer assistance provided by recipients — repayment from net sale proceeds goes back to the Fund.
- The department may impose sanctions for misuse, including suspension from applying for up to 24 months, other administrative measures (not unduly harming reputation), and standard criminal referrals for fraud/theft.
- The department may not require new-construction or rental-conversion projects funded by the Trust Fund to meet other department program application requirements and shall not restrict construction/sale of units funded from specified sources.
Department of Labor
- No added text affecting the Department of Labor or its budget/appropriations was found.

LB289 amends village and municipal procedures and the Local Option Municipal Economic Development Act. Key government entities affected:

- County board: may incorporate villages and appoint initial village trustees per petitioner-designated three- or five-member board.
- Election commissioner or county clerk and county canvassing board: receive and verify petitions, place trustee-number questions on statewide general-election ballots, and canvass results; village clerks provide petition forms.
- Village boards of trustees and city councils: may change trustee count via petition or board resolution; establishes election and term-staggering rules when switching between three and five trustees.
- City councils or village boards: may be designated to serve as boards of adjustment and must adopt rules consistent with statutory board-of-adjustment powers.
- U.S. Bureau of the Census: remains the population source for statutory thresholds.
The bill redefines “qualifying business” to expressly include retail trade, housing construction/rehabilitation, and early-childhood care and education; no funding or appropriation changes are included.
Additions: Adds procedures letting village voters decide at a statewide general election whether their village board will have three or five trustees. Key officials/agencies referenced: - Village clerk: provides petition forms. - Election commissioner or county clerk: assists with petitions, receives filings (… 
Adds procedures letting village voters decide at a statewide general election whether their village board will have three or five trustees. Key officials/agencies referenced:
- Village clerk: provides petition forms.
- Election commissioner or county clerk: assists with petitions, receives filings (≥70 days before the election), verifies signatures per section 32-631, places the question on the ballot, and conducts/counts the canvass.
- County canvassing board: completes canvass and declares results.
- References to statutory procedures if membership is increased (secs. 32-568, 32-569) or decreased (sec. 17-202).

Petition rules: signatures from at least 5% of village electors from the prior statewide general election; no post‑filing changes allowed. Term assignments at the first statewide general election after incorporation or a change are specified (which trustees serve two- vs. four‑year terms). No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are mentioned.

This bill amends duties and grant authority of the Economic Recovery and Incentives Division of the Department of Economic Development. The division shall award grants (50% advance, remainder paid monthly until paid or by Dec. 31, 2026) and may recoup or reduce payments for unused funds. It must prioritize grants to qualified census tracts (QCTs) in metropolitan-class cities and rely on studies under §81-12,242. The division will create a Qualified Census Tract Recovery Grant Program with allocations: up to $10M for QCTs in primary-class cities, up to $10M for QCTs outside metro/primary cities, and remaining funds for metro-class QCTs. Additional capped grants administered by the division include: $90M for a business park (with specified pre-release conditions), $6M for internships/crime prevention, $5M film production, $20M (metro) and $20M (primary) for affordable housing land prep, $5M to a county agricultural society, and $1M for postsecondary financial literacy. Grants using federal ARPA funds must meet Treasury guidance.
Additions: Requires that grant-eligible activity be limited to the boundaries of an inland port district within a metropolitan-class city and expressly prohibits use of grant funds in that city’s downtown and northern downtown areas. For the Department of Economic Development, this narrows where DED-administer… 
Requires that grant-eligible activity be limited to the boundaries of an inland port district within a metropolitan-class city and expressly prohibits use of grant funds in that city’s downtown and northern downtown areas. For the Department of Economic Development, this narrows where DED-administered grants may be spent but does not specify any new appropriations, funding amounts, or budget reallocations.

The bill defines "Department" as the Department of Economic Development and assigns it two explicit roles. Under the Aid to Municipalities Act the Department will receive and process municipal grant applications (on forms it prescribes), consider them in receipt order, and may approve grants within available appropriations; no individual grant may exceed $5 million. Amendments to section 13-522 require the Auditor to notify the Department (for cities and villages) of budget noncompliance; the State Treasurer and, where applicable, the Department must suspend distribution of state aid to the noncomplying municipal unit until compliance. Suspended funds are held six months and may be forfeited and redistributed if noncompliance continues.
Additions: Adds the Department of Economic Development as the defined "Department" administering the Aid to Municipalities Act. Adds the Department of Economic Development as the defined "Department" administering the Aid to Municipalities Act. Municipalities apply to the Department on a Department-prescribed form (request amount and project description). The Department must process applications in receipt order and may approve grants only within available appropriations; individual grants are capped at $5 million. The Department also is to receive notifications of noncompliance (for cities or villages). No new dollar appropriations or specific budget allocations are included—approvals are constrained to existing/available appropriations.

LB293 amends the Professional Employer Organization Registration Act (sections 48‑2706 and 48‑2708). Key agency-related provisions:

- Requires professional employer organizations (PEOs) offering self-funded health benefit plans to file quarterly reports and an annual report within 90 days after the plan fiscal year with "the department" detailing: financial statements; an actuary's solvency statement; confirmation of stop‑loss insurance (aggregate excess >125% of expected claims) issued by an insurer licensed in Nebraska; and a certificate of compliance. Stop‑loss policies must notify the PEO and the Commissioner of Labor at least 30 days before termination.

- Authorizes the department to hold compliance hearings, issue orders to comply within 30 days, and revoke a PEO's registration for noncompliance.

- Declares PEO‑sponsored employee welfare/health plans a single employee welfare benefit plan, exempting them from the Multiple Employer Welfare Arrangement Act, and treats the PEO as the employer under the Small Employer Health Insurance Availability Act; insurers must accept and insure eligible employees.

No appropriations or funding changes are included.
Additions: Adds requirements for professional employer organizations (PEOs) that offer health plans: plans must be fully insured or, if self‑funded, use a licensed third‑party administrator, hold assets in an ERISA-style trust, maintain actuarially sound reserves, notify employees the plan is self‑funded, and… 
Adds requirements for professional employer organizations (PEOs) that offer health plans: plans must be fully insured or, if self‑funded, use a licensed third‑party administrator, hold assets in an ERISA-style trust, maintain actuarially sound reserves, notify employees the plan is self‑funded, and file with the department quarterly and within 90 days after plan fiscal year end. Quarterly/annual reports to the department must include a financial statement, an actuary’s adequacy statement, evidence of aggregate stop‑loss insurance naming the PEO and requiring the insurer to give the PEO and the Commissioner of Labor 30 days’ written notice before termination, and a certificate of state-law compliance. The department (via 30 days’ written notice) may hold compliance hearings, issue corrective orders within 30 days after a hearing, and revoke PEO registration under the Professional Employer Organization Registration Act for failure to comply. No funding or appropriation changes are included.

LB294 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §81-3720 governing the County Visitors Improvement Fund. Administration remains with the county governing body, advised by the visitors committee created under §81-3717. The fund may make grants to public or nonprofit-owned visitor attractions for construction, expansion, exhibits, planning, or development. Annual grant amounts are limited to the greater of proceeds from a one-percent county sales tax designated for the Fund or $5,000. Grants may be pledged to secure bonds, may run up to 20 years, and must be funded annually per contract. Bonds secured by such grants are explicitly not general obligations or pledges of county faith and credit. The bill repeals the original section and takes effect immediately as an emergency measure.

LB295 touches the Department of Labor in three limited ways. It adopts the U.S. Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index (CPI‑U) as the index for annual cost‑of‑living adjustments and directs use of a substitute DOL index if CPI is discontinued; it also cites the DOL’s Medical Price Index to justify a separate medical cost‑of‑living supplemental annuity. The bill clarifies retirement coverage for Department of Labor employees employed before July 1, 1984 and paid from Title III or other federal funds: such employees remain excluded from the State Employees Retirement Act unless their contributory retirement plan/contract is terminated, in which case they become members effective the first day of the first pay period after termination and receive vesting credit for prior participation. No Department of Labor funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are changed.

No provisions specifically reference or alter duties, funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department of Labor. The added text amends Public Employees Retirement Board rules: it recognizes DHS/USCIS extensions of ID validity, creates a hardship exception to repayment of inadvertent benefit overpayments (including gross distributions), adjusts the method for calculating a 20‑hour‑per‑week threshold, clarifies allowable remote retirement‑planning access, and restricts use of state retirement system names/logos in financial solicitations. No Department of Labor budget or funding changes are included.

LB297 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §48-649.03 (Employment Security Law). It clarifies that the state's reserve-ratio and average combined tax-rate calculations use "total wages for contributory employers" when determining yield and planned yield for the Unemployment Trust Fund and the State Unemployment Insurance Trust Fund. The bill preserves the commissioner's authority to adopt rules and to lower scheduled yield factors when the reserve ratio is ≥ 0.70%. It fixes the rate-assignment scheme but makes a one-time change for tax year 2025: rate category 12 is set at 0.48. No specific appropriations or budget line-item changes are included. The act is effective on passage due to an emergency clause.

Summary: The bill creates and reorganizes legislative oversight offices and sets agency duties and information‑sharing rules: - Department of Correctional Services: establishes an Office of Inspector General within the Division of Legislative Oversight (appointment with legislative committee approval; ineligible if a recent DCS executive), requires prompt notification of deaths/serious injuries/hospitalizations, access to records (medical/mental‑health r… 
The bill creates and reorganizes legislative oversight offices and sets agency duties and information‑sharing rules:

- Department of Correctional Services: establishes an Office of Inspector General within the Division of Legislative Oversight (appointment with legislative committee approval; ineligible if a recent DCS executive), requires prompt notification of deaths/serious injuries/hospitalizations, access to records (medical/mental‑health records generally require consent except death investigations), subpoena authority, confidentiality and annual reporting; inmate/parole files are confidential with limited public release. Deputy public counsel for corrections has authority over DCS and local jails.

- Department of Health and Human Services and Department of Veterans' Affairs: deputy public counsel for institutions has authority over DHHS mental‑health institutions/regional behavioral health authorities and veterans institutions; DHHS must report/cooperate with child‑welfare Inspector General investigations.

- Department of Administrative Services: Accounting Administrator must furnish information to the Legislative Fiscal Analyst; building division must prepare cost analyses for projects ≥ $400,000 (threshold reset every four years); DAS employees prohibited from impermissible tax‑record disclosure.

- Department of Revenue: Tax Commissioner retains return confidentiality but must provide returns/secures audit workpapers on request to the Auditor/Legislative Audit Office for audits.

- Department of Labor, Department of Insurance, Department of Motor Vehicles: limited, specified tax‑return disclosures permitted — Labor for employment‑law administration and tax‑incentive audits (using Labor data/NAICS), DMV for IFTA enforcement, Insurance for tax‑credit administration.

Staffing for new oversight offices is authorized "within the amount available by appropriation" or "within available appropriations"; no specific appropriations or budget increases are included.
Additions: Added text creates expanded legislative oversight: establishes Offices (Public Counsel; Inspectors General for Child Welfare and the Correctional System) and a Legislative Audit Office with broad investigatory and subpoena powers over state agencies (including DAS, DOI, Labor, Corrections, DHHS, DMV… 
Added text creates expanded legislative oversight: establishes Offices (Public Counsel; Inspectors General for Child Welfare and the Correctional System) and a Legislative Audit Office with broad investigatory and subpoena powers over state agencies (including DAS, DOI, Labor, Corrections, DHHS, DMV, Revenue, Veterans’ Affairs). Agencies must provide records/personnel (30-day production), may negotiate privilege objections, and face expedited litigation in Lancaster County to compel or quash subpoenas. DHHS and the Department responsible for corrections are specifically required to notify the respective Inspector General when criminal investigations involving death or serious injury begin and end; agencies may enter secure information‑sharing agreements. The Legislative Auditor may hire staff “within the amount available by appropriation through the Division of Legislative Oversight” (no specific dollar amounts added). Any fees for counsel present during questioning are not charged to the offices or Legislative Council.

The bill directs the Department of Administrative Services to prescribe the attestation format for verifying U.S. citizenship, lawful presence, or "eligible alien" status for applicants seeking certain public benefits and professional/commercial licenses; agencies may allow electronic attestation if it is substantially similar to the format the Department prescribes. Separately, the bill provides that if a contributory retirement plan (per former section 48-609) is terminated, active employees of the Department of Labor in that plan at termination shall receive vesting credit for their years of participation. No appropriations, budget allocations, or other funding changes are included.
Additions: Adds definitions for "approved identification document" and "eligible alien" (authorized under 8 C.F.R. 274a.12 as of Jan 1, 2025) and provides that eligible aliens employed in Nebraska are entitled to employment-related public benefits, including retirement (State, County, School, Class V), benefit… 
Adds definitions for "approved identification document" and "eligible alien" (authorized under 8 C.F.R. 274a.12 as of Jan 1, 2025) and provides that eligible aliens employed in Nebraska are entitled to employment-related public benefits, including retirement (State, County, School, Class V), benefits under the Employment Security Law, deferred compensation (84-1504), scholarships/financial aid, and related family/dependent benefits regardless of relatives' immigration status. The Department of Administrative Services must prescribe the attestation format applicants use to verify eligible‑alien status. Implication for the Department of Labor: unemployment/Employment Security Law benefits must be made available to eligible aliens. No explicit funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB29 amends the Administrative Procedure Act to require state agencies to review all existing and pending rules beginning January 1, 2026 and every three years thereafter. Each agency head must designate an oversight individual and submit an electronic report to the Clerk of the Legislature by June 30 of the review year addressing: public health/safety/welfare necessity; cost‑benefit; effectiveness measurement; consideration of less‑restrictive alternatives; and whether the rule stemmed from state statute, federal mandate, or court order. The Legislature’s Reference Committee will refer reports to relevant standing committees, which must report to the Clerk by December 15 with recommended legislation or clarifications. Agency rulemaking is suspended during the review except for rules affecting health/safety, time‑sensitive matters, or those subject to statutory deadlines. No funding or appropriation changes are included.
Additions: Starting Jan 1, 2026, all state agencies must review all existing and pending rules every three years. Agency heads must appoint a review supervisor. Starting Jan 1, 2026, all state agencies must review all existing and pending rules every three years. Agency heads must appoint a review supervisor. Agencies must file an electronic, detailed report to the Clerk of the Legislature by June 30 of the review year addressing: public health/safety/welfare necessity; cost‑benefit; whether effectiveness is measured; consideration of less‑restrictive alternatives; and whether the rule arose from state statute, federal mandate, or a court decision. The Legislature’s Reference Committee will assign each agency report to the appropriate standing committee, which must file its recommendations by Dec 15 and may propose clarifying legislation. Rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act is suspended during the review, except for rules that affect health/safety/welfare, are time‑sensitive, or meet statutory deadlines. No funding or appropriation changes are included.

Summary: LB300 amends multiple school statutes to expand and clarify the Superintendent Pay Transparency Act. LB300 amends multiple school statutes to expand and clarify the Superintendent Pay Transparency Act. It requires boards of Class I–V school districts and boards of educational service units (ESUs) to ensure superintendent and ESU administrator compensation complies with the Act. Key provisions: (1) defines salary, benefits, and compensation (including employer contributions under the School Employees Retirement Act and Class V SERA); (2) caps total compensation for a superintendent or ESU administrator at five times the district’s/ESU’s beginning-teacher compensation for the same contract year; (3) declares contracts violating the cap invalid, prohibits expenditure of funds on them, requires forfeiture and return of excess pay, and mandates filing notice with the Commissioner of Education within 30 days; and (4) mandates pre-approval and post-approval publication of proposed and approved contracts and cost estimates (website publication permitted). No new appropriations or budget allocations are provided.

Adds compliance with a new Superintendent Pay Transparency Act: boards must set superintendent/administrator pay consistent with that Act and related sections. Defines Benefit (wide range of employer-paid items including retirement contributions, early-retirement inducements, annuities, insurance premiums, severance, cash awards, payment for unused leave), Compensation (salary plus benefits), Beginning‑teacher compensation (first‑year pay with maximum typical benefits), and Salary (gross wages including overtime and certain retirement/deferral contributions).

Imposes a cap: no contract may require paying a superintendent/administrator more than five times the beginning‑teacher compensation in the same school district or educational service unit. Violating contracts are invalid; excess pay must be forfeited and returned. Boards/officials must notify the Commissioner of Education within 30 days of learning of a violation and provide related compensation and cap calculations.

Agencies mentioned: school districts, educational service units, boards of education, Commissioner of Education, and references to state School Employees Retirement Acts and federal tax code sections. No direct changes to appropriations or new funding allocations are included.

Summary: LB302 ceases Nebraska’s observance of daylight saving time (effective only after Iowa, Kansas, South Dakota, and Wyoming enact similar laws) and harmonizes statutory time references. Key agency/departments and administrative effects: - Governor: retains discretion to extend annual leave in special cases. - Legislative Council / Executive Board: exercises that discretion for legislative employees. - Director of Personnel: required to adopt an… 
LB302 ceases Nebraska’s observance of daylight saving time (effective only after Iowa, Kansas, South Dakota, and Wyoming enact similar laws) and harmonizes statutory time references. Key agency/departments and administrative effects:

- Governor: retains discretion to extend annual leave in special cases.  
- Legislative Council / Executive Board: exercises that discretion for legislative employees.  
- Director of Personnel: required to adopt and promulgate rules to administer vacation leave provisions.  
- Employing agencies: must provide reasonable opportunity to use accrued vacation; if a reasonable written request to use leave is denied and the leave is forfeited, the agency must pay the cash equivalent within 30 days.  
- Public Employees Retirement Board: cash payments for denied-forfeited leave count as compensation only for defined contribution or cash-balance retirement plans.  

No appropriations, budget allocations, or other funding changes are included.
Additions: Adds a provision that Nebraska’s standard time follows the Uniform Time Act of 1966 for both central and mountain zones but that the state will not observe daylight saving time and is exempt from 15 U.S.C. 260a(a) (the federal DST advancement provision). The subsection becomes operative on January 1… 
Adds a provision that Nebraska’s standard time follows the Uniform Time Act of 1966 for both central and mountain zones but that the state will not observe daylight saving time and is exempt from 15 U.S.C. 260a(a) (the federal DST advancement provision). The subsection becomes operative on January 1 following the date when Iowa, Kansas, South Dakota, and Wyoming each enact similar laws. The provision is void if subsection (2) of §49-1301 becomes operative. No government agencies or departments are newly created or mentioned, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes.

Agencies and entities named: the Governor (appointing commission members), the Executive Board of the Legislative Council (appointing one member), the State Board of Education (approval authority for exclusions and for demonstrations of net savings from voluntary termination agreements), the Department (responsible for defining distance‑education/telecommunications expenditures for Network Nebraska), the Educational Service Unit Coordinating Council, the School Employees Retirement System of the State of Nebraska, and the Class V School Employees Retirement system. Fiscal changes: employer retirement contributions above baseline rates (7.35% for SERS; 7.37% for Class V) are allowable exclusions; 2024‑25 SERS excess contributions may be carried into 2025‑26 and 2026‑27 budget authority; Network Nebraska, early‑childhood, special grants, special education, and certain voluntary‑termination incentive amounts are clarified as exclusions. Adds appointment and term rules for a statutory commission: the Executive Board of the Legislative Council will appoint the member described in subdivision (1)(d) in January of odd‑numbered years for two‑year terms (initial appointee within 30 days of the act, serving until a successor in January 2027). Members from subdivisions (1)(a)–(c) serve ex officio. The Governor must appoint members in (1)(e)–(h) within 30 days of the act; initial staggering is specified (some three‑year, some two‑year), thereafter three‑year terms, with gubernatorial appointment to fill vacancies. Summary: LB304 directs the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to administer Nebraska’s social services program and to participate in the federal Child Care Subsidy/Child Care and Development Block Grant programs, extending child care assistance eligibility and transitional assistance rules (including a 10% earned-income disregard and provider accommodation provisions). LB304 directs the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to administer Nebraska’s social services program and to participate in the federal Child Care Subsidy/Child Care and Development Block Grant programs, extending child care assistance eligibility and transitional assistance rules (including a 10% earned-income disregard and provider accommodation provisions). DHHS must promulgate rules (subdivisions operative July 1, 2025), adopt an annual fixed-rate schedule for subsidy payments (effective Oct. 1 each year), and collaborate with a private nonprofit for an independent evaluation of prior income-eligibility changes if privately funded (evaluation due July 1, 2024). Funding: CCDBG funds shall cover costs from the eligibility changes; if insufficient, TANF funds may be used; no General Funds (except administration) shall be used. DHHS must also develop policy guidelines for additional cash assistance in extreme hardship cases.

- Caps approvals at $1,000,000 in credits per fiscal year, with priority for rural preceptors and prorating of credits when the annual limit is exceeded.  
- Grants the department rulemaking authority to implement the Preceptorship Tax Credit Act.  
- Adds the Preceptorship Tax Credit Act to the list of income tax credits in section 77-2715.07.  
- Separately, the Department of Revenue may recapture a residence purchase credit if residency requirements are not met.

Fiscal/financial effect: the department may approve up to $1,000,000 in tax credits per fiscal year, give approval priority to rural preceptors, prorate credits among requests received on the day the annual cap is exceeded, and prohibit transfer/sale of credits. LB306 directs three state agencies as follows:

- Department of Administrative Services: required to develop, maintain, and post a public database of school-district financial information (audit-based revenue, expenditures, assets/liabilities). The DAS budget administrator will set an implementation date on or before January 1, 2026. School districts must provide current and annual updates (and available historical data beginning 2005); DAS must update the database within 30 days of receipt.

- Department of Economic Development: will designate eligible programs of study for Nebraska Career Scholarships (in collaboration with the Board of Trustees, Board of Regents, or Coordinating Commission) based on periodic workforce-need reviews.

- Department of Health and Human Services: foster homes and residential service providers must be licensed/approved by DHHS for residency determinations; the state will pay education (and required transportation) costs for wards placed outside their resident district under rules and regulations prescribed by DHHS.

- Funding/appropriations: Boards and the Coordinating Commission shall allocate amounts appropriated under the Nebraska Career Scholarship Act among campuses/private colleges; the commission must establish a separate budget subprogram for private-college scholarship allocations.

Department of Administrative Services (DAS): New requirement for DAS to develop, maintain, and publish online a school-district financial database (revenue sources, expenditures, and balance sheets showing assets/liabilities) using most recent audit reports. School districts must provide audit-derived data annually (and historical data back to 2005 if available); DAS must update the database within 30 days of receipt. This bill designates the Commissioner of Labor and the Department of Labor as the administering authorities for the new Health Care Staffing Agency Registration Act. Health care staffing agencies must register annually with the Department and pay a $1,500 annual registration fee per Nebraska location (or a single $1,500 statewide fee for technology platforms without a physical Nebraska location) payable to the Department. The Commissioner may receive appeals, investigate complaints, conduct random audits, issue subpoenas, and be represented by Department counsel or the Attorney General. The Department must maintain a publicly accessible database of registered agencies, may adopt rules, and Section 81-401 is amended to add this Act to the list of laws the Department administers. Operative January 1, 2026.
Additions: Creates the "Health Care Staffing Agency Registration Act" placing primary administration with the Department of Labor and the Commissioner of Labor. Creates the "Health Care Staffing Agency Registration Act" placing primary administration with the Department of Labor and the Commissioner of Labor. Key Dept. of Labor duties: register agencies annually; collect $1,500 annual fees per operating location (or $1,500 statewide for non‑physical health care technology platforms); operate a public complaints system, investigate complaints, conduct random audits, and exercise subpoena and enforcement authority; maintain a publicly accessible database of registered agencies (dates of approval and expiration/revocation); and adopt rules to implement the Act. Appeal and enforcement procedures are assigned to the Commissioner (with Attorney General support available). No separate appropriations or explicit budget allocations are included; fee revenue is the only funding mechanism specified.

Summary: LB309 designates the Department of Environment and Energy as the lead agency to implement the Safe Battery Collection and Recycling Act. LB309 designates the Department of Environment and Energy as the lead agency to implement the Safe Battery Collection and Recycling Act. The department must review and approve or deny battery stewardship plans (120-day review), post approved plans and reports (excluding proprietary data), require plan amendments and participant notifications, adopt rules, and report to the Legislature’s Natural Resources Committee by May 30, 2028. Civil enforcement may be pursued by the Attorney General or county attorneys; civil penalties collected are remitted to the State Treasurer for constitutional distribution. The bill creates the Battery Stewardship Cash Fund, to be administered by the department and funded by fees collected under section 4; funds are restricted to carrying out the Act and may be invested by the state investment officer under existing state investment statutes.
Additions: Adds the Department of Environment and Energy (defined as "the department") as the lead agency to review, approve, conditionally approve, deny, and post battery stewardship plans and amendments, with specified timelines (plan submissions by Jan 1, 2027; department action within 120 days; revised pla… 
Adds the Department of Environment and Energy (defined as "the department") as the lead agency to review, approve, conditionally approve, deny, and post battery stewardship plans and amendments, with specified timelines (plan submissions by Jan 1, 2027; department action within 120 days; revised plan decisions within 90 days). The department must publish approved plans and annual reports (excluding proprietary data), review out‑of‑state studies and report to the Legislature's Natural Resources Committee by May 30, 2028, and may adopt implementing rules. Creates a Battery Stewardship Cash Fund, consisting of fees from section 4, administered by the department and investable by the state investment officer under Nebraska investment law. Civil penalties are remitted to the State Treasurer; enforcement may involve the Attorney General or county attorneys.

LB313 amends the Nebraska Workers' Compensation Act to (1) clarify subrogation rights of employers and workers' compensation insurers, explicitly allowing employer or insurer subrogation against third parties and permitting recovery beyond amounts actually paid as compensation; excess recoveries, after collection expenses, must be paid promptly to the employee and treated as an advance on future compensation. (2) Update third‑party settlement rules to require written agreement of the employee and the employer's workers' compensation insurer (or the employer if uninsured), or court approval as fair and reasonable. If distribution is contested, the court must deduct recovery expenses, pay one‑third of the remainder to the employee, reimburse the employer/insurer for past or future compensation obligations, and pay any remaining balance to the employee. No agency appropriations or budget changes are included.
Additions: Adds a three-step priority for distributing a recovery (after reasonable collection expenses): (a) one-third of the remainder to the employee or their personal representative; (b) from the next balance, the employer or workers' compensation insurer is reimbursed for all compensation already paid or… 
Adds a three-step priority for distributing a recovery (after reasonable collection expenses): (a) one-third of the remainder to the employee or their personal representative; (b) from the next balance, the employer or workers' compensation insurer is reimbursed for all compensation already paid or that it may be obligated to pay; and (c) any remaining balance goes to the employee or their personal representative. No government agencies, departments, or changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are referenced.

LB314 amends the Sports Arena Facility Financing Assistance Act. It narrows eligible uses of state assistance for privately owned sports complexes to: repayment for public infrastructure costs; leasing portions to a political subdivision (defined as a contractual lease between coapplicants at fair-market rent for up to 20 years); promotion of publicly available sporting events; or repayment to a nonprofit coapplicant subject to voter approval. It caps state-funded promotion: 10 years for arts/cultural events, 10 years for sporting events, and 5 years for complexes in cities of the second class or villages. For large public stadiums approved on or after July 19, 2024, state assistance may cover up to 100% of final project cost. It revises board approval procedures—approvals tied to voter approval of bond issues or issuance of a building permit within 24 months—and requires a majority board vote with the Governor as a member. Original sections 13-3106 and 13-3103 are repealed.
Additions: Adds a definition of "lease" as a contractual lease between the coapplicants referenced in §13-3102(1)(b) for an eligible sports arena at fair market rent, term not to exceed 20 years. Adds a definition of "lease" as a contractual lease between the coapplicants referenced in §13-3102(1)(b) for an eligible sports arena at fair market rent, term not to exceed 20 years. It also makes approvals required by §13-3103(1)(f) temporary: the board’s temporary approval becomes permanent if a building permit for the arena is issued within 24 months; if not, the temporary approval is void. Agencies implicated: the approving board and the building permit authority. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB315 amends Nebraska corporate statute to make the Secretary of State the central agency responsible for administering biennial reports and occupation taxes for domestic and foreign corporations, but expressly limits (sunsets) those recurring reporting and tax deadlines to periods before January 1, 2026. Duties retained/clarified for the Secretary of State include prescribing report form, receiving reports and occupation taxes, returning nonconforming filings, sending advance notices (mail or electronic), investigating and obtaining information, filing certificates of administrative dissolution or revocation, and maintaining liens for delinquent occupation taxes. The bill preserves rules for tax measurement (including the doubled schedule and $30,000 cap for foreign corporations) and repeals the prior sections. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Summary: LB319 directs the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to maximize use of federal SNAP options and funding, minimize use of state General Funds, hire necessary personnel, and file an annual report to the Legislature detailing options, actions, caseloads, and program costs. LB319 directs the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to maximize use of federal SNAP options and funding, minimize use of state General Funds, hire necessary personnel, and file an annual report to the Legislature detailing options, actions, caseloads, and program costs. DHHS must develop a state outreach plan meeting Food and Nutrition Service (U.S. Department of Agriculture) criteria, submit it to USDA FNS for approval and federal matching funds, and may accept gifts, grants, and donations; implementation may be deferred if private or federal funds are insufficient. DHHS shall create a TANF-funded categorical eligibility policy (raising gross income eligibility to 165% until Oct 1, 2025) and annually report administrative costs and federal funding availability. The Department of Labor may administer the SNAP Next Step Program only to the extent federal funds are available and is not to use General Funds for those processes.

Adds a SNAP eligibility restriction: under 21 U.S.C. 862 (as of Jan 1, 2025), persons convicted of a felony involving possession, use, or distribution of a controlled substance are eligible for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits under this subsection only if they (i) have completed their sentence or (ii) are serving parole, probation, or post‑release supervision. 

Agency effects: USDA/FNS must implement and enforce the restriction. No provisions change Department of Labor or HHS responsibilities. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB31 directs the State Board of Education to develop and distribute a model policy governing school district use of student surveillance, monitoring, and tracking technology. The model must require districts to inventory tools and provide vendor contact info, purchase/maintenance costs, tool descriptions and privacy protections, opt‑out availability, data‑sharing (including with law enforcement) and disciplinary implications, accommodations for students with disabilities, biometric/data storage/sharing practices, and available legal remedies. Districts must post the inventory on their websites and provide hard copies on request. Each school board must adopt a conforming written policy by May 1, 2026, for implementation in school year 2026–27. No appropriations or funding changes are included.

The State Board of Education (Department of Education) must develop and distribute a model policy governing school districts’ use of student surveillance, monitoring, and tracking technologies. Districts must post inventories online and provide hard copies on request. LB321 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §31-735 to revise election procedures for sanitary and improvement district trustees. Key administrative roles: election commissioners or county clerks receive candidate filings (no filing fee), administer sealed mail-ballot elections (must notify the district board by July 1), and set the record date (not more than 80 days before the election) based on register of deeds records. District clerks must mail election notices at least 65 days prior. The bill requires candidates representing entities to so designate and provide documentation (including for write-ins within 10 days), clarifies voter weights (per acre/platted lot), preserves rules for allocation of seats between resident property owners and all owners, and allows board-size reduction via articles amendment. No funding or appropriation changes.

Summary: LB323 amends statutes governing the Department of Transportation (DOT). LB323 amends statutes governing the Department of Transportation (DOT). For DOT construction contracts over $250,000 (as determined by the department), bid solicitations must be published on the department’s official web page at least 20 days before bid opening (newspaper publication remains required but web posting satisfies notice even if newspaper notice is defective). For contracts ≤ $250,000, DOT may either follow the above procedure or request bids from at least three potential bidders and may award on one responsive bid. DOT may annually adjust the dollar thresholds (Oct. 1) by the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers published by the U.S. Department of Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics, rounded to the next $1,000. DOT may not construct buildings exceeding the adjusted capital-construction dollar amount in section 81-1114.01 without legislative consent. No appropriations or budget allocations are specified.
Additions: Adds procurement-notice requirements for state agencies (affecting the Department of Labor and Department of Transportation): notices must be published in a newspaper and on the agency’s official web page at least 20 days before bid closing; the web posting satisfies the 20‑day requirement even if t… 
Adds procurement-notice requirements for state agencies (affecting the Department of Labor and Department of Transportation): notices must be published in a newspaper and on the agency’s official web page at least 20 days before bid closing; the web posting satisfies the 20‑day requirement even if the site is temporarily unavailable. Newspaper notices must identify the agency’s official bid webpage; if the webpage has been posted for 20 days, a defective or shortened newspaper notice will not invalidate the solicitation. Also inserts purchase/lease language and bars the department from awards with an estimated cost exceeding the adjusted dollar threshold for capital construction projects in section 81-1114.01(3). No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB324 amends the Business Improvement District Act’s protest and notice procedures, specifying actions by city authorities. Key agency references and changes:

- City council: continues to hold hearings, receive protests, and may continue hearings; must terminate proceedings if a mailed postcard vote yields fewer than 50% of returned postcards in favor when a special assessment or an occupation tax is proposed.
- City (administration): must mail hearing notices and a self‑addressed voting postcard to each record owner of assessable units (per county treasurer tax rolls) when a special assessment is proposed and to each user of space when an occupation tax is proposed; must publish notice in a legal newspaper.
- County treasurer: tax rolls are the source for owner mailing lists.
- Neighborhood associations: may register with the city to receive notice; registration and service methods follow city rules and regulations.

No changes to appropriations, funding, or budget allocations.
Additions: Adds voting procedures for creation or modification of business improvement districts requiring postcards mailed under section 19-4029.01 to record owners and users of space. If fewer than 50% of returning record-owner postcards (and fewer than the specified share of returning user-of-space postcard… 
Adds voting procedures for creation or modification of business improvement districts requiring postcards mailed under section 19-4029.01 to record owners and users of space. If fewer than 50% of returning record-owner postcards (and fewer than the specified share of returning user-of-space postcards) vote in favor, the proposed or modified district is not approved. When a special assessment is proposed, a self-addressed postcard must be included. Return methods reference subdivisions of sections 19-4027 and 19-4029.04. No government agencies or departments are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

LB325 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §44-211 to permit a five-year waiver of the statutory requirement that an insurance corporation have at least one Nebraska-resident director if the insurer files a sworn affidavit with the Department of Insurance. The affidavit must certify the insurer meets specified criteria (Nebraska principal offices; publicly traded or wholly owned affiliate of such; domiciled in Nebraska ≥25 years; >500 Nebraska employees subject to Nebraska income tax; unchanged ultimate controlling entity for 10 years, as defined by the Department of Insurance). If the insurer stops meeting the criteria during the five-year period it must notify the Department of Insurance and appoint a Nebraska-resident director within six months. No appropriations or funding changes are included.
Additions: Adds a five-year waiver process to the statutory requirement that an insurance corporation have at least one Nebraska-resident board member, administered by the Department of Insurance. An insurer may file a sworn affidavit (executed by its president or board chair) certifying it meets five criteria… 
Adds a five-year waiver process to the statutory requirement that an insurance corporation have at least one Nebraska-resident board member, administered by the Department of Insurance. An insurer may file a sworn affidavit (executed by its president or board chair) certifying it meets five criteria: principal executive offices in Nebraska; publicly traded or wholly owned affiliate of a publicly traded company; domiciled in Nebraska ≥25 years; employs >500 Nebraska employees subject to state income tax; and unchanged ultimate controlling entity for ten years. The affidavit may be renewed after five years. If the insurer stops meeting any criterion during the term, it must notify the Department, specify the failed criteria, and appoint a Nebraska-resident director within six months. No funding, appropriation, or budget changes are included.

Summary: LB326 explicitly defines "Department" as the Department of Insurance and "Director" as the Director of Insurance. LB326 explicitly defines "Department" as the Department of Insurance and "Director" as the Director of Insurance. It expands the Director's investigatory and enforcement role (including hearings, orders, penalties) and makes failure to respond to a written inquiry from the department within 15 working days an unfair trade practice. Health insurance lead generators and certain insurers must reimburse the Department for examination expenses per the Insurers Examination Act. The Director must transmit covered insolvency claims to the Nebraska Property and Liability Insurance Guaranty Association and will receive recovered sums from the association to handle per Chapter 77 procedures. Mutual insurance holding companies must file annual statements (by March 1) and audits (by June 1) with the Director. The bill preserves a 20% premium-tax-offset mechanism tied to director-prescribed certificates of contribution.

The added provisions expand definitions and regulatory authority overseen by the Department of Insurance (the director): they define “customer,” “health insurance lead generator,” “lead generating device,” and “recording,” require health insurance lead generators to keep books, records and complete call recordings accessible for director examination (retain current year plus two prior years), and authorize enforcement by the director. Changes to the insurer/association law: broaden the definition of covered claims to include claims after policy transfers/assumptions (with conditions), limit association liability for cybersecurity coverage to $300,000 per single insured event, and give the guaranty association rights to review/contest pre‑liquidation settlements, assert statutory defenses/offsets, and seek to set aside judgments entered by default or failure to defend. Confidentiality agreements with rehabilitators/liquidators are required. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Summary: LB327 shifts financial and administrative responsibility for probation from counties to the State. Key agency roles and budgetary changes: - Supreme Court: adopts interpreter standards; may adopt rules to implement the act; will receive appropriations to pay probation-related expenses and interpreter services. - State Court Administrator: selects the implementation date between July 1, 2026 and July 1, 2027 and coordinates transition with coun… 
LB327 shifts financial and administrative responsibility for probation from counties to the State. Key agency roles and budgetary changes:

- Supreme Court: adopts interpreter standards; may adopt rules to implement the act; will receive appropriations to pay probation-related expenses and interpreter services.  
- State Court Administrator: selects the implementation date between July 1, 2026 and July 1, 2027 and coordinates transition with counties.  
- State: becomes responsible for salaries and travel of probation staff; expenses for district principal offices; office space/facilities; drug testing (with existing exceptions); and comprehensive IT procurement/support. These costs are to be paid from funds appropriated to the Supreme Court.  
- Counties: must collaborate on a coordinated transition.  
- Probation administrator: prepares budget and appropriation requests for Supreme Court submission.
Additions: Adds an implementation date, set by the State Court Administrator between July 1, 2026 and July 1, 2027. Adds an implementation date, set by the State Court Administrator between July 1, 2026 and July 1, 2027. Beginning on that date, the state (via funds appropriated to the Supreme Court) will assume payment for probation services — including district principal office operations, office space and facilities, probation staff salaries and travel, and comprehensive IT (technical support; hardware like printers/scanners/phones/mobile devices; software licensing; network and Internet services). County officials must coordinate with the State Court Administrator to ensure a smooth transition. The Supreme Court may adopt rules to implement the section.

LB329 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §28-316.01 to expand and clarify definitions used in the statute. The bill retains criminal classifications and penalties for sexual abuse by a school employee (first-, second-, and third-degree offenses as Class IIA, IIIA, and IV felonies, respectively). The original section is repealed. No agencies beyond the State Department of Education are referenced, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes.

109-1-LB331_IntroWithdrawnLegislature 109, Session 1 (2025)LB331_Intro_Copy.docxDOCXDepartment of Health and Human Services, Department of Revenue
Summary: The bill gives the Department of Revenue (Tax Commissioner) broad administration and enforcement authority for a new consumption tax: register/audit sellers; collect/remit tax receipts (remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the General Fund); design forms and tax‑exempt certificates; designate collectors and require surety; summon records, seize assets, garnish wages, file liens; set penalties and appeals; operate a hotline and fraud‑rewa… 
The bill gives the Department of Revenue (Tax Commissioner) broad administration and enforcement authority for a new consumption tax: register/audit sellers; collect/remit tax receipts (remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the General Fund); design forms and tax‑exempt certificates; designate collectors and require surety; summon records, seize assets, garnish wages, file liens; set penalties and appeals; operate a hotline and fraud‑reward program; publish monthly interest rates; maintain employee training; and provide an annual in‑person report to the Legislature’s Revenue Committee beginning 2029. Rules are required by Sept. 1, 2025; applications available by Oct. 1, 2027. Collection‑agreement recoveries are limited to finally assessed, unappealed taxes and capped at 12 months. Department of Revenue employees face a Class IV felony for unauthorized disclosure; permitted disclosures and deidentified reporting provisions are detailed. Beginning 2028, agencies (including Revenue) must file annual budget requests by Sept. 15 subject to CPI limits. The Department of Health and Human Services must certify developmental‑disability homestead exemption eligibility on forms prescribed by the Department of Revenue; annual recertification is not required unless the medical condition changes. No specific appropriations to either agency are provided.
Additions: Department of Revenue - Replaces Nebraska income, sales/use, property, motor vehicle, and inheritance taxes with a statewide 7.5% "consumption tax" effective Jan 1, 2028; Dept. of Revenue (Tax Commissioner) administers registration, collection, audits, enforcement (liens, garnishment, criminal penal… 
Department of Revenue
- Replaces Nebraska income, sales/use, property, motor vehicle, and inheritance taxes with a statewide 7.5% "consumption tax" effective Jan 1, 2028; Dept. of Revenue (Tax Commissioner) administers registration, collection, audits, enforcement (liens, garnishment, criminal penalties), large-seller remittance/security rules, tax‑exempt certificates (rules by 9/1/2025; application online/paper by 10/1/2027), transitional inventory credit, and other compliance provisions.  
- Consumption tax receipts are collected by the Department of Revenue and remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the General Fund; the State Treasurer disburses revenue and the Dept. of Administrative Services administers/disburses agency shares.  
- Departmental obligations: maintain employee continuing education; begin annual audit/activity reporting to the Legislature in 2029; penalty-abatement and confidentiality rules updated.  
Department of Health and Human Services

LB338 (Wordekemper) prohibits life, disability, and long-term care insurers from using genetic information — including solicitation or genetic test results — to deny, limit, or set differential premiums absent a clinical diagnosis. The bill mirrors protections in the federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act (29 U.S.C. 1182) and relies on Nebraska definitions in section 48-236. Permitted insurer activities include reviewing medical records, asking about family history, and considering documented clinical diagnoses. Enacted by the Nebraska Legislature (Banking, Commerce and Insurance Committee origin). No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds legislative findings citing the federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act and establishes protections preventing life, disability, and long‑term‑care insurers from using genetic information (or applicants' decisions about genetic testing) to cancel, limit, deny coverage, or set premium… 
Adds legislative findings citing the federal Genetic Information Nondiscrimination Act and establishes protections preventing life, disability, and long‑term‑care insurers from using genetic information (or applicants' decisions about genetic testing) to cancel, limit, deny coverage, or set premium differentials in the absence of a clinical diagnosis. Insurers also may not require or solicit genetic tests or test results. Carved‑out exceptions allow insurers to review medical records as part of underwriting, ask about family history, and consider clinical diagnoses. Definitions defer to section 48‑236. No government agencies or departments beyond "The Legislature" or funding/appropriations are mentioned.

Summary: LB340 enacts the Asbestos Trust Claims Transparency Act and the Asbestos Claims Priorities and Over‑Naming Reform Act, imposing court-directed procedures and evidentiary rules. Courts may require claimants to file or supplement asbestos trust claims, produce trust governance documents (deemed admissible and not privileged), and provide affidavits; defendants may move 60 days before trial and a court cannot set trial earlier than 90 days after com… 
LB340 enacts the Asbestos Trust Claims Transparency Act and the Asbestos Claims Priorities and Over‑Naming Reform Act, imposing court-directed procedures and evidentiary rules. Courts may require claimants to file or supplement asbestos trust claims, produce trust governance documents (deemed admissible and not privileged), and provide affidavits; defendants may move 60 days before trial and a court cannot set trial earlier than 90 days after compliance. Courts must hold evidentiary hearings to determine prima facie impairment under specified medical standards (AMA Guides, American Thoracic Society) and may limit discovery until prima facie proof is resolved. Defendants receive setoffs for trust recoveries, allocated proportionally. The bill amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §25‑224 to toll the limitations period for non‑malignant asbestos conditions until a qualifying diagnosis or death. No funding or appropriations are included.
Additions: Adds detailed procedures for asbestos litigation: claimants must file all applicable asbestos trust claims, produce trust‑claim materials and affidavits, and supplement filings; courts may order additional trust filings, delay trials, admit trust materials as evidence, and allow defendants discovery… 
Adds detailed procedures for asbestos litigation: claimants must file all applicable asbestos trust claims, produce trust‑claim materials and affidavits, and supplement filings; courts may order additional trust filings, delay trials, admit trust materials as evidence, and allow defendants discovery from trusts and setoffs for trust payments. Creates the "Asbestos Claims Priorities and Over‑Naming Reform Act" with definitions (including AMA Guides) and medical report standards, requires evidentiary hearings to establish prima facie impairment, limits discovery until prima facie is shown, and allows limited consolidation and tolling of statutes of limitations. Mentioned entities: courts, asbestos trusts, American Medical Association, American Thoracic Society, American Board of Internal Medicine, American Osteopathic Board of Internal Medicine. No government agencies, appropriations, or budget changes are referenced.

"Department" is defined as the Department of Revenue. The department is the licensing and regulatory authority for fantasy contest operators: it receives applications (including a $5,000 nonrefundable application fee), conducts background investigations, issues or denies licenses, and may adopt rules (with limits — it may not regulate individual contest rules or reclassify contests as sports wagering). Initial license fees are set (existing in‑state operators: 10% of adjusted gross fantasy contest receipts from the prior year or $5,000, whichever is less; new operators: $5,000 plus a supplemental 10% remittance). The Fantasy Sports Consumer Protection Fund is created and administered by the department; license and application fees are credited to it and invested per state law. The department administers self‑exclusion, maintains a prohibited‑participant list, directs forfeited prizes to problem‑gaming charities, may enforce civil penalties (collected penalties are remitted to the State Treasurer for distribution under Article VII, §5), and may cooperate with law enforcement.

The added provisions designate the "Department" as the Department of Revenue and assign it primary regulatory, licensing, enforcement, and rulemaking duties for fantasy contest operators (with limits on regulating contest rules or platforms). The department must: process applications and background checks, issue/deny licenses, adopt rules (including geolocation, anti‑fraud/AML, and problem‑gaming standards), operate a self‑exclusion list, receive operator reports, refer investigations to law enforcement, and assess civil penalties (up to $1,000 per violation, $10,000 max per transaction).

Financially, a $5,000 nonrefundable application fee is required; initial license fees are 10% of prior-year adjusted gross receipts or $5,000 (whichever is less) with supplemental 10% obligations for some new entrants. The Fantasy Sports Consumer Protection Fund is created, administered by the department, to receive all license/application fees and fund program administration; funds may be invested per state law.

LB344 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §46-740 to clarify groundwater allocation in areas the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) has found fully appropriated (§46-714) or designated overappropriated (§46-713). Key agency provisions:
- DNR retains authority to designate fully appropriated/overappropriated areas.
- Natural resources districts (NRDs) may amend municipal allocations made before Nov. 1, 2005.
- Integrated management plans (IMPs), rules, or orders generally may not limit municipal or nonmunicipal commercial/industrial use until Jan. 1, 2026; after that date such users may be limited and base allocations are defined.

- Exemptions remain for users regulated under the Industrial Ground Water Regulatory Act and the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

Summary: LB349 amends Nebraska statutes to expand oversight by the Nebraska Power Review Board to explicitly cover "electric energy storage resources" and revises related definitions (including "electric supplier" and "privately developed renewable energy generation facility"). LB349 amends Nebraska statutes to expand oversight by the Nebraska Power Review Board to explicitly cover "electric energy storage resources" and revises related definitions (including "electric supplier" and "privately developed renewable energy generation facility"). Construction or acquisition of generation facilities, electric energy storage resources, or transmission lines carrying >700 volts now generally requires board application/approval, subject to existing exemptions and a specific exemption for privately developed renewable facilities that comply with section 70-1014.02. Enforcement: the board’s executive director may assess a $500 fine and require cure within 20 days if a private electric supplier began construction less than 30 days before required notice; failure to comply mandates cease of construction. The bill establishes hearing procedures before the board and assigns hearing costs to suppliers found in violation. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Summary: LB34 amends Nebraska time statutes to enable a transition to year‑round daylight saving time and to harmonize time references across state law. It: (1) establishes future operative standard times as UTC‑5 (central) and UTC‑6 (mountain) in 49‑1301, contingent on federal authorization (including any order by the U.S. Secretary of Transportation) and adoption by three adjacent states; (2) renders current daylight‑saving provisions null when that sub… 
LB34 amends Nebraska time statutes to enable a transition to year‑round daylight saving time and to harmonize time references across state law. It: (1) establishes future operative standard times as UTC‑5 (central) and UTC‑6 (mountain) in 49‑1301, contingent on federal authorization (including any order by the U.S. Secretary of Transportation) and adoption by three adjacent states; (2) renders current daylight‑saving provisions null when that subsection becomes operative (49‑1302); (3) adjusts statutory election poll and ballot‑receipt hours by time zone (32‑908); and (4) standardizes sick and vacation leave accounting to 11:59 p.m. central time and directs the Director of Personnel to adopt implementing rules (81‑1323, 81‑1328). Agencies mentioned include employing state agencies, the Director of Personnel, the Governor, the Legislative Council/Executive Board, and the Public Employees Retirement Board; federal offices referenced include the U.S. Secretaries of Transportation, Commerce, and the Navy. No funding, appropriation, or budget changes are included.
Additions: Added language sets Nebraska's standard time as UTC−5 in the central zone and UTC−6 in the mountain zone. It defines Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) as maintained by the General Conference on Weights and Measures and interpreted or modified for the United States by the U.S. Secretary of Commerce in… 
Added language sets Nebraska's standard time as UTC−5 in the central zone and UTC−6 in the mountain zone. It defines Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) as maintained by the General Conference on Weights and Measures and interpreted or modified for the United States by the U.S. Secretary of Commerce in coordination with the U.S. Secretary of the Navy. The provision becomes operative on the first Sunday in November after (1) it is authorized by U.S. law or an order of the U.S. Secretary of Transportation or is no longer in conflict with such federal law/order, and (2) three adjacent states adopt laws establishing a single year‑round standard time. The section will be nullified if subsection (2) of §49‑1301 becomes operative. No agencies are assigned funding and no appropriations or budget changes are included.

- Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS): Judges may commit defendants to DHHS for competency restoration, including state hospitals, other state-owned/-operated facilities, or contract providers under DHHS-proposed alternative treatment plans (court review within five days). DHHS must file such reports with the court. If a DHHS-committed defendant remains lodged in a county jail, DHHS shall reimburse the county for lodging (daily lodging, food, medical services, transportation, other necessary costs). Reimbursement is $100 per day per defendant for each day after the first 30 days, adjusted annually each July 1 by the CPI-U.

- Department of Correctional Services (DCS): Emergency protective custody placements may include admission to a Department of Correctional Services facility. Persons with prior sex-offense convictions taken into emergency custody must be admitted to a jail or DCS facility unless a medical/psychiatric emergency requires a medical facility; transfer occurs once the emergency has passed.

Summary: The bill directs the State Board of Education, using the State Department of Education’s student identifier system, to implement statewide systems for tracking individual student achievement and student discipline.
