The bill directs the State Board of Education, using the State Department of Education’s student identifier system, to implement statewide systems for tracking individual student achievement and student discipline. The department must maintain a publicly available, de-identified discipline database searchable by district, school building, offense, discipline type, law‑enforcement involvement, restraint, and seclusion. School districts must annually report individual student discipline incidents (suspensions, expulsions, alternative assignments, physical interventions, restraints, seclusions, offenses warranting long‑term removal, and law‑enforcement contacts). Each district must designate a discipline data coordinator and publish contact information. The Department of Education will annually analyze and electronically report achievement and discipline data, disaggregated by demographics, to the Governor, Legislature, ESUs, learning communities, and the public. The Commissioner of Education may enforce noncompliance, up to accreditation actions. No funding changes or appropriations are included.

- The Department (State Board/Department of Education) will post the annual, disaggregated reports online (by demographic groups, discipline types, and academic/discipline progress indicators); reports must not identify individual students.
- Commissioner of Education may notify districts of material noncompliance, allow time to cure, and take remedial actions up to treating noncompliance as an accreditation violation.
- No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB355 assigns several responsibilities to the Department of Economic Development (DED): allocate state financial assistance to certified development districts (50% equally, 20% by population per the latest federal decennial census—DED may determine unincorporated county population if census data are unavailable—and 30% by proportional share of local governments) and verify local dues, capping assistance accordingly. Fees equal to 0.5% of ImagiNE Nebraska incentives are remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the ImagiNE Nebraska Cash Fund, which DED will administer. DED must annually update workforce-housing construction cost limits using the Producer Price Index published by the U.S. Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics. DED will administer job-training grants, audit recipients, and require annual reporting on trainee outcomes and matching contributions. The bill also amends the Nebraska Innovation Hub Act to define “Department” and “Director” as DED and its director; operative date July 1, 2025, with an emergency clause.

Summary: LB357 creates and consolidates regulatory authority in a seven‑member State Racing and Gaming Commission (Governor‑appointed) that selects a Governor‑approved executive director, may hire staff, license racetrack enclosures and gaming operators, adopt rules, levy fines, and require market and socioeconomic studies to be filed with the Governor and the Legislature’s General Affairs Committee. LB357 creates and consolidates regulatory authority in a seven‑member State Racing and Gaming Commission (Governor‑appointed) that selects a Governor‑approved executive director, may hire staff, license racetrack enclosures and gaming operators, adopt rules, levy fines, and require market and socioeconomic studies to be filed with the Governor and the Legislature’s General Affairs Committee. Background checks are conducted by the Nebraska State Patrol with FBI checks at the applicant’s expense. Fiscal changes: establishes/renames the Racetrack Gaming Fund (State Treasurer to transfer the Racing Cash Fund balance); investment by the State Investment Officer with investment earnings credited to the General Fund beginning Oct. 1, 2024; imposes a one‑time $5 million operator license fee (payable over five years), a $50,000 annual review fee, and a 20% annual tax on gross gaming revenue. The bill also narrows equine‑activity immunity, creates liability exceptions for certain negligent or intentional acts, and repeals numerous related statutes.
Additions: - Nebraska Racing and Gaming Commission: defines "licensed racetrack enclosure," will issue racetrack enclosure licenses (separate from horseracing-meet licenses), sets application and renewal fees of $10,000, and three-year license terms; existing horseracing licensees are deemed to hold racetrack… 
- Nebraska Racing and Gaming Commission: defines "licensed racetrack enclosure," will issue racetrack enclosure licenses (separate from horseracing-meet licenses), sets application and renewal fees of $10,000, and three-year license terms; existing horseracing licensees are deemed to hold racetrack enclosure licenses until the commission rules on applications.  
- State Treasurer: directed to transfer any money in the Racing and Gaming Commission's Racing Cash Fund on the act's effective date to a new Racetrack Gaming Fund.  
- Funding/payment terms: an initial $5 million license fee is referenced with $1 million due each year thereafter until paid; language ties certain license fees and gross tax receipts under specified horseracing statutes to the scheme while excluding taxes under section 2-1208.01 and horseracing administration receipts.  
- Nebraska State Patrol and FBI: applicants must provide fingerprints to the Nebraska State Patrol, which submits them to the FBI for national criminal-history checks and reports results to the commission.

- The unspecified "board" (and its executive director) must receive written notice ≥30 days before construction, review certifications (decommissioning plan, security bond by year six unless a local government has enacted decommissioning rules), and issue a written acknowledgement within ten days if requirements are met; the board may bring enforcement actions for bond-plan noncompliance.

LB365 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §68-911 to impose specific duties on the Department of Health and Human Services (the department). Key provisions require the department to: provide coverage and reimbursement for self-measured blood pressure monitoring services by Jan. 1, 2026 (device, appropriately sized/ replacement cuffs, patient training, and data reporting); provide continuous glucose monitor coverage per prior deadlines and expansion (with intent that no more than $600,000 annually be appropriated from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund and excess funded by that fund); seek federal approval to extend postpartum coverage; submit a waiver/state plan for two medical respite facilities (funded by the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund); provide electric personal-use breast pumps and ten lactation consultations (legislative intent for an appropriation equal to a 145% rate increase); and cover translation/interpretation services (funded by the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund).

By January 1, 2026, the Department of Health and Human Services must provide coverage and reimbursement under the medical assistance program for self-measured blood pressure monitoring for all eligible beneficiaries. Covered services must include: (a) a validated blood pressure monitor; (b) appropriately sized and replacement cuffs as needed; (c) patient education and training on device setup, use, clinical accuracy, calibration, and measurement procedures; and (d) collection of patient- or caregiver-reported readings for submission to providers to inform or adjust treatment plans. Summary: LB366 creates a Legislative Economic Analysis Unit and a Chief Economist and amends the Administrative Procedure Act. Agencies (boards, commissions, departments, etc.) must publish proposed rules in a statewide newspaper and electronically submit to the Legislature and the Chief Economist a report (rule text, concise statement, major/nonmajor classification, related actions, proposed effective date) and any cost‑benefit analysis including job imp… 
LB366 creates a Legislative Economic Analysis Unit and a Chief Economist and amends the Administrative Procedure Act. Agencies (boards, commissions, departments, etc.) must publish proposed rules in a statewide newspaper and electronically submit to the Legislature and the Chief Economist a report (rule text, concise statement, major/nonmajor classification, related actions, proposed effective date) and any cost‑benefit analysis including job impacts before filing with the Secretary of State. The Unit must report on each major rule to the committee of jurisdiction within 15 legislative days, assessing procedural compliance and regulatory impacts; agencies must cooperate. Major rules may not be published until ratified by the Legislature or after 60 legislative days; emergency major rules require Governor approval with a published justification and are effective up to 90 days (renewable once). Courts may review whether statutory requirements for a rule’s effect or major classification were met. No funding or appropriation changes.
Additions: Requires the Legislature (within one month) to provide an email/electronic address for delivery of rules and related information. Before any agency files a rule with the Secretary of State, the agency must publish it in a statewide newspaper and electronically submit to the Legislature and the Chief… 
Requires the Legislature (within one month) to provide an email/electronic address for delivery of rules and related information. Before any agency files a rule with the Secretary of State, the agency must publish it in a statewide newspaper and electronically submit to the Legislature and the Chief Economist: the rule, a concise statement, major/nonmajor classification and rationale, related regulatory actions with individual/aggregate economic effects, proposed effective date, and a complete cost‑benefit analysis (including jobs added/lost, public vs. private). The Legislative Economic Analysis Unit must report on each major rule to the subject committee within 15 legislative days, assessing procedural compliance, private‑sector impacts, and regulatory impact. Major rules cannot be published until ratified by the Legislature or 60 legislative days pass (with limited Governor exceptions requiring a published justification). Courts may review whether procedural requirements were met and whether a rule is a major rule. No funding or appropriation changes are included.

Bill amends the Uniform Credentialing Act to prohibit licensed practitioners under the Medicine and Surgery, Mental Health, Nurse, Pharmacy, and Psychology practice acts from providing conversion therapy to persons under 19. It adds provision of conversion therapy to disciplinary grounds enforced by the state department responsible for credentialing and by licensing boards (including pharmacy board recommendations to the department) and to causes for action under the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Pharmacy technician registration discipline is updated to include these grounds. The Licensee Assistance Program remains available. The bill bars expenditure of state or political‑subdivision funds for providing, referring to, or covering conversion therapy. No specific appropriations or new budget allocations are included.

Adds a ban on licensed health professionals (under the Medicine and Surgery, Mental Health, Nurse, Pharmacy, and Psychology Practice Acts) from providing conversion therapy to anyone under 19, with statutory definitions for conversion, gender-identity, and sexual-orientation conversion therapies. Violations are treated as deceptive trade practices under the Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Exempts clergy/religious counselors acting in a pastoral (non‑healthcare) capacity. Budget language prohibits any state or political‑subdivision funds from being expended to conduct, refer for, or provide health‑benefits coverage for conversion therapy. No specific state agencies or new appropriations are named; licensing boards and enforcement under existing deceptive‑practices law are implicated.

LB368 creates the Nebraska Youth in Care Bill of Rights and assigns implementation duties to state child‑welfare entities. The bill requires "the department" to: facilitate joint‑sibling placement and visitation, inform children of placement/visitation rights, facilitate reunification and family visitation consistent with law, provide transition planning and access to vital records and medical/educational files, ensure confidentiality, and explain reasons for denied visits/placements. Caseworkers must be trained on and provide written notice of the rights (with specified timing and acknowledgments) and explain a grievance process; the department must acknowledge grievances within three business days. Court‑appointed guardians ad litem must review and discuss rights with children and escalate alleged infringements to the court. The Nebraska Strengthening Families Act Committee will monitor implementation. No appropriations or budget changes are included.

Summary: LB36 consolidates and clarifies the statutory authority of the Department of Transportation (the Department), reaffirming its power to plan, construct, maintain, operate and enter agreements (including with the United States and adjoining states) for the state highway system and interstate bridges. The bill expressly authorizes the Department to establish and operate mitigation banks and in‑lieu‑fee programs for transportation projects (threatene… 
LB36 consolidates and clarifies the statutory authority of the Department of Transportation (the Department), reaffirming its power to plan, construct, maintain, operate and enter agreements (including with the United States and adjoining states) for the state highway system and interstate bridges. The bill expressly authorizes the Department to establish and operate mitigation banks and in‑lieu‑fee programs for transportation projects (threatened/endangered species, wetlands, habitat), adopt implementing rules, and enter cooperative agreements. The Department may acquire real property—including purchase, donation or condemnation—and redesignate the state highway system; it may establish wetlands banks sized up to 150% of projected mitigation needs. State agencies must give priority to the Department’s mitigation resources. Owners of mitigation bank property acquired after July 1, 2026 must pay sums in lieu of lost ad valorem taxes to affected counties. The bill contains no explicit appropriations or new Department budget allocations.
Additions: Creates authority for the Department of Transportation to establish, operate, and use mitigation banks and in‑lieu‑fee programs to provide compensatory mitigation for DOT-administered transportation projects (impacts to threatened/endangered species/habitat, wetland dredge/fill, and habitat restorat… 
Creates authority for the Department of Transportation to establish, operate, and use mitigation banks and in‑lieu‑fee programs to provide compensatory mitigation for DOT-administered transportation projects (impacts to threatened/endangered species/habitat, wetland dredge/fill, and habitat restoration/creation/enhancement/preservation). State agencies are urged to give priority to these DOT programs when reviewing mitigation plans. The department may enter cooperative agreements with public or private parties, acquire real property (purchase, donation, bequest, or eminent domain) for mitigation purposes, and adopt rules to implement the program. Properties acquired after July 1, 2026, must pay a sum in lieu of lost ad valorem taxes to the county. No specific new appropriations, budget allocations, or funding amounts for DOT implementation are specified.

LB371 amends the Uniform Civil Remedies for Unauthorized Disclosure of Intimate Images Act to expressly cover images created by computer generation or digital manipulation. Key changes:
- Expands definitions so a "depicted individual" and "private" intimate images include computer-generated or digitally manipulated images made without consent.
- Creates a civil cause of action for intentional or threatened disclosure of private intimate images when the defendant knew or recklessly disregarded lack of consent, the image’s privacy, and identifiability.
- Clarifies that consent to creation or prior consensual sharing does not by itself permit further disclosure; nonconsensual sexual conduct or uncovering preserves a reasonable expectation of privacy even if created in public.

No state agencies or departments are mentioned. No funding, appropriations, or budgetary changes are included.

LB373 amends statutes governing county road designation, maintenance, and vacation procedures, affecting county and municipal officials. Key agency impacts:

- County boards: retain authority to open/maintain section-line roads (section lines now declared public roads but not required), to initiate vacations/abandonments, and must adopt resolutions setting hearings and recording outcomes.
- County highway superintendent or designee: may be directed to study road use and submit written reports to the county board; reports and resolutions are permanent records in the county clerk’s office.
- County surveyor or, if none, a licensed professional land surveyor: must perpetuate government corners with monuments and records; lost corners located per §§23-1907–1908.
- Planning and public works directors and governing bodies of metropolitan/primary/first-class cities: receive notice and must approve vacations when within city zoning jurisdiction.
- Register of Deeds: must receive and index vacating resolutions within 30 days.

No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are changed.

Adds procedures authorizing county boards to propose vacating or abandoning public roads previously declared under former section 39‑1410, including: no study requirement for such vacations/abandonments; triggering a public hearing either upon receipt of the report required by section 39‑1722 or by county board resolution; county responsibility to fix the hearing time/place; and required notice to persons identified in section 39‑1724. The additions also reference sections 23‑1907 and 23‑1908 concerning causing and placing monuments and assign duties to the directed superintendent or other designated person to cause those monuments to be set. No state agency other than county boards and the county superintendent (or designated person) is newly created or mentioned, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

LB377 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §37-101 governing the Nebraska Game and Parks Commission. The commission remains nine members (eight district, one at-large), appointed by the Governor with the Legislature’s consent. Qualifications retained include Nebraska residency and citizenship, at least three members engaged in agriculture, a maximum of five members from the same political party, and district residency for district representatives; loss of those qualifications vacates the office. The bill specifies four-year terms beginning January 15, limits reappointment after serving three full terms, and clarifies vacancy appointments are for the remainder of the term. Recess appointment, gubernatorial removal procedures (with hearing) and filing of removal records with the Secretary of State remain. The act repeals the original section. Requires every public and private two- and four-year college or university in Nebraska to file quarterly reports with the Attorney General and electronically to the Legislature detailing "reportable funding" (foreign contracts, gifts, grants, donations, payments, etc., over $50) received from defined foreign sources. Reports must include amount, type and purpose, foreign source identity/address, and copies of related contracts; the Attorney General prescribes the reporting format and must post reports on the AG's website. The Attorney General is charged with enforcement and may impose civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation and order forfeiture of unreported funds. Payments by a natural person foreign payer for an individual student’s tuition or related fees are exempt. No appropriations or budget allocations are specified.

LB379 amends §68‑1724 of the Welfare Reform Act to set a cumulative 24‑month limit on cash assistance for recipient families with children, with extensions if the state fails to meet terms of the self‑sufficiency contract or if no suitable job is available. The bill requires the department to develop policy guidelines permitting additional assistance for recipient families facing “extreme hardship.” It establishes transitional child‑care assistance eligibility up to 200% of the federal poverty level before Oct. 1, 2026, and 185% thereafter, allows families to contribute up to 20% of gross income, and expresses legislative intent for sliding‑scale transitional health coverage up to 185% FPL. It includes various eligibility and program‑management provisions (school attendance, minor parents, two‑parent families). No new appropriations or budget allocations are specified.

LB37 adopts the Railroad Safety Act and amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §75-109.01 to expressly vest the Public Service Commission (PSC) with jurisdiction over "railroad carrier safety" pursuant to the new Act and cited statutes. The bill defines terms (referencing Federal Railroad Administration timetables and federal regs for several definitions), limits trains carrying hazardous substances on state main lines to 8,500 feet, and provides a civil-liability rule where train lengths over 7,000 feet may affect recoveries in crash cases. It also confirms the PSC is not granted jurisdiction over railroad labor relations. The act repeals the original §75-109.01 and §17-225, becomes operative July 1, 2026, and contains no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.
Additions: Adds definitions (many referencing federal regs) and safety rules. It designates the Public Service Commission as “Commission” and cites the Federal Railroad Administration and numerous federal statutes/regulations (49 U.S.C.; 49 C.F.R.). Adds definitions (many referencing federal regs) and safety rules. It designates the Public Service Commission as “Commission” and cites the Federal Railroad Administration and numerous federal statutes/regulations (49 U.S.C.; 49 C.F.R.). New substantive requirements: rail trains carrying hazardous substances on main lines are limited to 8,500 feet; in lawsuits, if a train exceeded 7,000 feet and length caused harm, plaintiff recovery cannot be reduced for comparative fault. The Act explicitly does not give the Commission authority over railroad–employee labor relations. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

The bill assigns the Division of Medicaid and Long-Term Care of the Department of Health and Human Services the following duties:

- Enforce contractor compliance with federal/state laws and rules governing mental health and substance use disorder coverage, including EPSDT for children and youth.
- Publish contractors' surveys, financial analyses, contract audits, parity reports, and parity compliance results.
- Ensure provider access and parity for mental health/SUD services via regulation and review of claims, reimbursement procedures, network adequacy, and rate adequacy.
- Establish monthly electronic communications to all Medicaid providers about amendments or changes to managed-care contracts.
- Define "network adequacy."
- Annually post network adequacy assessment criteria and each managed care organization's compliance on the Department website.

No explicit funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department are specified.

Summary (Department of Health and Human Services)

- DHHS must provide a clear written justification when commencing a provider audit and limit records requests to documents proportional to the services audited. Providers get 90 days after notice of overpayment to adjust a claim in certain circumstances.
- Onsite audits require at least ten business days' advance notice and a good-faith effort to agree on timing.
- Written overpayment notices must include ten specified items (patient, dates, amount, claim ID, detailed basis/evidence, payment method, adjustment/appeal procedures, recovery method) and overpayments cannot be recouped for at least 60 days after notice.
- Program integrity contractors may not recoup until appeals are exhausted (except verified credible fraud), must provide appeal procedures at audit start, and must respond to provider inquiries within 10 business days.
- Credible allegation of fraud must be verified by DHHS; fraud defined to include intentional deception under law.
- Contracts for recovery may limit contingency fees to no more than 12.5% and must comply with federal law.
- The Division of Medicaid and Long-Term Care must enforce parity and access for mental health/substance use services (including EPSDT), publish contractor surveys/analyses/audits/parity reports, define and annually post network adequacy criteria and MCO compliance, ensure network/provider access and reimbursement review, and create monthly electronic communications with Medicaid providers about MCO contract changes.

No explicit changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB381 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §68-974 governing program integrity and recovery-audit contractors for the Medical Assistance program. Key agency references and changes:
- "The department" (Medicaid administering agency) must coordinate with contractors and federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) at audit commencement and retain statutes/policies in audit records.
- CMS and the department conduct/coordinate program integrity audits; recovery audits must exclude capitated Medicaid managed-care claims, non-primary insurance claims, and claims currently or previously audited; audits of managed-care claims must be coordinated with the managed care organization.
- New provider protections/timelines: one-year payment lookback (except fraud), 180-day determination letters, 10-business-day onsite notice, 90-day post-audit documentation window, 60-day no-recoupment after adverse notice, appeal processes, and public annual contractor metrics on the department website.
- Annual December 1 electronic report to the Legislature on contracts, parties, issues, estimated recoveries, and savings.
No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are changed.
Additions: Adds requirements for the department and its contractors overseeing audits and overpayment recovery. Key points: - The department must provide written justification to a provider before commencing an audit. - Payments become final after one year from payment date (except for fraud). - Records reques… 
Adds requirements for the department and its contractors overseeing audits and overpayment recovery. Key points:
- The department must provide written justification to a provider before commencing an audit.
- Payments become final after one year from payment date (except for fraud).
- Records requests are limited to documents relevant and proportional to the services audited (per subsection 12).
- Onsite audits require at least ten business days' advance notice; requested documentation after an onsite audit cannot be required sooner than 90 days from the provider’s request date.
- Overpayment notices must include detailed information (beneficiary, dates, amount, claim identifiers, evidence/basis, payment method/date, adjustment procedure, appeal rights, recovery method) and overpayments cannot be recouped for at least 60 days after notice.
- Contracts that violate these rules are unenforceable.
- Program integrity and audit-recovery contractors may not recoup until appeals are exhausted (unless credible fraud) and must provide appeal procedures, contact info at audit commencement, and answer provider questions within ten business days.
- An incomplete provision requires the department to submit an electronic filing. No funding or appropriation changes are included.

LB384 amends §77-1633 (Property Tax Request Act). It applies to political subdivisions (counties, cities, school districts, community colleges) and adds that a majority of the elected members of each participating subdivision's governing body must attend the county-organized joint public hearing on proposed property tax requests exceeding allowable growth. County clerks (or designees) organize hearings (Sept. 14–24, after 6 p.m.), notify participants, and prepare a report within 10 days. Political subdivisions must electronically send required presentation data to the county assessor by Sept. 4; the assessor arranges postcard printing. Initial postcard printing costs are paid from the county general fund and subsequently allocated proportionally to participating subdivisions based on parcel counts. The bill repeals the original section.

Summary: LB388 amends statutes governing judicial nominating commissions and assigns specific roles to state officials and agencies. Key agency responsibilities and changes: - Governor: appoints successor Supreme Court judges on commissions, citizen members, and fills citizen vacancies promptly; notified when additional citizen appointments are needed for quorum. - Nebraska Supreme Court / Clerk of the Supreme Court: Clerk solicits lawyer nominations (no… 
LB388 amends statutes governing judicial nominating commissions and assigns specific roles to state officials and agencies. Key agency responsibilities and changes:

- Governor: appoints successor Supreme Court judges on commissions, citizen members, and fills citizen vacancies promptly; notified when additional citizen appointments are needed for quorum.
- Nebraska Supreme Court / Clerk of the Supreme Court: Clerk solicits lawyer nominations (now may use the Court’s attorney licensure portal), mails or electronically delivers ballots, ensures secrecy/validity, and sets ballot counting date; Supreme Court justice chairs each commission (nonvoting) and the designated justice may not be one originally selected from that district.
- Nebraska State Bar Association (Executive Council/Executive Director): nominates additional lawyer candidates if party-specific nominations are insufficient, designates alternate lawyer members upon Clerk notification, and fills alternate vacancies.
- Secretary of State and Attorney General: serve on the ballot-counting board (or their alternates).

Other changes: residency and voter-registration requirements for lawyer members; four-year terms and alternate-member rules; caps on consecutive service (maximum 12 years; over 10 years disqualifies reelection); electronic nomination deadlines (Oct. 1) and Executive Council deadline (Nov. 1); hearing and submission timelines (first public hearing within 60 days; names to Governor within 90–120 days). A change in residency or party registration automatically terminates commission membership.

No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds procedures involving the Nebraska Supreme Court and the judicial nominating commission, and assigns roles to the Clerk of the Supreme Court and the Executive Council of the Nebraska State Bar Association (NSBA). Key points: - Notices may be delivered electronically via the Supreme Court’s attor… 
Adds procedures involving the Nebraska Supreme Court and the judicial nominating commission, and assigns roles to the Clerk of the Supreme Court and the Executive Council of the Nebraska State Bar Association (NSBA). Key points:
- Notices may be delivered electronically via the Supreme Court’s attorney licensure portal by Oct. 1 of even-numbered years; nominations due by Nov. 1.
- Vacancies on judicial nominating commissions: an alternate lawyer of the same political party fills the unexpired term; if none, a nonpartisan alternate may fill it. If no suitable alternates exist, the Clerk of the Supreme Court uses prior certified election results to promote the highest‑vote alternate who meets constitutional requirements to preserve party balance.
- For unexpired‑term vacancies the Clerk notifies the NSBA Executive Council, which must designate lawyers meeting statutory qualifications.
- Temporary vacancies for meetings are filled under the same rules; interested lawyer members must resign before notice publication to be eligible for nomination.
No funding, appropriations, or budget changes are included.

Additions: The added language eliminates educational service units' property tax levy authority beginning FY2028-29 and creates a state-funded replacement payment stream beginning in 2029. The added language eliminates educational service units' property tax levy authority beginning FY2028-29 and creates a state-funded replacement payment stream beginning in 2029. For 2029 each ESU receives its 2027 levy amount increased 3.5%; for 2030+ each ESU receives the prior year distribution increased 3.5%. The Department of Revenue is assigned to annually calculate each ESU's distribution and certify those amounts to the State Treasurer and the ESU. LB38 amends Nebraska's Geologists Regulation Act to clarify administration and authority of the Board of Geologists (seven Governor‑appointed members, five‑year terms, eligibility and reimbursement per state law). The board's powers include licensing, issuing seals, certificates of licensure and certificates of authorization to organizations, temporary permits, Nebraska‑specific examinations, roster maintenance, rulemaking, enforcement, and accepting verified records from the National Association of State Boards of Geology. The Attorney General is designated legal advisor; the board may employ counsel. The Secretary of State is prohibited from issuing business certificates or registering trade names containing "geology" unless the board has issued a certificate of authorization or eligibility letter. Fee caps are established: individual licensure up to $300, geologist‑intern enrollment $100, organizational authorization $300, emeritus status $100, plus an administrative collection fee up to $100 and potential roster fees. No appropriations or budget allocations are included.

The board may issue certificates of authorization to organizations, adopt exams/standards (including those of the National Association of State Boards of Geology), set application/renewal fees, charge an extra administrative fee up to $100, charge for roster copies, and may waive a first reexamination fee. Creates the Give to Enable Support Act establishing the Give to Enable Support Cash Fund and the Give to Enable Support Program. The State Treasurer will administer the fund and program (program begins Jan. 1, 2026), accept private contributions only (no transfers from the General Fund), approve participant applications annually (Jan. 1–June 1) as funding allows, establish accounts under existing sections 77-1401 to 77-1409, and adopt rules. The State Investment Officer will invest fund balances pursuant to the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and Nebraska State Funds Investment Act. The bill amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §77-2716 to permit a Nebraska income tax reduction for contributions to the Give to Enable Support Cash Fund (subject to existing contribution limits: $5,000 married filing separately; $10,000 other returns). The original §77-2716 is repealed.
Additions: Creates the Give to Enable Support Cash Fund and the Give to Enable Support Program, both administered by the State Treasurer. The fund will accept private contributions only (expressly prohibiting transfers from the General Fund) and any investable balances will be managed by the state investment o… 
Creates the Give to Enable Support Cash Fund and the Give to Enable Support Program, both administered by the State Treasurer. The fund will accept private contributions only (expressly prohibiting transfers from the General Fund) and any investable balances will be managed by the state investment officer under the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and the Nebraska State Funds Investment Act. The program begins January 1, 2026; the State Treasurer will accept applications each year Jan 1–June 1, approve as many applicants as available fund resources permit, establish accounts by April 1 following approval, fund them at least to the minimum required to open, set higher amounts at their discretion, and adopt implementing rules and regulations. No new appropriations or General Fund allocations are authorized.

LB396 amends procedures for certain Nebraska electric districts and related agencies (public power districts, public power and irrigation districts under Chapter 70, art. 6; rural power districts under Chapter 70, art. 8; and agencies created under §§18-2426 to 18-2434) and audit filing requirements.

Key provisions:
- Budget requirements (§13-516): these districts/agencies must prepare written proposed budgets showing prior two years' revenues/expenditures, current-year estimates, and a fiscal policy summary. Proposed budgets must be available at the entity’s principal headquarters at least seven days before the board meeting adopting the budget. A newspaper notice (at least seven days prior) must state the meeting time/place and where the proposed budget is available. Changes made before the meeting must be posted; the public may testify and a written record is required; adopted-budget changes must be summarized and available for inspection.
- Audit filing (§70-623): annual CPA audits (per §84-304.01) must be kept at the district’s principal place of business and filed with the Auditor of Public Accounts within 180 days after fiscal year end.

No appropriations or funding allocations are included.

Organizational plate fee reduced from $70 to $40 effective Oct. 1, 2025; plate revenues split (commonly 60% DMV Cash Fund / 40% Highway Trust Fund); certain veteran fees ($5 alphanumeric; $40 personalized-message) are allocated to the Nebraska Veteran Cemetery System Operation Fund per stated splits. DMV CDL/records expansions include posting medical/self‑cert data, verification duties, portal access fees (per‑record and bulk rates), and creation of an Operator's License Services System Replacement and Maintenance Fund (implementation by 7/1/2032); investment earnings credited to the General Fund beginning 10/1/2024.

Fee changes: personalized-message disabled veteran and Purple Heart plates carry a $40 fee (25% to DMV Cash Fund; 75% to Nebraska Veteran Cemetery System Operation Fund); Cornhusker plates $70 (60% DMV Cash Fund; 40% to Highway Trust Fund); commercial fertilizer trailer registration $1 (effective Jan 1, 2026); RV registration schedules set; record-request fees allocated between License Plate Cash Fund and Records Management Cash Fund. Bill amends the Mutual Finance Assistance Act. It authorizes mutual finance organizations formed under the Interlocal Cooperation Act or Joint Public Agency Act, requires three-year agreements, and sets uniform property tax levy rules (each member must levy an agreed rate in one of the three years, and no more than that rate in other years). It excludes levies for bonded indebtedness and lease-purchase contracts in existence on or after July 1, 1998. The bill revises eligibility for distributions from the Mutual Finance Assistance Fund to rural or suburban fire protection districts and mutual finance organizations that (a) have an assumed population of 30,000+ or (b) contain at least 60% of a county’s assumed population residing outside cities of the first/primary/metropolitan class. It defines “assumed population” using U.S. Bureau of the Census estimates and population certifications under section 77-3,119. Operative date: October 1, 2025. No specific appropriations are added.

Summary: LB3 amends Nebraska law governing selection and certification of presidential electors. Key agency roles: - Governor: receive convention-certified elector names; serve certificates by registered/certified mail; notify electors of meeting time; include a security feature in the federal certificate of ascertainment; appoint substitutes for vacancies and submit amended certificates as needed. - Secretary of State: receive certifications from party… 
LB3 amends Nebraska law governing selection and certification of presidential electors. Key agency roles:

- Governor: receive convention-certified elector names; serve certificates by registered/certified mail; notify electors of meeting time; include a security feature in the federal certificate of ascertainment; appoint substitutes for vacancies and submit amended certificates as needed.
- Secretary of State: receive certifications from party conventions; be provided lists by the Governor; supply and examine presidential/vice‑presidential ballots; accept and count only ballots consistent with each elector’s required pledge; affix the state seal to canvass abstracts.
- Board of State Canvassers: authorize opening county abstracts, prepare statewide abstracts, and declare the party whose electors receive the highest statewide vote as elected.

Other changes: conventions must select five presidential electors; electors must pledge to vote for the presidential/vice‑presidential candidates who received the highest number of votes statewide (effectively a statewide winner‑take‑all allocation). No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB400 amends the Nebraska Workers' Compensation Act (section 48-1,110, Reissue Revised Statutes) to establish rebuttable presumptions that certain cancers in firefighters arose out of and in the course of employment. Key administrative points: the presumptions apply to currently employed firefighters (diagnosed during employment); to retired professional firefighters with diagnosis timing tied to years of service (different rules for retirements before vs. on/after Jan. 1, 2026); and to volunteer firefighters regardless of retirement date. Purchased service credit in a retirement system may not be used to calculate years of service for these presumptions. Claims filed under the post-2026 retiree rule are limited to medical benefits only. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are specified.
Additions: Adds specific carcinogen findings (hydrocarbons linked to urinary tract/ureteral cancer; benzene and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons linked to uterine cancer) and creates rebuttable presumptions that firefighter cancers are work‑related: any cancer diagnosed during employment; for retirees (profess… 
Adds specific carcinogen findings (hydrocarbons linked to urinary tract/ureteral cancer; benzene and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons linked to uterine cancer) and creates rebuttable presumptions that firefighter cancers are work‑related: any cancer diagnosed during employment; for retirees (professionals retiring before Jan 1, 2026, and all volunteers) diagnosed within up to 60 months after last work, using a period = 3 months × full years worked; for professionals retiring on/after Jan 1, 2026, diagnosed within a post‑separation period equal to years worked if <20 years, or at any time for ≥20 years. Purchased retirement service credit cannot be used to calculate years. Claims under subsection (7) after retirement are limited under the Nebraska Workers' Compensation Act to medical benefits only. No funding, appropriation, or specific agency budgets are changed.

Creates an Office of Grants in the executive branch. The office is led by a Director of Grants, appointed by the Governor (serving at the Governor’s pleasure), selected after a nationwide search and required to have at least ten years’ experience writing or managing federal grants. The Director may appoint additional staff "for which adequate funding is available" (no specific appropriation in the bill). Duties: identify national (including federal) grant programs available to state agencies, political subdivisions, and private Nebraska organizations; assist those entities with identification, applications, and compliance; and develop a statewide plan to maximize grant funding by July 1, 2026, with annual updates. Creates an Office of Grants in the executive branch headed by a Director of Grants (Governor‑appointed, serves at pleasure, nationwide search, 10+ years federal grant experience) and additional staff as funded. No specific appropriations or budget allocations are made; staffing is tied to “adequate funding.”

LB406 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §2-1201 to (re)define the State Racing and Gaming Commission. Key provisions: the seven-member commission is appointed by the Governor with legislative confirmation and removable for cause; membership set by congressional-district representation (as of Jan 1, 2010) plus at-large seats with specified initial appointment dates and subsequent four-year terms; political- and residency-based limits on composition; vacancies filled by gubernatorial appointment. Member pay is $1,000 per month, adjustable biennially up to the change in the CPI for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers. Members are reimbursed under §§81-1174–81-1177, must be bonded/insured per §11-201, and may not hold financial interests in licensed racetracks or authorized gaming operators. The bill repeals the original section. No new appropriations are specified.

Specifically (section 43-251.01): juveniles described in subdivision (3) of section 43-247 may not be placed in an adult correctional facility, the Department of Correctional Services’ secure youth confinement facility, a youth rehabilitation and treatment center, or committed to the Office of Juvenile Services; juveniles described in subdivisions (1), (2), or (4) of section 43-247 may not be assigned or transferred to an adult correctional facility or the Department’s secure youth confinement facility. Adds procedures for juveniles ages 13–15 charged with specified felonies: juvenile court has exclusive original jurisdiction and may transfer cases per section 8. After disposition, the county attorney may move to dismiss the juvenile petition and refile in district court; the court must hold a hearing within 15 days, the juvenile has counsel and may present evidence, and the court must decide within 30 days with written findings. The court retains the case unless the county attorney proves by a preponderance that the juvenile is not amenable to rehabilitation. Orders are immediately appealable to the Court of Appeals on an expedited docket. If transferred, the juvenile is arraigned as an adult and applicable statutes of limitations are tolled for one year. Most admissions in these proceedings are inadmissible later, with limited exceptions. No changes to funding, appropriations, or Department of Correctional Services budgets are included.

LB408 creates the Special Education Teacher Forgivable Loan Program to be administered by "the department" (the bill-designated state department). The department may award up to 25 forgivable loans per academic year per eligible institution (state colleges in Nebraska and the University of Nebraska) to students seeking initial special education teacher certification. The department contracts with recipients, determines annual/total loan amounts, and forgives 20% per compliant postgraduation year (or proportional forgiveness if fewer than five years of loans). The State Board of Education may adopt rules. Repayments from noncompliant recipients (with 5% simple interest) are remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the General Fund. The bill includes no explicit appropriations or new budget allocations.

LB409 amends membership of the Nebraska Power Review Board. It requires that, upon the first vacancy or term expiration among the existing three at-large positions after the bill’s effective date, the five-member board must include: at least one engineer, at least one attorney, at least one licensed journeyman electrician who is affiliated with a nonprofit labor organization holding a 501(c)(5) exemption and selected from a list provided by that organization, and two additional persons. Appointment remains by the Governor with legislative approval. The board continues to employ an executive director, submit a biennial report to the Governor (with electronic copies to the Clerk of the Legislature and the Department of Environment and Energy), and may report to the Natural Resources Committee. Member compensation limits remain: $100/day (max $7,000/yr), SPP designee $250/day (max $35,000/yr), aggregate SPP pay cap $40,000/yr.

LB40 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §21-193 (Nebraska Uniform Limited Liability Company Act) to specify publication requirements for LLC notices. Notices of organization, amendments to the certificate of organization, mergers, conversions, and domestications must be published for three successive weeks in a legal newspaper of general circulation near the LLC’s designated office; dissolution notices follow the publication procedure in §21-150. Proof of publication must be filed with the Secretary of State. If required publication is belatedly completed and filed, prior and subsequent LLC acts are validated. The original §21-193 is repealed. No state agency funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are changed.

Grant amounts: $2,500 annually for years 1–6 of full‑time Nebraska teaching; $3,000 for years 7–15; $4,000 from year 16 onward. Effective July 1, 2025, "the department" is required to automatically provide teacher retention grants. Grant amounts by years of full‑time Nebraska service: $2,500 per year (years 1–6); $3,000 per year (years 7–15); $4,000 per year (year 16 onward). LB412 amends paternity statutes to authorize alleged biological fathers to intervene in juvenile-court paternity proceedings. Key government entities mentioned: district courts (where child is domiciled or found), juvenile courts, county courts, county sheriffs (service of process), counties, and the State of Nebraska. Procedural changes: the juvenile court may order genetic testing and require the juvenile be produced; no filing fee may be charged for the complaint and supporting affidavit. Funding changes: the juvenile court may allocate payment for genetic testing to the complainant, the county, or the state at its discretion. The bill also expands the statutory definition of child (under 18) and adds “reasonable education” to the definition of support.

Adds a definition of "child" as a person under 18 (regardless of whether born out of wedlock) and authorizes the juvenile court, when ordering genetic testing or establishing paternity, to consider: the child's age; the child's relationship with any presumptive parent, any parent whose rights were established by acknowledgment or court finding, and the complainant; whether establishing paternity would benefit or harm the child; and any other factor the court deems relevant. No other government agencies or departments are mentioned, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

LB413 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §70‑655 governing public power districts, public irrigation districts, and public power and irrigation districts. It explicitly authorizes district boards to set and differentiate rates for electrical energy, water service/storage and other commodities (including ethanol and hydrogen) based on objective criteria (load size, load factor, firm/nonfirm service, technology risks, length of commitment, etc.). Boards may negotiate commercial/industrial rates effective up to five years; rates for customers participating in state or local economic development projects (and adding >500 kW with ≥60% annual load factor) cannot be below incremental production cost. The changes also apply to entities under the Electric Cooperative Corporation Act, Nebraska Nonprofit Corporation Act, agencies created under the Municipal Cooperative Financing Act, and municipalities. Mergers may sustain differing predecessor rates up to five years if supported by cost‑of‑service or rate studies. The bill repeals the original section. No appropriations or budget changes are included.

Upon request by the bill’s referenced "director," a county attorney or the Attorney General may issue subpoenas for records (coroner and autopsy reports, law‑enforcement records, medical and mental‑health records, EMS data, PDMP data, toxicology, employment, school records, etc.). Adds requirements for suicide mortality review teams to enter a cooperative agreement with the Nebraska Violent Death Reporting System (NVDRS) to share and store review-related data. At the director's request, a county attorney or the Attorney General may subpoena records (e.g., coroner, autopsy, law enforcement, medical, probation/corrections, EMS, prescription monitoring) which must be entered into NVDRS and provided to the review team as an aggregate narrative. LB416 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §25-21,185.11 to clarify the legal effect of releases, covenants not to sue, and similar agreements. Under the amendment, a release discharges the released party from liability to the claimant and reduces the claimant’s claim against remaining defendants by the released party’s share of the obligation as determined by the trier of fact. A release also precludes the released party from being made a party or, if already named, provides a basis for dismissal; however, that party’s negligence remains subject to allocation under §25-21,185.09. The bill further states such releases do not abrogate joint and several liability of other liable parties. The original section is repealed. No state agencies, appropriations, or budget allocations are affected.
Additions: Adds a provision that a release, covenant not to sue, or similar agreement between a claimant and one or more liable parties does not eliminate the joint and several liability of any other parties liable on the same claim. No government agencies or departments are referenced and there are no funding…

Summary: LB417 assigns administration of the Nebraska Promise Program to the Board of Regents of the University of Nebraska and establishes the College Promise Act. The Coordinating Commission for Postsecondary Education will administer a College Promise Fund to distribute payments to community and state colleges, with the Legislature authorized to transfer funds; the bill declares the Legislature's intent to fully fund the Fund annually for the total val… 
LB417 assigns administration of the Nebraska Promise Program to the Board of Regents of the University of Nebraska and establishes the College Promise Act. The Coordinating Commission for Postsecondary Education will administer a College Promise Fund to distribute payments to community and state colleges, with the Legislature authorized to transfer funds; the bill declares the Legislature's intent to fully fund the Fund annually for the total value of tuition waivers. The state investment officer will invest any available fund balances. The Coordinating Commission must also develop an appeals process. The State Board of Education and the State Department of Education retain roles in statewide assessments, student data tracking and reporting, and the State Board must recommend career‑readiness assessments. The act takes effect immediately under an emergency clause.

- Legislature: authorizes transfers into the College Promise Fund; intent language directs full annual funding equal to the total value of waivers.

LB419 amends statutes governing Nebraska veterans services. Key agencies and offices affected:
- Department (Veterans' homes): continues to provide long‑term care at Nebraska veterans homes and clarifies eligible service (including Nebraska National Guard active duty and training).
- Office of the Director of Veterans' Affairs: retains responsibility for administering income from the Nebraska Veterans' Aid Fund and for approving or denying aid applications.
- County veterans service officers, state service officers, recognized veterans organizations and the state service office are explicitly identified as authorized originators/representatives for aid applications.
- State Treasurer and Legislature: existing fiscal controls remain—expenditures for assistants, clerical staff, and the state service office require specific legislative appropriation; interest from the Aid Fund cannot be used to organize/maintain veterans organizations; the $12 million trust and its income remain protected, with principal reverting to the state treasury upon trust completion.

No new appropriations or dollar allocations are established in the bill.

Bill LB420 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §84-1501 to revise composition and appointment provisions for the Public Employees Retirement Board. The board consists of nine appointed members plus the state investment officer (nonvoting, ex officio). Seven appointees must be active or retired participants in systems the board administers; two appointees must be nonstate employees with at least ten years' experience in organizational management or in actuarial/employee-benefit-plan administration. Specified member seats represent: School Employees Retirement System (teacher and administrator), Nebraska Judges Retirement System, Nebraska State Patrol Retirement System, Retirement System for Nebraska Counties, State Employees Retirement System, and (effective Sept. 1, 2024) a teacher in a Class V school retirement system (previously nonvoting ex officio). Appointments are by the Governor with legislative approval; terms are staggered, vacancies filled by gubernatorial appointment, and members removable for cause. No funding or appropriation changes.

LB425 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §77-3506 (homestead exemptions). It requires certification of veteran/disability status from the United States Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) for eligible claimants, generally annually but with VA certification only required in subsequent years evenly divisible by five. The bill clarifies that homesteads in specified categories (veterans, unremarried or qualifying surviving spouses, etc.) receive 100% of the exempt amount, and adds a new category effective January 1, 2026: veterans rated at least 80% but less than 100% service‑connected disabled (and their qualifying surviving spouses) are eligible for an exemption equal to the veteran’s VA disability percentage. No agencies other than the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs are expressly referenced, and the bill contains no funding, appropriation, or budget allocations.

Adds a tax-exemption formula and a new eligibility class effective January 1, 2026. For homesteads described in new subdivision (2)(g), a portion of the exempt amount will be excluded from taxation equal to the veteran’s VA disability percentage. The new (g) defines eligible persons as veterans discharged honorable or general, receiving compensation from the United States Department of Veterans Affairs for a service‑connected disability of at least 80% but under 100%, who are not already eligible for full exemption under sections 77-3526 to 77-3528; it also covers an unremarried surviving spouse and a surviving spouse who remarries after age 57. No agencies beyond the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs are added, and no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are specified.

LB427 directs the State Treasurer to establish individual educational savings accounts for K–12 students enrolled at approved or accredited public, private, denominational, or parochial schools. The State Board of Education must adopt a list of qualified educational expenses and post it on the State Department of Education website; appeal rights are provided. The bill creates the Student Savings Account Support Fund, administered by the State Treasurer (or a third‑party manager under the Treasurer’s supervision); fund assets are invested by the state investment officer pursuant to the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and Nebraska State Funds Investment Act. Beginning July 1, 2026, the Treasurer must transfer $1,500 annually from the Support Fund into each enrolled student’s account. The Treasurer will monitor, audit, and investigate misuse, referring suspected crimes to the Nebraska State Patrol; restitution is required. The State Board may adopt implementing rules; terminated accounts revert to the General Fund.

Adds multiple education and fiscal duties to state agencies. The State Board of Education must adopt a list of qualified educational expenses, post it on the State Department of Education website, hear appeals to add expenses, and may adopt rules. The State Treasurer (or a third‑party manager under the Treasurer's supervision) must create and administer a new Student Savings Account Support Fund, invest available money via the state investment officer under existing investment acts, establish individual educational savings accounts beginning July 1, 2026, and annually transfer $1,500 from the Support Fund into each enrolled student's account. The Treasurer will monitor, audit, investigate misuse, interview suspects, and refer crimes to the Nebraska State Patrol; restitution must be returned to the account. Account funds revert to the General Fund on ineligibility, graduation, or death.

LB429 regulates how school boards may interact with professional employees' organizations. The bill requires school boards to provide equal access to any professional employees' organization when granting use of employees' physical or electronic mailboxes, permission to attend or display materials at employee meetings or orientations, and posting signage or materials in schools. Bill LB430 amends sections 79-265, 79-265.01, and 79-268 of Nebraska law governing school discipline. Key agency/department roles: school districts must develop elementary disciplinary policies; school principals and district superintendents carry notification, investigation, suspension, and hearing duties; the Student Discipline Act procedures apply.

Notable changes:
- Short-term suspension notice (principal) must be sent within 24–72 hours and include conduct, reasons, prior school interventions, available resources, and an actionable plan to keep the student in school; principals must document efforts to confer with parents.
- Pre-K–2 suspension prohibition gains exceptions for bringing a deadly weapon onto school property/vehicles/activities and for violent behavior causing potential physical harm.
- Long-term suspension/expulsion procedures require decision and superintendent filing within two school days, certified-mail notice with resources, actionable remediation plan, hearing rights, ability to complete missed work, records/witness disclosure, and a hearing-request form. Principals may suspend pending hearings to prevent interference or injury.

No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included. The prior versions of the amended sections are repealed.
Additions: Added provisions require schools to document: actions taken to discontinue or alleviate a student's behavior before suspension; resources the school can provide or recommend; and an actionable plan for handling the behavior going forward focused on keeping the student in school. Added provisions require schools to document: actions taken to discontinue or alleviate a student's behavior before suspension; resources the school can provide or recommend; and an actionable plan for handling the behavior going forward focused on keeping the student in school. The additions also clarify that conduct including bringing items onto school property and violent behavior causing physical harm to students or staff are covered. No government agencies or departments are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

LB433 amends State Personnel and State Employees Retirement Act provisions affecting several named agencies:

- Department of Banking and Finance and Department of Insurance: deputies and examiners are exempted from the State Personnel System (except those who remain covered).
- Department of Correctional Services: chief executive officers of all correctional facilities and the department medical director are exempt; pharmacists, physicians, psychiatrists, and psychologists employed by the department are also exempt.
- Department of Health and Human Services and Department of Veterans' Affairs: pharmacists, physicians, psychiatrists, psychologists, service area administrators, and facility operating officers are exempt from the State Personnel System.
- Department of Labor: active participants in a terminated contributory retirement plan/contracts under former section 48-609 shall receive vesting credit for years of participation.

No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations appear in the bill.

- Deputy directors and attorneys hired after the bill’s effective date will serve at the will of the agency director; their salaries are set by the director and approved by the Governor.  
- incumbents in those roles may permanently elect to convert to at‑will status by written notice; until they do they remain in the State Personnel System.  
- Temporary employees who return to state service without a 120‑day break must rejoin the retirement system within 30 days; the definition of "temporary employees" is clarified for certain legislative hires.

LB436 amends the Nebraska Regulation of Health Professions Act to clarify review and rulemaking roles for the director, the division, the board, and technical committees. The division must adopt rules establishing standards for applying statutory criteria. The director manages letters of intent, accepts applications within set timelines, and may set review order. For unregulated professions, technical committees will be six appointed members plus a board-designated chair (with conflict restrictions and composition limits); for scope changes to regulated professions, the existing regulatory entity serves as the technical committee. Committees must conduct public fact‑finding hearings, consider scientific evidence, consult applicants and opponents, comply with the Open Meetings Act, and file written findings and recommendations with the board and director, including recommending the least‑restrictive regulation if approving. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

For unregulated professions or professions without such a regulatory entity, a different process is referenced (text incomplete). No specific state agencies beyond the profession’s regulatory entity are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

LB438 requires authorized gaming operators, beginning on the implementation date designated by the Tax Commissioner, to check a collection system before paying sports-wagering winnings and, if a winner has outstanding state tax liability or other debt, deduct the identified amount and remit that deducted amount to the Department of Revenue to be credited against the debt per section 9-1306.  

The bill also reallocates gross gaming tax distributions: for non-sports wagering, 75% to state (2.5% Compulsive Gamblers Assistance Fund; 2.5% General Fund; 70% Property Tax Credit Cash Fund) and 25% to county/city as specified. For sports wagering, taxes are remitted to the State Treasurer: 2.5% Compulsive Gamblers Assistance Fund, 5% Racing and Gaming Commission Racetrack Gaming Fund, 27.5% Property Tax Credit Cash Fund, 20% General Fund, and 45% Education Future Fund.

Added provisions define "online sports wagering platform" and "platform provider," require sports wagering to be conducted by an authorized gaming operator (or a vendor contracted with one) and require online platforms to submit controls for commission approval before use. Financially, the bill specifies that the tax under section 9-1203 on gross gaming revenue from sports wagering must be remitted to the State Treasurer and allocated: 2.5% to the Compulsive Gamblers Assistance Fund, 5% to the Racing and Gaming Commission's Racetrack Gaming Fund, 27.5% to the Property Tax Credit Cash Fund, 20% to the General Fund, and 45% to the Education Future Fund. The Department of Revenue would administer/collect and remit these tax receipts according to the new allocation.

For tax years beginning on or after Jan 1, 2026, the Department will accept applications, verify eligibility, approve or deny within 30 days, and certify refundable income tax credits to qualifying homeowners and renters who reside in their Nebraska principal residence at least six months. The Department may adopt rules. LB43 amends statutes governing electric generation and transmission. It revises definitions (including "foreign adversary" and "military installation") and requires owners to notify and certify to the board (and its executive director) that facilities within a ten‑mile radius of specified U.S. Air Force installations contain no electronic-related equipment or components manufactured by a foreign adversary. Retail suppliers compliant with NERC critical infrastructure protection (CIP) standards may certify that compliance instead. The board may preapprove use of such equipment only where no reasonable alternative exists and withholding it would cause greater harm. Privately developed renewable energy facilities must notify the board 30 days before construction, submit decommissioning plans and security, enter joint transmission development agreements, and consult the Nebraska Game and Parks Commission on species impacts; the executive director must acknowledge exemptions within ten days. The board retains hearing and enforcement powers. No changes to funding or appropriations. Emergency clause makes the act effective on passage.
Additions: Adds definitions and new compliance steps for electric suppliers and facility owners. Key agencies and references: - United States Air Force (certain silos/bases identified by 31 C.F.R. citations as of Jan 1, 2025). - The board (entity receiving certifications and preapproval requests). - North Amer… 
Adds definitions and new compliance steps for electric suppliers and facility owners. Key agencies and references:
- United States Air Force (certain silos/bases identified by 31 C.F.R. citations as of Jan 1, 2025).
- The board (entity receiving certifications and preapproval requests).
- North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) — facilities connected at ≥100 kV and meeting specified nameplate/injection thresholds must certify future compliance with NERC critical infrastructure protection requirements.
- Federal regulations: foreign adversary defined by 15 C.F.R. 791.4 (as of Feb 7, 2025).

Requirements:
- Before building or acquiring generation/transmission >700 volts within 10 miles of a military installation, suppliers/owners must consult vendors and file a one‑time written certification to the board that no electronic-related equipment/components are manufactured by a foreign adversary, and must notify the board if compliance later lapses.
- The board may preapprove use of such equipment only if no reasonable alternative exists and nonuse would cause greater harm.

No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Summary: Creates the Education Leave and Support Act and establishes the State Education Leave Fund and Education Retention Fund, both administered by the State Department of Education. Beginning Jan. 1, 2026, a 0.35% payroll fee on certificated teachers' taxable wages is collected from employees, remitted quarterly to the State Treasurer, and matched by employers; all receipts are credited to the State Education Leave Fund. The fund, investable by the st… 
Creates the Education Leave and Support Act and establishes the State Education Leave Fund and Education Retention Fund, both administered by the State Department of Education. Beginning Jan. 1, 2026, a 0.35% payroll fee on certificated teachers' taxable wages is collected from employees, remitted quarterly to the State Treasurer, and matched by employers; all receipts are credited to the State Education Leave Fund. The fund, investable by the state investment officer under existing state investment law, reimburses school districts (beginning July 1, 2026) for substitute-teacher costs for the first six weeks of a teacher's FMLA leave; reimbursements capped at actual daily substitute cost as determined by the department. Surplus (>20% of projected annual needs) may be transferred by the State Treasurer to the Education Retention Fund for shortages and professional development. The department must report annually to the Legislature; funds are auditable by the Auditor of Public Accounts; misuse triggers repayment and departmental penalties.
Additions: Creates a new revenue stream and two state funds administered by the State Department of Education. Beginning Jan 1, 2026, a 0.35% payroll fee on certificated teachers' wages is collected by school districts and remitted quarterly to the State Treasurer; employers must remit an equal matching amount… 
Creates a new revenue stream and two state funds administered by the State Department of Education. Beginning Jan 1, 2026, a 0.35% payroll fee on certificated teachers' wages is collected by school districts and remitted quarterly to the State Treasurer; employers must remit an equal matching amount. Proceeds are credited to the newly created State Education Leave Fund, administered by the Department of Education and invested by the state investment officer under existing investment laws. The fund (reimbursements begin July 1, 2026) reimburses districts for substitute-teacher costs for the first six weeks of a teacher's FMLA leave, up to actual daily cost as set by the department; reimbursed teachers need not use sick/personal leave. The Department must report annually to the Legislature. Excess (>20% of projected needs) may be transferred by the Treasurer to an Education Retention Fund (also DOE‑administered) for addressing shortages and professional development. The Auditor of Public Accounts will audit the Education Leave Fund; misuse by districts triggers repayment and departmental penalties.

LB441 amends the Building Construction Act (section 71‑6401) to authorize virtual building inspections by "authorized inspectors"—individuals credentialed by the state agency, county, city, or village issuing permits or third‑party inspectors registered/licensed with the State of Nebraska and contracted per project specifications (excluding self‑inspections). Virtual inspections are permitted when: the inspection involves a residential building under three stories and <10,000 sq ft; the permit holder supplies an onsite personnel list; and the inspection is conducted live with both permit holder and inspector (except nonstructural reinspections, which may use submitted photos/video). All inspections for permits or structural scopes must be performed by authorized inspectors. Adds definitions and procedures for building inspections involving state agencies, counties, cities, and villages. Key points: authorized inspectors must be credentialed by the permitting state agency, county, city, village, or be a State of Nebraska–registered/licensed third‑party contractor (self‑inspections excluded). Inspection records are defined as pass/fail results with reasons tied to the permit address. Permitting entities may allow live virtual inspections for residential buildings under three stories and 10,000 sq ft if the permit holder lists onsite personnel; nonstructural reinspections may use submitted video/photos. All building or structural inspections must be performed by an authorized inspector. Inspection records must be made public if the structure remains standing when requested. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Summary: The bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services to administer a new state child care subsidy program and authorizes contracting with other social agencies. Beginning October 1, 2026, the department must provide child care assistance to families with incomes from 130%–400% of the federal poverty level, adopt rules implementing eligibility (including a 10% gross-earned-income disregard after 12 continuous months, sliding-scale cost-sh… 
The bill requires the Department of Health and Human Services to administer a new state child care subsidy program and authorizes contracting with other social agencies. Beginning October 1, 2026, the department must provide child care assistance to families with incomes from 130%–400% of the federal poverty level, adopt rules implementing eligibility (including a 10% gross-earned-income disregard after 12 continuous months, sliding-scale cost-sharing, and criminal-history checks), and establish an annual fixed-rate reimbursement schedule effective each October 1. Beginning October 1, 2025, the department must allow certain accommodations and enrollment flexibilities for household members. Funding is provided by a 0.52% payroll tax (0.39% employer / 0.13% employee); General Funds may not be used to cover state costs, including administrative costs, attributable to the income-eligibility changes beginning October 1, 2026. The program must prioritize apprentices for highest assistance.
Additions: DHHS must administer expanded social services and implement a state child-care subsidy program. Key DHHS duties: provide child care assistance to families earning 130%–400% of FPL effective Oct 1, 2026; require providers to meet Child Care Licensing Act criminal-history checks; apply a sliding‑scale… 
DHHS must administer expanded social services and implement a state child-care subsidy program. Key DHHS duties: provide child care assistance to families earning 130%–400% of FPL effective Oct 1, 2026; require providers to meet Child Care Licensing Act criminal-history checks; apply a sliding‑scale, cost‑share for benefits with a 10% gross‑earned‑income disregard after 12 continuous months and at each redetermination; adopt rules for reasonable‑accommodation and enrollment exceptions (effective Oct 1, 2025); set an annual fixed-rate reimbursement schedule (effective Oct 1 each year) that may include higher rates for infants or children with special needs but not exceed providers’ private charges; and prioritize highest assistance for qualified apprentice workers. Funding: a 0.52% payroll tax (0.39% employer / 0.13% employee) funds the program; General Funds cannot pay state costs from the eligibility expansion beginning Oct 1, 2026.

LB443 amends the Nebraska Criminal Code to create the offense of unlawful squatting and assigns specific duties to law enforcement. LB446 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §71-602 (vital records).
