LB604 amends initiative and referendum procedures, assigning specific duties to state officers and clarifying judicial review.

Key agency actions:
- Secretary of State: must transmit proposed measure to the Revisor of Statutes for a form/draftsmanship review (completed within 10 business days), keep filings confidential for five days, prepare petition forms, post measure text and circulation notice on the Secretary of State website upon receipt of a sample petition, and—if refusing placement for legal insufficiency other than lack of signatures—announce the refusal and state reasons at the time of posting (failure to state reasons waives those defenses).
- Revisor of Statutes: review and recommend form/draftsmanship changes.

Judicial process and jurisdiction:
- Residents may seek mandamus in Lancaster County District Court within 10 days of a refusal announcement.
- Sponsor of record must be named as a defendant in suits to enjoin placement.
- Challenges to legal sufficiency (except signature insufficiency) must be filed within 60 days after posting (or by petition-filing deadline if earlier).
- Lancaster County District Court has original jurisdiction; if the suit does not assert signature insufficiency, the Nebraska Supreme Court may hear the case under original jurisdiction if practicable and on petition. Appeals to the Court of Appeals must be filed within ten days; Administrative Procedure Act appeal procedures do not apply.
Budget/funding changes: none.
Additions: Adds duties and timelines for the Secretary of State and the Supreme Court: the Secretary of State must post a measure’s text and a circulation notice on the Secretary of State website until the petition-filing deadline and, if refusing to place a measure on the ballot for any legal insufficiency ot… 
Adds duties and timelines for the Secretary of State and the Supreme Court: the Secretary of State must post a measure’s text and a circulation notice on the Secretary of State website until the petition-filing deadline and, if refusing to place a measure on the ballot for any legal insufficiency other than lack of signatures, must announce that refusal the same day and state the reason (failure to state a reason waives those defenses). Lawsuits challenging non‑signature legal insufficiencies must be filed within 60 days of the circulation posting (or by close of business on the last petition‑filing day if the 60th day falls after that deadline). If practicable, the Supreme Court shall hear such non‑signature challenges under its original jurisdiction upon petition. Officials or residents may raise substantive facial insufficiency without ripeness dismissal; the section does not limit other post‑enactment suits. No funding or appropriation changes are included.

Summary: LB605 requires each public school board to adopt a policy governing student participation as a transgender student in school-sponsored extracurricular activities and in activities governed by any athletics or activities association of which the school is a member. LB605 requires each public school board to adopt a policy governing student participation as a transgender student in school-sponsored extracurricular activities and in activities governed by any athletics or activities association of which the school is a member. The policy must specify required documentation (student registration, written statements from student and parent/guardian, corroborating statements), require submission and cooperation by the school board and school administrators/athletic directors with any applicable athletics or activities association for association-level determinations, and set default team eligibility by biological sex as listed on the birth certificate unless a board approves participation as a transgender student. The bill clarifies the policy shall not be construed to encourage medical treatment and does not alter cross-gender participation rules. No funding, appropriations, or budgetary changes are included.
Additions: Adds requirements directing local school boards (via school administrators or athletic directors) to: receive written requests from a student and parent identifying the student as transgender and desired activities; determine eligibility under a board policy; and, when required, submit eligibility a… 
Adds requirements directing local school boards (via school administrators or athletic directors) to: receive written requests from a student and parent identifying the student as transgender and desired activities; determine eligibility under a board policy; and, when required, submit eligibility applications and any documentation to relevant athletics or activities associations of which the school is a member. Permits sharing student registration, parental/student statements, and corroborating documentation with those associations. States eligibility for sex‑separated teams defaults to the biological sex on the birth certificate unless board approval or a cross‑gender policy applies. Clarifies the policy does not encourage medical transition. No funding, appropriations, or budget changes.

Summary: The bill consolidates parole functions into the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), abolishing the Division of Parole Supervision and assigning parole powers/duties to the DCS director. The bill consolidates parole functions into the Department of Correctional Services (DCS), abolishing the Division of Parole Supervision and assigning parole powers/duties to the DCS director. DCS will maintain electronic parole files, receive presentence reports, provide record access to oversight bodies, set performance metrics, direct risk-and-needs assessments and training, supervise parolees, run reentry programming (including a technical‑violation residential pilot), and establish sanction matrices and community supervision procedures. DCS may contract with private providers for community work‑release and reentry centers, use designated legislative funds for agreements, and is the intended recipient of a $1,000,000 General Fund appropriation to implement that Act. Parolees owe a $25 monthly programming fee remitted to the Parole Program Cash Fund. The director may certify overcrowding (140% capacity) to expedite releases. DHHS may subpoena records for licensing investigations. Department of Revenue employees are excluded from the “law enforcement officer” definition (sec. 81‑1401).
Additions: Department of Correctional Services: Added provisions require the department to maintain all records and files for the Board of Parole, including records for individuals under lifetime community supervision (sec. 83-174.03), while not preventing the department from also keeping daily records for the… 
Department of Correctional Services: Added provisions require the department to maintain all records and files for the Board of Parole, including records for individuals under lifetime community supervision (sec. 83-174.03), while not preventing the department from also keeping daily records for the Board of Pardons. Other additions clarify director/department implementation duties and authorize continued in‑facility correctional treatment, medical care, or vocational training when it will substantially enhance an offender’s ability to lead a law‑abiding life after release. References to the Community Corrections Act and board responsibilities were expanded.

Department of Health and Human Services / Department of Revenue: No substantive additions or funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes are included for these agencies in the provided text.

Summary: LB607 centralizes implementation, oversight, and enforcement with the Nebraska Department of Environment and Energy (and its Director). Manufacturing sites are removed from the Integrated Solid Waste Man… 
LB607 centralizes implementation, oversight, and enforcement with the Nebraska Department of Environment and Energy (and its Director). The Department will approve battery stewardship plans, adopt rules, set fees (including a manufacturer registration fee of $1,000 under the Minimum Recycled Content Act), audit reports, and conduct a 2027 assessment of large/noncovered batteries. Manufacturing sites are removed from the Integrated Solid Waste Management Act “facility” definition but remain subject to state manufacturing rules for air, water, waste, and land use. Landfill/solid‑waste disposal fees rise to $2.25 (2026), $3.25 (2027), and $4.25 (2028) per unit; proceeds split 50% to the Integrated Solid Waste Management Cash Fund (Department use) and 50% to the Waste Reduction and Recycling Incentive Fund (grants/reimbursements), with political‑subdivision reimbursements capped at 5% of prior‑year fees. The Department administers the Minimum Recycled Content Act (reporting begins 1/1/2027), may join a multistate clearinghouse, levies penalties (e.g., $0.20/lb for recycled‑content shortfalls in year one), and manages the Incentive Fund (may deduct admin costs; includes up to $1.5M/year for scrap‑tire projects through 6/30/2029). Penalties and fees are remitted via the State Treasurer; the state investment officer may invest fund balances. The act becomes operative January 1, 2026.
Additions: Adds definitional and program language and assigns implementation and enforcement to the Department of Environment and Energy (including the Director and departmental divisions). Key agency actions and fiscal elements: - Manufacturing/process definitions (depolymerization, gasification, pyrolysis,… 
Adds definitional and program language and assigns implementation and enforcement to the Department of Environment and Energy (including the Director and departmental divisions). Key agency actions and fiscal elements:

- Manufacturing/process definitions (depolymerization, gasification, pyrolysis, solvolysis, recovered feedstock) and subjects manufacturing facilities to Department air/water/waste/land rules; owners must properly dispose of onsite post‑use polymers within 60 days after ceasing operations.  
- Disposal fee schedule for applicable materials: $2.25 (2026), $3.25 (2027), $4.25 (2028).  
- Creates the Environmental Stewardship of Batteries Act administered by the Department: establishes producer/stewardship-organization duties, statewide collection standards, reimbursement to local governments for demonstrable costs, required departmental fees to cover implementation, reporting/confidentiality rules, and enforcement (civil penalties up to $1,000/day; up to $10,000/day for repeated violations). Appeals to the Environmental Quality Council. Department must complete assessments and report by set deadlines.  
- Establishes Minimum Recycled Content Act under the Department: annual registration (default $1,000, adjustable), reporting, third‑party certification, per‑pound civil penalties (initially $0.20/lb), and penalty remittance to the State Treasurer.

- The bill adds “correctional officer” defined to include individuals employed full-time by a jail or by the Department of Correctional Services.

Department of Revenue
- Applicants and recipients must file documentation with the Department of Revenue proving employment, residential status, or eligible-disabled status when applying for tuition waivers and annually while receiving benefits; tuition‑waiver agreements require annual tax returns filed with the Department to verify Nebraska residency for five years post‑award.

LB60 (2025) amends section 9‑829 of the State Lottery Act. Summary: LB614 amends and restates extraterritorial zoning provisions in sections 16-901 and 17-1001. LB614 amends and restates extraterritorial zoning provisions in sections 16-901 and 17-1001. Key government entities affected: cities of the first and second class, villages, county boards, boards of adjustment, and joint planning commissions/departments. The bill:

- Clarifies ETJ distances: city of the first class retains a two-mile ETJ generally but is one mile for purposes of sections 70-1001–70-1020; cities of the second class and villages retain a one-mile ETJ generally but are one-half mile for those same sections.
- Confirms municipalities may apply local ordinances in their ETJ and allows boards of adjustment to exempt qualifying farm buildings (on 20+ acre farmsteads producing ≥$1,000/year) consistent with comprehensive plans.
- Requires cities/villages to notify county boards at least 30 days before final action on ETJ zoning changes and allows county comment, with exceptions for counties over 100,000 population or where joint planning exists.
Original sections are repealed. No appropriations or funding changes.
Additions: Adds authority for cities (first- and second-class) and villages to allow their boards of adjustment to exempt certain farm buildings within their extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction from zoning, property-use, building, electrical, plumbing, and related ordinances (including those under section 16-… 
Adds authority for cities (first- and second-class) and villages to allow their boards of adjustment to exempt certain farm buildings within their extraterritorial zoning jurisdiction from zoning, property-use, building, electrical, plumbing, and related ordinances (including those under section 16-240) when consistent with the jurisdiction’s comprehensive development plan, per sections 19-907 to 19-915. Defines "farm building" by reference to section 77-1359: located on a farmstead of 20+ acres producing $1,000+ in farm products annually. No state agencies, departments, or funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are created or altered.

Summary: LB615 (Introduced by Sen. J. Cavanaugh) amends Nebraska’s election statute (rev. §49-1401) to define and prohibit deceptive, fraudulent deepfakes of candidates and to require conspicuous disclosures for synthetic media. It authorizes candidates to seek injunctive or other equitable relief through the courts to prohibit publication of prohibited deepfakes. Specified exceptions reference radio/television broadcasters, cable/satellite operators, int… 
LB615 (Introduced by Sen. J. Cavanaugh) amends Nebraska’s election statute (rev. §49-1401) to define and prohibit deceptive, fraudulent deepfakes of candidates and to require conspicuous disclosures for synthetic media. It authorizes candidates to seek injunctive or other equitable relief through the courts to prohibit publication of prohibited deepfakes. Specified exceptions reference radio/television broadcasters, cable/satellite operators, internet news outlets and periodicals when material is bona fide news, paid broadcasts with good-faith verification, federally required candidate advertising, or satire/parody. The bill cites “federal law” where applicable but does not name or create any state agency or department, nor does it include any changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations. The original §49-1401 is repealed.
Additions: Added provisions require deceptive audiovisual material to be labeled as "Image," "Video," or "Audio"; visual disclosures must be legible and for videos remain on screen the entire duration; audio disclosures must be clearly read at start, end, and at least every two minutes for recordings longer th… 
Added provisions require deceptive audiovisual material to be labeled as "Image," "Video," or "Audio"; visual disclosures must be legible and for videos remain on screen the entire duration; audio disclosures must be clearly read at start, end, and at least every two minutes for recordings longer than two minutes. Candidates harmed by deceptive deepfakes may seek injunctive or equitable relief. Exemptions cover radio/TV broadcasters (including cable/satellite operators, programmers, producers) airing such material as bona fide news coverage or when federal law requires airing candidate ads, paid broadcasts where the broadcaster made a good‑faith authenticity check, regularly published news outlets that disclose inaccuracies, and satire/parody. No specific government agencies or departments are named, and there are no changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

Summary: LB616 authorizes local authorities and law enforcement to enforce red‑light violations using automatic license plate reader (ALPR) systems subject to conditions. LB616 authorizes local authorities and law enforcement to enforce red‑light violations using automatic license plate reader (ALPR) systems subject to conditions. The Department (DMV) must approve driver's safety training curricula and fees and promulgate rules. Local authorities must offer violators a choice to pay a civil fee or attend an approved driver's safety training program; if the violator chooses training the program fee is waived. Red‑light violations enforced via ALPR will not generate points under the DMV point system and no warrant may issue for failure to pay or attend. Unpaid fees become a registration renewal block; the county treasurer collects and allocates fee proceeds to the county, local school system, school district, city, and village in the vehicle's tax district. The bill also expands statutorily permitted ALPR uses (e.g., identifying unregistered/uninsured or stolen vehicles) and limits admissibility of ALPR‑derived evidence to enforcement proceedings under the section.

[NOTE: Budget-related content may be missing from this summary. Please review manually.]
Additions: Added provisions authorize local authorities to enforce red‑light violations using automatic license plate reader systems if: the alleged violator may pay a fee or enter a driver's safety training program under pretrial diversion (sections 29‑3605 to 29‑3609); the training fee is waived; no DMV poin… 
Added provisions authorize local authorities to enforce red‑light violations using automatic license plate reader systems if: the alleged violator may pay a fee or enter a driver's safety training program under pretrial diversion (sections 29‑3605 to 29‑3609); the training fee is waived; no DMV points (per §60‑4,182) are assessed; and no warrant may issue for failure to pay or participate. Unpaid fees become a registration renewal hold—must be paid to the county treasurer per §60‑392. The county treasurer must allocate fee proceeds to the county, local school system/school district, city, and village in the vehicle’s tax district. Evidence from ALPRs is limited to enforcement of this section. No statewide appropriation or new agency created.

Summary: LB620 (2025) creates the Neighborhood Revitalization Act, authorizing district courts to bring in rem proceedings to declare deteriorated real property public nuisances, appoint receivers, and enforce abatement plans. LB620 (2025) creates the Neighborhood Revitalization Act, authorizing district courts to bring in rem proceedings to declare deteriorated real property public nuisances, appoint receivers, and enforce abatement plans. Key government actors: district courts (jurisdiction, plan approval, lien establishment, auction oversight), municipal corporations (inspection duties, may be petitioner, authorized to access and secure parcels and charge owners for costs, required to provide periodic updates), county registers' offices/registers of deeds and clerks (recording petitions, liens, and receiver deeds), and taxing authorities (receiver must satisfy delinquent property tax liens within 30 days; receiver's lien is first priority except for general property tax liens per §§77-203, 77-207). Receivers may pay outstanding municipal fines, penalties, and taxes. No line-item appropriations, funding changes, or new state budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds procedures giving courts (district courts) authority to proceed in rem against a “subject parcel” and to appoint receivers. Identifies municipal corporations (cities, towns, villages), county clerks, county register/register of deeds, and courts as key actors: municipal corporations must be not… 
Adds procedures giving courts (district courts) authority to proceed in rem against a “subject parcel” and to appoint receivers. Identifies municipal corporations (cities, towns, villages), county clerks, county register/register of deeds, and courts as key actors: municipal corporations must be notified, may inspect parcels, may access and secure parcels (costs charged to the owner), and must provide periodic updates to the court. Receiver powers include taking possession, paying operating costs, insurance, pre‑receivership mortgages, outstanding municipal fines/assessments and state/local taxes (delinquent property tax liens must be fully satisfied within 30 days). Receiver’s liens are first priority except for general property tax liens (refs. to sections 77‑203, 77‑207). Certification of prospective receivers occurs through the applicable court with financial and organizational documentation. No new appropriations or budget allocations are specified.

The bill assigns multiple responsibilities and funding changes to the Department of Economic Development (DED) and references the Department of Revenue (including the Tax Commissioner).

- DED: The Affordable Housing Trust Fund may finance community projects, the new Statewide Housing Assistance Program, and departmental expenses as appropriated. DED sets matching-fund requirements for for‑profit recipients, must allocate at least 30% of annual funds to each congressional district, announce ≥90‑day application periods, develop a qualified allocation plan prioritizing lowest‑income projects and homebuyers, may recapture unspent awards, and may contract for services. The Statewide Housing Assistance Program will be administered by a nonprofit contracted by DED, provide downpayment loans (lien, payable on title transfer) up to $30,000, and be subject to DED rules. DED must report detailed fund, budget, and program metrics annually, including deposits from section 76-903.

- Department of Revenue/Tax Commissioner: Tax Commissioner designs documentary stamp tax stamps; taxpayers may seek declaratory rulings from the Department of Revenue; the department will not overturn county assessor sale‑qualification determinations without review. Documentary stamp tax set at $2.55 per $1,000 with remittance: $0.50 retained by register; $1.25 to the Affordable Housing Trust Fund; $0.25 to Site and Building Development Fund; $0.25 to Homeless Shelter Assistance Trust Fund; $0.30 to Behavioral Health Services Fund.
Additions: Creates a Statewide Housing Assistance Program administered by a nonprofit contractor overseen by the Department of Economic Development. Creates a Statewide Housing Assistance Program administered by a nonprofit contractor overseen by the Department of Economic Development. The program provides statewide downpayment assistance as a loan (secured by a lien) repayable on transfer of title, capped at $30,000 per homebuyer. Eligibility and application rules are to be set by the department; priority goes to lowest‑income buyers and buyers in enterprise zones, federal opportunity zones, or areas declared extremely blighted. No provisions in the added text change Department of Revenue responsibilities, nor are specific appropriations, funding sources, or budget allocations specified.

- Register of Deeds: continues to require and forward prescribed statements to the county assessor; exceptions added so recorded easements and mineral leases generally need no statement except for conservation, preservation, and easements that seek the new recreational trail exemption.
- County Assessor & Property Tax Administrator: county assessors must process statements per instructions of the Property Tax Administrator and forward to the Tax Commissioner.
- State Records Administrator: retains records retention/disposition oversight.

Section 77‑202 is amended to add a property tax exemption for a portion of property as provided by the new Act. Operative date: January 1, 2026. No funding, appropriation, or budget allocations are included. Original sections are repealed.

Adds requirements that guidance address: alignment with public access and conservation goals; procedures for certifying the public benefit of qualifying easements (including connectivity to existing or planned trail systems); and methods to ensure ongoing compliance with the act’s public-purpose requirements. It also clarifies that easements (and a portion of taxpayer-owned property) may qualify for the property tax exemption under the Recreational Trail Easement Property Tax Exemption Act. No specific government agencies are named and no funding or appropriation changes are included.

LB629 creates the "County Initiative and Referendum Act," reserving initiative and referendum powers to the qualified electors of each Nebraska county. The Act governs use of initiative to enact and referendum to amend or repeal measures that affect county governance and that fall within the legislative authority of a county board. It defines "circulator" (person soliciting petition signatures) and "measure" (ordinance, charter provision, or resolution subject to county board authority) and expressly excludes actions authorized under the Nebraska Advantage Transformational Tourism and Redevelopment Act. No state agencies or departments beyond county boards are added or altered, and the bill contains no funding, appropriation, or budgetary provisions.
Additions: Creates the "County Initiative and Referendum Act," reserving initiative and referendum powers to qualified electors of each county and governing use of initiative to enact and referendum to amend or repeal county governance measures. Creates the "County Initiative and Referendum Act," reserving initiative and referendum powers to qualified electors of each county and governing use of initiative to enact and referendum to amend or repeal county governance measures. Defines "circulator" as anyone who solicits petition signatures and "measure" as any ordinance, charter provision, or resolution within a county board's legislative authority (subject to statutory exceptions). Explicitly excludes actions authorized by the Nebraska Advantage Transformational Tourism and Redevelopment Act. No state agencies beyond county boards are added and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes.

Appropriates $19,000,000 General Fund for FY2025-26 to the Department of Administrative Services (Program 245). DAS is directed to provide these funds to the Office of the Chief Information Officer to establish interoperable communications between state agencies and volunteer departments via portable/mobile radios, programming, installation, and training through a grant program. Eligibility is based on department needs/size. The CIO may not charge subscription, programming, or training fees to volunteer departments after receiving a grant. The Legislature intends all grant funds be distributed by June 30, 2028. The act takes effect immediately as an emergency measure.

Appropriates $19,000,000 General Fund for FY2025‑26 to the Department of Administrative Services (Program 245). DAS must pass these funds to the Office of the Chief Information Officer to fund a grant program that: (1) purchases and installs portable/mobile radios and associated programming to establish interoperable communications between state agencies and volunteer departments; and (2) provides training for interoperability with the Statewide Radio System. Grant eligibility is based on each volunteer department’s size and radio needs. Recipients may not be charged subscription, programming, or training fees after receiving a grant. Legislature intends all grant funds be distributed by June 30, 2028. Volunteer department defined per §35‑901.

LB631 amends §79-3111 to clarify administration and funding of the School Emergency Response Mapping Fund. The fund is administered by the Nebraska Department of Education, consists of legislative transfers and gifts/grants/bequests, and is to be used for grants to facilitate implementation of mapping data under §79-3110. Available funds are to be invested by the state investment officer pursuant to the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and the Nebraska State Funds Investment Act. The bill repeals the original section and takes effect immediately under an emergency clause.

LB632 requires health care facilities that perform elective abortions to provide individualized disposition of the remains of aborted unborn children by cremation or interment (burial). Summary: LB633 amends §79-239 and creates the Nebraska Option Enrollment Tuition Account Program. Key state entities: State Board of Education (board), State Department of Education, and the Commissioner of Education. Parents may appeal to the State Board (hearings unde… 
LB633 amends §79-239 and creates the Nebraska Option Enrollment Tuition Account Program. Key state entities: State Board of Education (board), State Department of Education, and the Commissioner of Education. Changes require rejecting school districts to send written notices specifying reasons, appeal procedures to the State Board, and the option to decline appeal and request a tuition account. Parents may appeal to the State Board (hearings under the Administrative Procedure Act; district bears burden on capacity defenses) or request an account, which the board must issue upon timely request. Districts must annually report rejected-application data to the State Department; the Commissioner compiles and electronically reports to the Legislature each September. The board may use up to 5% of scholarship account funds for program administration or contracting and may adopt rules. The bill repeals the original section and takes effect immediately as an emergency measure.
Additions: Creates the Nebraska Option Enrollment Tuition Account Program and assigns administrative duties to the State Board of Education. If a parent/guardian submits a request plus a copy of a public school district rejection notice to the Board within 30 days of notification, the Board must issue an optio… 
Creates the Nebraska Option Enrollment Tuition Account Program and assigns administrative duties to the State Board of Education. If a parent/guardian submits a request plus a copy of a public school district rejection notice to the Board within 30 days of notification, the Board must issue an option enrollment tuition account. Defines terms (Board, eligible student, parent, program). An eligible student meets compulsory attendance requirements if program conditions are met. Clarifies the State of Nebraska gains no additional authority over public, private, or denominational schools via the program. The Board may adopt rules and may use up to 5% of scholarship account funds for program administration or to contract with a third party.

Summary: LB634 establishes the Legislative Sunset Review Act, creating a Legislative Sunset Review Committee within the Legislature (members appointed by the Executive Board of the Legislative Council and including the Appropriations Committee chair). LB634 establishes the Legislative Sunset Review Act, creating a Legislative Sunset Review Committee within the Legislature (members appointed by the Executive Board of the Legislative Council and including the Appropriations Committee chair). The committee receives staff support from legislative divisions and staff, is chaired by elected committee members, and begins reviews in 2027 on a five‑year cycle. Reviewable entities must file detailed electronic reports with the Clerk of the Legislature (performance data, compliance, advisory committees, overlap/duplication, corrective actions including Auditor of Public Accounts findings, etc.). The committee may access records of reviewable entities, state agencies, and officers and request their assistance. The bill abolishes the Legislature’s Planning Committee, becomes operative January 1, 2026, and repeals specified obsolete statutes. No new appropriations or funding allocations are included.
Additions: Creates a Legislative Sunset Review Committee composed of the chair of the Appropriations Committee, five legislators appointed by the Executive Board of the Legislative Council (with geographic representation), and others; chair/vice-chair elected by the committee. Initial appointments begin as soo… 
Creates a Legislative Sunset Review Committee composed of the chair of the Appropriations Committee, five legislators appointed by the Executive Board of the Legislative Council (with geographic representation), and others; chair/vice-chair elected by the committee. Initial appointments begin as soon as possible after Jan 1, 2026; staff support comes from legislative divisions and staff. The committee must publish a review schedule on the Legislature's website, begin reviews in 2027, and review each "reviewable entity" every five years. Reviewable entities must electronically file detailed performance, budgetary, procurement (including small/minority business goals), advisory‑committee and compliance information with the Clerk of the Legislature; data must be validated by the entity's administrator. The committee may review costs, alternatives (including privatization), request assistance and records from state agencies/officers, and inspect files. References include the Auditor of Public Accounts, public records statutes (secs. 84‑712 to 84‑712.09) and the Open Meetings Act. No funding or appropriation changes are specified.

This bill expands the regulatory authority of the State Athletic Commissioner to include professional bare-knuckle mixed martial arts, professional mixed martial arts on ice, professional muay thai, amateur muay thai, and amateur kickboxing. It authorizes the commissioner to issue licenses (promoter fee $100–$300; referee $10–$40; matchmaker $10–$100; physicians/managers/judges/timekeepers/contestants $10–$20), require bonds (amateur minimum $1,000; professional minimum $5,000), and collect a tax of 5% on gross receipts (including 5% of television rights) for covered events. The commissioner may adopt rules, limit events, suspend or fine licensees (administrative fines remitted to the State Treasurer), implement a banned-substances list and testing, and impose escalating penalties for violations (first offense up to $1,500 or 40% of purse; second up to $3,000 or 70%; third up to $5,000 or 100% and possible lifetime suspension). Original sections are repealed.

Summary: LB636 allows counties to seek state reimbursement for medical services provided to county jail inmates. LB636 allows counties to seek state reimbursement for medical services provided to county jail inmates. It assigns the Jail Standards Board authority to receive and determine eligibility of county reimbursement claims (certified by county boards), require supporting information, audit county records (at least every two years), promulgate rules, and request warrants from the State Treasurer to pay approved amounts to county treasurers (credited to county general funds). Claims must be filed within 45 days after each quarter-end; claims caused by jail or employee negligence, recklessness, or intentional misconduct are ineligible. The Legislature caps annual appropriations for the Jail Standards Board’s eligible criminal court cost reimbursement at $21 million beginning FY2025-26. The bill also amends sheriffs’ fee provisions (33-117) and distress-warrant fee/commission rules (77-1720), including mileage and minimum charges, and takes effect immediately due to an emergency clause.
Additions: Adds procedural and funding rules centering on the Jail Standards Board and county officials. Key points: - Counties must submit certified reimbursement claims to the Jail Standards Board within 45 days after each quarterly period; late claims are ineligible. - If approved, the Jail Standards Board… 
Adds procedural and funding rules centering on the Jail Standards Board and county officials. Key points:
- Counties must submit certified reimbursement claims to the Jail Standards Board within 45 days after each quarterly period; late claims are ineligible.
- If approved, the Jail Standards Board requests a warrant from the State Treasurer to pay the county treasurer; amounts credit the county general fund.
- The Jail Standards Board has sole authority to determine eligible medical costs, may obtain additional information, audit county records at least biennially, promulgate rules, and will not reimburse costs caused by jail/county negligence or misconduct.
- Beginning FY2025‑26, legislative appropriations for the Jail Standards Board’s eligible criminal court cost reimbursements are capped at $25 million annually.
- County sheriffs may charge fees for additional officers serving a warrant (minimum $10), not to exceed existing rate limits.

This bill amends the Nitrogen Reduction Incentive Act and tasks the Nebraska Department of Natural Resources (DNR) with administering the program, with authority to collaborate with natural resources districts. DNR must (1) determine per‑acre incentive rates (not less than $10/acre) and review targets biennially, and (2) apply for a $25 million grant from the Nebraska Environmental Trust Fund payable as five $5 million annual installments; if awarded, proceeds are remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Nitrogen Reduction Incentive Cash Fund. DNR must establish a subaccount for Trust funds, report monthly interest to the State Treasurer (who transfers a like amount back to the Trust), may apply for other grants (credited to the cash fund), and funds are invested by the state investment officer. The Act now terminates December 31, 2030, and takes effect immediately.
Additions: Creates a requirement that the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) apply, before the FY2025‑26 application deadline, for a $25 million grant from the Nebraska Environmental Trust Fund, payable in five $5 million annual installments. If awarded, the grant proceeds are to be remitted to the State Tr… 
Creates a requirement that the Department of Natural Resources (DNR) apply, before the FY2025‑26 application deadline, for a $25 million grant from the Nebraska Environmental Trust Fund, payable in five $5 million annual installments. If awarded, the grant proceeds are to be remitted to the State Treasurer and credited to the Nitrogen Reduction Incentive Cash Fund to support projects consistent with that fund's purposes. DNR must establish a subaccount in the Nitrogen Reduction Incentive Cash Fund to track grant receipts. Monthly, DNR will calculate interest earned on that subaccount and notify the State Treasurer, who will transfer an equal amount from the Nitrogen Reduction Incentive Cash Fund back to the Nebraska Environmental Trust Fund. No other appropriations are specified.

LB640 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §47‑502 to modify good‑time credit for persons confined in city or county jails, including those serving custodial sanctions following parole or probation violations. After the 15th day of confinement, the bill makes the aggregate remaining term—explicitly including the sum of any consecutive sentences received at or during confinement—eligible for reduction at a rate of one day for each day without a breach of discipline or jail regulation violation. The original section 47‑502 is repealed. No state agencies, appropriations, or budgetary allocations are specified.

LB641 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §68-919 concerning Medicaid estate recovery by the Department of Health and Human Services. It reaffirms the department's authority to recover medical-assistance payments from a recipient's estate (held in abeyance until spouse/qualified children conditions lapse), limits foreclosure in specified sibling/adult-child caregiving situations (allowing physician attestation), permits the department to certify whether reimbursement is due upon application and to release estate property accordingly, allows admission of department payment records in probate, authorizes waiver or compromise of claims for hardship, and preserves recovery rights from third-party tort recoveries with pro rata contribution to attorney fees. No funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes are included.

Adds standards limiting estate recovery and lien foreclosure for Medicaid recipients: DHHS must accept a physician's written attestation that a sibling, adult child, or other relative provided care that delayed the recipient's institutional admission — such attestation is sufficient to (1) prevent foreclosure on the lien described and (2) exclude a retained life‑estate interest in real estate (if the life estate was recorded ≥12 months earlier and the relative resided solely and continuously with the recipient and satisfies the department). Clarifies that care may be reimbursed or unreimbursed. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB642 (Artificial Intelligence Consumer Protection Act) empowers the Nebraska Attorney General to investigate compliance: during an investigation the AG may require deployers or contracted third parties to produce risk‑management policies, impact assessments, and related records within 90 days, review them for compliance, and treat disclosed materials as nonpublic (allowing trade‑secret designation). The bill permits cooperation with law enforcement and requires compliance with subpoenas and government inquiries. LB643 allows a taxpayer to appeal to the Department of Revenue asserting that their single‑family residential property was offered for sale at fair market value for at least 90 days with no good‑faith offers. If the Department of Revenue sustains the appeal, the taxpayer may claim Nebraska income tax deductions for interest, taxes paid on, or maintenance of that property. The bill contains no provisions altering Department of Revenue funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.
Additions: Adds exceptions and an appeal process administered by the Department of Revenue: individuals generally cannot claim Nebraska income tax deductions for interest, taxes, or maintenance on single-family residential property except for (a) their principal residence, (b) property owned by qualified nonpr… 
Adds exceptions and an appeal process administered by the Department of Revenue: individuals generally cannot claim Nebraska income tax deductions for interest, taxes, or maintenance on single-family residential property except for (a) their principal residence, (b) property owned by qualified nonprofits, or (c) owners who sold at least 10% of their single-family holdings during the year to owner-occupants or 5% to first-time homebuyers. It allows a taxpayer to appeal to the Department of Revenue showing a property was offered at fair market rate for 90 days with no good-faith offers; a successful appeal permits those deductions. No funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes are included.

The Attorney General will require registration, maintain public records, run a public portal, transmit filings to the U.S. Secretary of State, issue civil investigative demands, adopt rules, and report semiannually to the Legislature. The Nebraska Accountability and Disclosure Commission Cash Fund is amended to receive specified fees and penalties; funds may be invested and transferred to the General Fund. Adds extensive duties for the Nebraska Attorney General: registration, retention, public posting and transmission of registrants' filings to the U.S. Secretary of State, sharing information with state and federal agencies, operating a public portal (per section 12), issuing civil investigative demands, adopting rules, and reporting biannually to the Legislature. Summary: This bill amends retirement funding and benefit provisions and names responsible state actors. This bill amends retirement funding and benefit provisions and names responsible state actors. Key agency roles:
- Retirement Board and its actuary: certify state deposits and determine required transfers to the School Retirement Fund and Service Annuity Fund; administrator of Class V systems must provide member data.
- Director of Administrative Services and State Treasurer: execute certified state transfers/appropriations to the School Retirement Fund.
- State investment officer: invest Service Annuity Fund assets.
- Legislature/Appropriations Committee: may review and authorize additional transfers to Class V district systems.

Funding changes:
- Employee contribution to the School Retirement Fund becomes a tiered rate (7.25%–9.75%) effective July 1, 2025 based on funded ratio.
- State contribution to the School Retirement Fund becomes tiered (0%–2% of payroll) from July 1, 2025 based on funded ratio.
- State continues targeted transfers to Class V district funds and the Service Annuity Fund to pay normal cost and amortize unfunded liabilities; additional transfers require legislative approval.

Nebraska State Patrol: survivor benefits increase from 75% to 100% of the officer’s annuity beginning July 1, 2027 in applicable circumstances. The act is effective on passage due to an emergency clause.
Additions: Adds required state transfers and new contribution formulas for school retirement plans and survivor benefits. Key agencies/entities: the State, Class V school districts and their retirement systems, the School Retirement Fund, and the retirement board (annual actuarial valuation per §84-1503). Fund… 
Adds required state transfers and new contribution formulas for school retirement plans and survivor benefits. Key agencies/entities: the State, Class V school districts and their retirement systems, the School Retirement Fund, and the retirement board (annual actuarial valuation per §84-1503). Funding changes:
- Beginning July 1, 2025, employee contribution rates to the School Retirement Fund are tiered by funded ratio: 9.75%, 8.75%, 8.00%, or 7.25% of compensation.
- State deposits into the School Retirement Fund are tiered by funded ratio: 2.0% of member compensation if <96%; 0.7% if 96%–<100%; none at ≥100%. Transfers to Class V district retirement systems are to be made annually by July 1. Legislature states these state transfers do not assume district funding liabilities.
- Survivor annuity benefits changed to 100% of officer’s annuity to surviving spouse and dependent children beginning July 1, 2027.

Summary: LB64 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §44-3614 to revise eligibility and premium rules for Medicare supplement policies. LB64 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §44-3614 to revise eligibility and premium rules for Medicare supplement policies. It allows insurers to vary premiums for persons under 65 who are eligible for Medicare due to disability, provided differences are actuarially sound and not unfairly discriminatory, and caps the under-65 premium at no more than 150% of the premium for a similarly situated 65‑year‑old. It also provides that an individual under 65 who is eligible for a Medicare supplement because of disability becomes subject to the same open enrollment rules applicable to age‑65 enrollees beginning the first day of the first month in which the individual turns 65. The bill repeals the original section. No state agencies or departments are named, and there are no appropriations or budget changes included.

The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission must collaborate with the Departments of Agriculture and Revenue and DHHS on cultivation, processing, manufacture, distribution, transport, testing, and sale. Department of Correctional Services (DCS) employees and jail staff are ineligible for medical cannabis licenses; persons sentenced to DCS for controlled‑substances violations must attend drug‑abuse treatment and counseling while incarcerated. LB655 creates statutory conscience-based objection rights for health care providers and payors and designates enforcement and reporting pathways to government agencies. Complaints may be filed with the Attorney General; providers may also report to "the department," any state agency charged with protecting medical conscience, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, or the Office for Civil Rights. The Attorney General may investigate (administer oaths, take depositions, issue subpoenas), commence civil actions for damages or injunctive relief, award attorney's fees, and adopt rules to implement enforcement. The bill preserves EMTALA and state emergency-treatment obligations. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds a “right of medical conscience” allowing health care providers and payors to opt out of providing or paying for specific services on conscience grounds. It authorizes disclosures and complaints to employers, the Attorney General, “the department,” any state agency charged with protecting medica… 
Adds a “right of medical conscience” allowing health care providers and payors to opt out of providing or paying for specific services on conscience grounds. It authorizes disclosures and complaints to employers, the Attorney General, “the department,” any state agency charged with protecting medical conscience, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (including the Office for Civil Rights), or other federal agencies. The Attorney General may investigate, adopt implementing rules, issue subpoenas, take depositions, compel evidence and witnesses, and commence civil actions for damages, injunctive relief and attorney’s fees. EMTALA emergency-treatment obligations remain unaffected. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

- Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS): required to pursue all SNAP options to maximize federal funding and minimize General Fund use, hire necessary personnel, and submit an annual report to the Health and Human Services Committee (due Dec. 1) detailing options, actions, caseload, costs and expenditures. DHHS must develop a state outreach plan meeting Food and Nutrition Service (USDA) criteria, may accept gifts/grants/donations, partner with counties/nonprofits, contract to allow costs to be paid from private or federal funds, submit the plan to FNS and request federal matching funds, and may be exempt from implementing the plan if insufficient private/federal funds. DHHS shall create a TANF-funded policy to establish categorical eligibility and temporarily raise gross income limits to 165% of OMB poverty guidelines until Oct. 1, 2025, and must annually report evaluations, administrative cost impacts, and federal funding availability to the HHS Committee and Legislative Fiscal Analyst. DHHS also must not seek SNAP work‑requirement waivers and must assign eligible 16–59 year olds to employment and training programs.

- Department of Labor: SNAP Next Step Program participation is encouraged for SNAP households with income between 131%–165% of OMB poverty guidelines (subject to program availability); the Legislature intends that the Department of Labor not use General Funds for these processes and that participation depend on available federal funds.

- Department of Agriculture: Prohibited from seeking, applying for, accepting, or renewing any SNAP work‑requirement waivers (7 U.S.C. 2015(o)) and from using the federal exemption option in 7 U.S.C. 2015(o)(6)(E), except where federal law expressly requires.

No appropriations, funding increases, or budget allocations are included.

LB657 amends the Nebraska Criminal Code (section 28-101) to create the offense of "assault on a sports official." It defines "athletic contest" and "sports official" (including those duly registered by local, state, regional, or national organizations that provide training). The offense is committed when a person intentionally or knowingly causes bodily injury to a sports official immediately before, during, or after an athletic contest, and is classified as a Class IV felony. Referred to the Judiciary Committee. No agencies, departments, or budget appropriations are named or altered, and the bill contains no funding changes.

Adds definitions for "athletic contest" and "sports official" (including those registered with local, state, regional, or national organizations that provide education/training). Establishes the offense of assault on a sports official when a person intentionally or knowingly causes bodily injury to such an official immediately before, during, or after an athletic contest, with knowledge (or reasonable awareness) that the victim is a sports official. Classifies the offense as a Class IV felony. No specific government agencies or departments are named, and there are no funding, appropriation, or budget changes.

The bill amends the Nebraska Pure Food Act to assign powers and duties to the Department of Agriculture and explicitly authorizes the department to investigate all credible complaints that food products are misbranded or falsely advertised as meat products. Creates definitions for "agricultural food animal" and for various "manufactured‑protein" products (cultivated-, insect-, and plant‑protein) and defines "identifying meat term" and "qualifying term." Establishes labeling and storage rules that can render a manufactured‑protein product misbranded or falsely advertised—e.g., requiring a conspicuous qualifying term near any meat-identifying term and physical separation/distinctive shelf tags when offered at food establishments. Summary: Bill LB659 amends the Election Act to impose procedural and reporting duties on election commissioners and county clerks using vote-counting devices. Bill LB659 amends the Election Act to impose procedural and reporting duties on election commissioners and county clerks using vote-counting devices. They must run three independent pre-count accuracy tests (by the commissioner/clerk, a chief deputy or opposite‑party registered voter, and the device installer/operator). Commissioners/clerks must certify test completion dates and provide anticipated completion dates and a written election‑day procedures plan to the Secretary of State (SoS); the SoS must post certifications online. County central committees supply watcher credentials (one per party); watchers/observers must comply with section 32‑1525. The bill also clarifies device security, ballot handling, storage of device media, and procedural limits on early tabulation. No funding or appropriations are included.
Additions: Adds pre-count testing and reporting requirements involving local election officials and the Secretary of State. Election commissioners or county clerks must run at least three independent tests of vote‑counting devices (including the installed counting program) before counting begins, conducted by:… 
Adds pre-count testing and reporting requirements involving local election officials and the Secretary of State. Election commissioners or county clerks must run at least three independent tests of vote‑counting devices (including the installed counting program) before counting begins, conducted by: (a) the election commissioner/county clerk; (b) the chief deputy or a registered voter of a different party; and (c) the installer or device operator. Each political party may appoint one watcher via the county central committee; other observers only as authorized. Watchers/observers must meet section 32‑1525 rules and cannot be excluded unless an unobstructed CCTV (or similar) view is provided. County officials must certify testing completion (and provide an anticipated completion date) to the Secretary of State, who will post the certification on the Secretary of State website. No funding or appropriation changes are included.

LB65 affects DHHS and the Department of Correctional Services (DCS). For DHHS, the bill retains authority to accept juveniles into temporary care/custody when secure detention is unnecessary (sec. 43‑254), requires DHHS to pay costs of a committed juvenile’s support, study, or treatment not covered by the parent (sec. 43‑290), and keeps existing procedures for remitting support payments and agency transfers to the Director of Administrative Services. Placements in state (non‑adult) institutions are charged to the committing county on a per‑diem set by the institution head. For DCS, the Nebraska Crime Victim Fund may, when available, transfer certified amounts to the DCS Facility Cash Fund (and the Supreme Court Automation Cash Fund) to pay initial implementation costs of Laws 2010, LB510; distributions revert after reimbursement (sec. 33‑157). No new appropriations or specific budget line items are established.
Additions: Summary (focus: Dept. of Correctional Services, Dept. of Health and Human Services) - The added language exempts any "individual described in section 1 of this act" from court- and program-related fees and costs across multiple statutory provisions: probation fees, court costs, laboratory/sample co… 
Summary (focus: Dept. of Correctional Services, Dept. of Health and Human Services)

- The added language exempts any "individual described in section 1 of this act" from court- and program-related fees and costs across multiple statutory provisions: probation fees, court costs, laboratory/sample collection fees, juvenile pretrial diversion and filing fees, and other local program participation fees.  
- For Department of Correctional Services implications: probation-related fees and fees for participation in non‑probation programs may not be imposed on these individuals, shifting any otherwise chargeable fees to counties (fees "shall be paid by the county" in some instances). This likely reduces fee revenue and shifts costs to county budgets; no DCS appropriation is provided.  
- For Department of Health and Human Services implications: courts may inquire about existing health coverage for juveniles and may order parents/guardians to continue paying deductibles if coverage exists, but the bill does not create new DHHS funding or appropriations.  
- No explicit changes to state appropriations or direct budget allocations for DCS or DHHS are included.

Highlights regarding specified agencies:

- Department of Administrative Services (DAS)/State Building Division: DAS oversight is expanded—authorized agencies must obtain approval from the Director of Administrative Services before executing design‑build or construction manager‑general contractor contracts; the state building division must adopt procurement guidelines and will adjust statutory dollar thresholds (currently $100,000) for construction every four years using a construction‑cost index. The division retains facilities planning, construction, and administration duties, remits rental proceeds to the State Building Revolving Fund and State Building Renewal Assessment Fund, and administers the State Emergency Capital Construction Contingency Fund.

- Department of Transportation (DOT): The Division of Aeronautics (DOT) must create and maintain a List of Secure Drones Authorized for Purchase by Jan 1, 2026, and, effective Jan 1, 2027, only drones cleared by that list may be purchased; state funds are prohibited for purchases of drones excluded by the list.

- Department of Correctional Services (DCS): Buildings and grounds owned, leased, or operated by DCS are exempt from certain DAS facilities‑administration provisions (maintenance, custodial, security, parking, and related duties).

Summary of added provisions affecting specified agencies:

- Department of Administrative Services (DAS): Authorized agencies must obtain DAS (or designee) approval before executing design‑build or construction manager–general contractor contracts; DAS’s State Building Division will adopt procurement guidelines and DAS must adjust specified dollar‑amount thresholds for inflation every four years using a construction‑cost index. DAS is listed as a consulting party for the Secure Drone Purchasing Act and may be asked to provide reports to legislative committees.

- Department of Transportation (DOT): The Division of Aeronautics must create and maintain a "List of Secure Drones Authorized for Purchase" by Jan 1, 2026, and will clear devices under the Secure Drone Purchasing Act. Effective Jan 1, 2027, state agencies and, practicably, political subdivisions may only acquire drones cleared by the division; state funds are prohibited for purchases of unapproved drones.

- Department of Correctional Services (DCS): Not specifically named; it would be subject as an "authorized agency" to DAS approval requirements for alternative contracting and to the drone purchase prohibitions.

- Funding/appropriations: No new appropriations. Key fiscal changes: DAS indexing of dollar thresholds and an explicit ban on using state funds after Jan 1, 2027 to buy unapproved drones.

Summary: This bill assigns specific duties to state entities regarding retirement-system investments. This bill assigns specific duties to state entities regarding retirement-system investments. Key agency actions:

- Nebraska Investment Council (appointed members): deemed fiduciaries for statewide retirement-system assets; must follow prudent-investor standards, avoid investments whose sole/primary objective is economic or social development, and must not engage with designated "restricted entities." Upon publication of a restricted-entity list, the council must identify and divest related holdings as soon as practicable.

- State investment officer: subject to the same restricted-entity prohibition for Public Employees Retirement Board assets; must follow Nebraska Investment Council directions; file monthly operational reports (within 15 days) to the Governor, State Treasurer, Auditor of Public Accounts, Department of Administrative Services, and council; and provide semiannual electronic reports to the Legislative Nebraska Retirement Systems Committee and Clerk detailing restricted-entity holdings (first due Jan 15, 2026).

- State Treasurer: must publish a list of restricted entities by Oct 1, 2025, and update it at least every six months.

No appropriations or funding changes are included. The act takes effect upon approval (emergency declared).
Additions: Added duties and restrictions for retirement-system investing: appointed members of the council and the state investment officer (for systems administered by the Public Employees Retirement Board) are prohibited from investing in "restricted entities" and must identify and divest any existing holdin… 
Added duties and restrictions for retirement-system investing: appointed members of the council and the state investment officer (for systems administered by the Public Employees Retirement Board) are prohibited from investing in "restricted entities" and must identify and divest any existing holdings "as soon as practicable" after the State Treasurer publishes the restricted-entity list. The State Treasurer (or designee) must create and publish that list by October 1, 2025, and update it at least semiannually. The definition references multiple federal lists and agencies (Office of Foreign Assets Control/Treasury, Department of Defense, Commerce (Entity/Denied/Unverified/Military End User lists), FCC, Department of Homeland Security, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, SEC, and federal presidential executive orders). The state investment officer must file semiannual electronic reports to the Nebraska Retirement Systems Committee of the Legislature and the Clerk of the Legislature (first due Jan 15, 2026). No funding or appropriation changes are included.

LB662 requires each state agency to produce a federal funding inventory detailing federal receipts and related obligations. Required elements include: amounts and sources (grant/program names); purposes of the receipts; positions and other resources obligated by each award; citations to applicable federal law, regulation, or grant provisions; an operating plan if federal receipts fall by 10% or more from the prior fiscal year; the specific actions or results the agency promised to receive funds; the state statutory objective served; and a schedule of receipts with foreseeable end dates. The bill applies to every state agency; it does not itself create or change appropriations or budget allocations.

Agencies must identify positions and other resources/obligations tied to each federal award and cite the governing federal law/regulation or grant provision. Adds reporting requirements for state agencies receiving federal funds. Agencies must identify positions and other resources/obligations tied to each federal award and cite the governing federal law/regulation or grant provision. They must also provide: (e) an operating plan if federal receipts drop 10%+ from the prior year; (f) a detailed description of actions/results promised to obtain the federal receipts; (g) the state statutory objective served by accepting the funds; and (h) a list of federal receipts with foreseeable end dates and the expected schedule of receipts. No new appropriations or budget allocations are specified.

Summary: LB663 amends county planning law (section 23‑114.01). Key agency-related changes: - Requires each county planning commission member and each county board member to complete two hours of role‑specific education per term, developed and presented by the respective county attorney. - Establishes procedural deadlines for the county planning commission and county board to determine application completeness (30 days), to notify applicants of deficienci… 
LB663 amends county planning law (section 23‑114.01). Key agency-related changes:

- Requires each county planning commission member and each county board member to complete two hours of role‑specific education per term, developed and presented by the respective county attorney.
- Establishes procedural deadlines for the county planning commission and county board to determine application completeness (30 days), to notify applicants of deficiencies (within 10 days), to re‑determine completeness after additional materials (30 days), and to grant/deny or recommend decisions within 90 days of a complete application.
- Requires commissions/boards to issue written factual findings supporting conditional use/special exception decisions and presumes applicants will comply with applicable local, state, and federal requirements (burden of proof on challengers).
- Retains appeal routes to the county board or district court as presently structured.

No changes to state funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Creates procedures involving county-level bodies and other agencies: requires each county commissioner and county board member to complete two hours per term of role-specific education developed and presented by the county attorney. Clarifies that planning commissions and county boards must base con… 
Creates procedures involving county-level bodies and other agencies: requires each county commissioner and county board member to complete two hours per term of role-specific education developed and presented by the county attorney. Clarifies that planning commissions and county boards must base conditional use permits/special exceptions solely on county zoning, may not condition approval on obtaining other federal, state, or local permits, and do not relieve applicants of separate permit obligations to those agencies. Establishes a presumption the applicant will comply with local, state, and federal requirements (burden on challenger). Sets deadlines: planning commission — 30 days to check completeness, 10-day notice if incomplete, 30 days after supplemental info, and 90 days to decide or recommend; county board follows analogous 30/10/30/90 timelines. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Summary: LB664 amends Nebraska’s Administrative Procedure Act to change how state agencies handle rulemaking and legal challenges. Agencies must solicit public comment before notice publication and must allow any person to submit supportive or opposing comments or materials electronically or by mail without requiring in-person travel. In rule challenges, the petition for declaratory judgment must be filed in district court (county of petitioner’s residenc… 
LB664 amends Nebraska’s Administrative Procedure Act to change how state agencies handle rulemaking and legal challenges. Agencies must solicit public comment before notice publication and must allow any person to submit supportive or opposing comments or materials electronically or by mail without requiring in-person travel. In rule challenges, the petition for declaratory judgment must be filed in district court (county of petitioner’s residence, principal business, Lancaster County, or the county of the agency’s headquarters), and the agency is required to be a party to the proceeding. Courts may invalidate rules that are unconstitutional, exceed an agency’s statutory authority, or were adopted without required statutory procedures (excluding the Negotiated Rulemaking Act). Agencies are prohibited from restricting venue. The bill takes effect immediately; no funding or appropriation changes are included.
Additions: Adds procedural protections for "agency" rulemaking: agencies must allow any person to submit comments for or against proposed rules, accept submissions electronically or by mail, and may not require in-person travel. Judicial petitions challenging agency action may be filed in district court in the… 
Adds procedural protections for "agency" rulemaking: agencies must allow any person to submit comments for or against proposed rules, accept submissions electronically or by mail, and may not require in-person travel. Judicial petitions challenging agency action may be filed in district court in the petitioner’s county of residence, the petitioner’s principal place of business, Lancaster County, or the county where the agency has its headquarters. Agencies are prohibited from restricting venue contrary to this section. No agencies are newly created and no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are changed.

Summary — LB665 (2025)

LB665 amends the Animal Health and Disease Control Act. It (1) adopts by reference federal animal disease traceability rules (9 C.F.R. part 86, as of Jan. 1, 2020) and authorizes the Nebraska Department of Agriculture to employ USDA APHIS Veterinary Services program standards for disease prevention and control; (2) defines "foreign adversary" by reference to 15 C.F.R. 791.4 (as of Jan. 1, 2025); (3) prohibits use in Nebraska of electronic identification devices manufactured by entities with direct or indirect ties to such foreign adversaries and bars the Department of Agriculture from requiring foreign‑manufactured electronic ID devices; and (4) restates related legislative findings. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Defines "foreign adversary" by reference to 15 C.F.R. 791.4 (as of Jan 1, 2025). Establishes Nebraska policy: protect and conserve livestock, prioritize private property rights over government bureaucracy, and treat foreign actors using surveillance tech against livestock production as a security th… 
Defines "foreign adversary" by reference to 15 C.F.R. 791.4 (as of Jan 1, 2025). Establishes Nebraska policy: protect and conserve livestock, prioritize private property rights over government bureaucracy, and treat foreign actors using surveillance tech against livestock production as a security threat. Prohibits application of any electronic identification device for livestock if manufactured by an entity with direct or indirect ties to a foreign adversary. Further bars "the department" (the state agency administering animal identification) from requiring use of foreign‑manufactured electronic animal identification devices to identify or track livestock. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Summary: LB666 amends §86‑1505 (Rural Communications Sustainability Act), directing the Nebraska Public Service Commission (PSC) to act expeditiously, upon request by an incumbent or competitive provider after a granting agency’s final payment under a broadband deployment program, to: (1) relieve the incumbent carrier of eligible telecommunications carrier (ETC) and carrier‑of‑last‑resort (COLR) obligations in the affected deployment project area if the g… 
LB666 amends §86‑1505 (Rural Communications Sustainability Act), directing the Nebraska Public Service Commission (PSC) to act expeditiously, upon request by an incumbent or competitive provider after a granting agency’s final payment under a broadband deployment program, to: (1) relieve the incumbent carrier of eligible telecommunications carrier (ETC) and carrier‑of‑last‑resort (COLR) obligations in the affected deployment project area if the granting agency found the competitive provider compliant; (2) — consistent with PSC procedural rules — determine allocations and distributions of support from the Nebraska Telecommunications Universal Service Fund for that area; and (3) coordinate with the Federal Communications Commission and consult the carriers to decide whether ETC/COLR obligations tied to Nebraska Universal Service Fund support should transfer to the competitive provider. The bill repeals the original section. No specific appropriations or dollar amounts are included.

Summary: LB667 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §60‑1438 (Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act) to revise warranty compensation and dispute procedures. It creates a formula and audit process for determining dealer compensation for parts (dealer-submitted repair orders, manufacturer audit, 45-day effective period), defines "fair wholesale value," limits burdensome documentation requirements, and allows manufacturers/distributors to request up to 100 additional repa… 
LB667 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §60‑1438 (Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act) to revise warranty compensation and dispute procedures. It creates a formula and audit process for determining dealer compensation for parts (dealer-submitted repair orders, manufacturer audit, 45-day effective period), defines "fair wholesale value," limits burdensome documentation requirements, and allows manufacturers/distributors to request up to 100 additional repair orders to verify declared rates. The bill expressly assigns the manufacturer the burden to justify denials and authorizes dealer complaints to the board under the Act; the board may find unreasonable denials to violate the Act and enforce remedies. It also clarifies recall, claim‑submission, payment, audit, chargeback, and appeal timelines, extends coverage to separately warranted components, and excludes recreational vehicles. No appropriations or funding changes are made.
Additions: No government agencies or departments are mentioned and there are no funding, appropriations, or budget changes. No government agencies or departments are mentioned and there are no funding, appropriations, or budget changes.

Summary of added provisions:
- When calculating parts compensation, only retail sales unrelated to warranty repairs may be used; markups for parts on recommended maintenance (oil, filters, fluids, brakes, spark plugs, wipers, tires, etc.) cannot be used. The Motor Vehicle Industry Regulation Act is cited as governing denials.
- If a franchisor supplies a part free or at reduced cost for warranty work, the franchisor must pay the dealer the dealer’s cost plus the dealer’s markup, computed using the part’s “fair wholesale value” (the greatest of dealer cost, franchisor price-schedule cost, or cost of a substantially identical franchisor-listed part).
- Manufacturers/distributors may request up to 100 additional repair orders (from a dealer-selected 90‑day period within the prior 12 months) to review labor/markup rates, may adjust warranty payment rates if nonwarranty rates are lower, and dealers have 30 days to rebut. Such requests cannot occur more than once per 12 months.
- Parties may mutually agree on rates.

Summary: LB668 amends multiple statutes involving the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). LB668 amends multiple statutes involving the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS). Key provisions referencing DHHS:

- DHHS must notify subjects of adult- and child-protection investigations of the right to contest and may amend/expunge identifying information or remove substantiated reports; subjects cannot be entered on registries while a timely appeal is pending and final DHHS order is outstanding.
- DHHS maintains the central registry of child protection cases, will cross-reference court-ordered name changes, and must report annually to the Governor and legislative committee chairs on minor-subject entries.
- DHHS may charge a records-check fee (not to exceed $5), remit receipts to the State Treasurer for credit to the Health and Human Services Cash Fund, waive fees for hardship, and use fees to defray records-check costs.
- Case managers for DHHS juvenile custody and voluntary cases must be DHHS employees, except prevention cases may use contracted providers.
Additions: Department of Health and Human Services must notify any person before entering them on adult or child protection registries of their right to contest. A subject has 14 calendar days after the department’s determination notice to appeal; if a proper appeal is filed, the department may not enter the p… 
Department of Health and Human Services must notify any person before entering them on adult or child protection registries of their right to contest. A subject has 14 calendar days after the department’s determination notice to appeal; if a proper appeal is filed, the department may not enter the person’s name on the registry until a final departmental order is issued. Appeals proceed under the Administrative Procedure Act. The bill also allows a case manager for “prevention cases” to be a contracted provider and defines a prevention case as one where (1) at least one juvenile meets the department’s “candidate for foster care” criteria under the Families First Prevention Services Act (section 471(e)(4)), (2) ongoing child welfare services are not required to keep the child safe, and (3) the family voluntarily engages community services. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
