Summary: The bill references the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) in several specific duties: it defines "hospital" as an institution licensed by DHHS under the Health Care Facility Licensure Act; requires that DHHS publish printed informational materials (including alternatives to abortion and instructions for finding immediate medical assistance after taking mifepristone) which physicians must notify patients about; directs DHHS to compile… 
The bill references the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) in several specific duties: it defines "hospital" as an institution licensed by DHHS under the Health Care Facility Licensure Act; requires that DHHS publish printed informational materials (including alternatives to abortion and instructions for finding immediate medical assistance after taking mifepristone) which physicians must notify patients about; directs DHHS to compile and maintain a geographically arranged list of providers/facilities offering ultrasounds (noting those offering free services) for physicians to furnish on request; and makes civil liability for failure to inform about those printed materials contingent on DHHS having published and made them available. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Adds requirements that licensed health personnel must privately ask and evaluate pregnant women about coercion to have an abortion, interpersonal/domestic violence, and human trafficking; post the national domestic violence and human trafficking hotline numbers in a manner that ensures privacy; and,… 
Adds requirements that licensed health personnel must privately ask and evaluate pregnant women about coercion to have an abortion, interpersonal/domestic violence, and human trafficking; post the national domestic violence and human trafficking hotline numbers in a manner that ensures privacy; and, if a woman discloses coercion or victimization, provide those numbers and offer a confidential telephone call. Staff must document that the questions were asked and that hotline information and call opportunity were offered. For the Department of Health and Human Services, this creates new compliance, licensing, training, and oversight duties to enforce these requirements. No new funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included in the added text.

LB66 adopts the Uniform Health‑Care Decisions Act, establishing statewide rules for advance health‑care directives, powers of attorney for health care, default surrogates, capacity determinations, and guardianship interactions. Government entities affected include Nebraska courts (timelines and standards for hearings, capacity findings, and guardian authority), health‑care institutions and their medical records administrators (duty to document directives and transfer patients when refusing care), and responsible health‑care professionals (notification duties, ability to require surrogate declarations, and permitted refusals). Nursing homes and assisted‑living facilities are referenced by statutory definition (including the Social Security Act nursing‑facility definition and section 71‑5903), with owner/operator/employee status affecting surrogate eligibility. Emergency medical responders receive a limited liability carve‑out. No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Adds definitions and procedures for advance health-care directives, powers of attorney, default surrogates, capacity determinations, and rights/remedies. Government entities referenced: the federal Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. §1396r(a)(1)) for the nursing home definition; state courts/judicial branch for findings of capacity, guardianship actions, and related hearings; and state licensing/certification authorities implicitly referenced for “health‑care institutions” and assisted‑living facilities (see cross‑reference to section 71‑5903). Also references emergency medical responders and the role of guardians appointed by courts. No specific changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Beginning January 1, 2020, the department shall use the Nebraska Early Childhood Professional Record System to document staff training levels and verify minimum training. Required content includes SIDS, abusive head trauma, crying plans, and child abuse. The department must provide or arrange statewide training and information at registration/licensure or annually, require providers receiving inservice training to submit their Social Security number, and review/update rules for the Governor at least every five years. No funding or appropriation changes are included.

The added language requires each public and nonpublic school to adopt and annually update a safety plan (using the state school security director’s model if desired) that at minimum addresses fire, tornado/weather, vehicle evacuation, and other drills. LB675 amends statutes governing the Board of Educational Lands and Funds (BELF). Key agency actions:

- BELF must give an Indian tribe with jurisdiction over reservation lands a first right of refusal to purchase (new §72-212) or lease (amended §72-232) school lands located within reservation boundaries. 
- BELF retains rulemaking authority over leases, including a mandated soil conservation program. 
- BELF may enter land-exchange agreements with the United States and, with the Governor’s written approval, with individuals or Indian tribes; for exchanges or sales of school lands within a reservation BELF must determine the transaction is not detrimental to state interests. 
- Definitions reference sections 81-2509 and 43-1503. No funding or appropriation changes.

Adds that when state school/educational lands fall within an Indian reservation, the Indian tribe with jurisdiction has a first right of refusal to purchase (sales under 72-208, 72-257, 72-257.01, 72-258) or to lease (leases under 72-232–72-239) those lands from the Board of Educational Lands and Funds. Authorizes the Board, with the Governor’s written approval, to enter agreements with tribes to sell or exchange state educational lands for equal-area/value lands, provided the Board finds such transactions are not detrimental to state interests. Definitions reference sections 81-2509 and 43-1503. No funding or appropriation changes.

LB676 amends the Certified Nurse Midwifery Practice Act and related credentialing statutes. It expands the Board’s (the licensing board referenced in the Uniform Credentialing Act) duties to monitor CNM scope of practice, recommend disciplinary action, and adopt rules for promulgation by the department (per §38-126), including approved certification organizations/programs and professional liability insurance. The bill authorizes the Board to require Accreditation Commission for Midwifery Education accreditation for CNM programs; revises definitions (adding “consultation,” broadening “collaboration” to working with other health care providers, and defining “health care provider” as those licensed under the Uniform Credentialing Act); removes practice-agreement language; clarifies CNM scope (prescribing, dispensing manufacturer-provided samples, pronouncing death, newborn care through 28 days). It also amends §44-2803 to expressly include certified nurse midwives under the Nebraska Hospital‑Medical Liability Act. Several statutory sections are repealed. No appropriations or funding changes are included.
Additions: Adds the Accreditation Commission for Midwifery Education and references the Uniform Credentialing Act. Defines "consultation" (CNM seeks physician/other health care provider advice), "health care provider" (licensed under the Uniform Credentialing Act), and "referral" (CNM directs patient to anothe… 
Adds the Accreditation Commission for Midwifery Education and references the Uniform Credentialing Act. Defines "consultation" (CNM seeks physician/other health care provider advice), "health care provider" (licensed under the Uniform Credentialing Act), and "referral" (CNM directs patient to another provider). Expands/clarifies certified nurse midwife scope: comprehensive perinatal and gynecologic care, primary female care, newborn care to 28 days, ordering tests/treatments, dispensing manufacturer-provided sample meds, prescribing within scope, and pronouncing death/signing death certificates if allowed by law. Requires collaborative, consultative, and referral networks. No funding, appropriation, or budget changes.

LB677 requires the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission to coordinate with the Department of Agriculture, Department of Revenue, and Department of Health and Human Services to ensure cultivation, processing, manufacture, distribution, transportation, testing, and sale of medical cannabis comply with the Act. The bill bars certain public employees — specifically including Department of Correctional Services staff and peace officers — from holding medical cannabis licenses. Persons convicted of controlled‑substances offenses and sentenced to the Department of Correctional Services must receive drug‑abuse treatment and counseling while incarcerated. The bill exempts vehicles used by the Department of Health and Human Services, Department of Correctional Services, Military Department, Department of Agriculture (for special investigations), and Tax Commissioner enforcement staff from state vehicle‑lettering requirements. Fiscal change: sales/use tax proceeds from aircraft sales or leases are credited to the Department of Transportation Aeronautics Capital Improvement Fund.
Additions: - Department of Agriculture: Added duty to collaborate with the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission on cultivation, processing, manufacture, distribution, transport, testing, and sale. No direct funding or appropriation changes. - Department of Correctional Services: Employees of jails or the Depa… 
- Department of Agriculture: Added duty to collaborate with the Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission on cultivation, processing, manufacture, distribution, transport, testing, and sale. No direct funding or appropriation changes.

- Department of Correctional Services: Employees of jails or the Department of Correctional Services are barred from holding licenses; possession/use of medical cannabis is prohibited in jails, correctional facilities, and youth centers. No funding changes.

- Department of Health and Human Services: Required to collaborate with the Commission; health-care facility consumer-access and restriction provisions added (may restrict smoking/vaping, specify locations, but cannot unreasonably limit access unless federal benefits/licenses at risk). No funding changes.

- Department of Revenue: Required to collaborate with the Commission; sales/use tax proceeds from dispensary sales are allocated (proceeds credited to the School District Property Tax Relief Credit Fund). Medical Cannabis Control Fund created; licensing/application fees (listed amounts) are remitted to that fund for administration/enforcement. Bonding premiums for commission employees are paid from the General Fund.

- Department of Transportation and Military Department: No substantive mentions or funding changes in the added text.

LB67 (Sexual Assault Emergency Care Act) charges "the department" and its director with complaint intake, investigation, and enforcement for hospital compliance. The department may investigate, convene informal conferences (using department staff or a contracted peer review organization), hold hearings under departmental rules, and issue decisions appealable under the Administrative Procedure Act. Remedial authority: a first substantiated complaint triggers a written warning and required correction; second and subsequent substantiated complaints carry a $1,000 fine either per affected sexual assault survivor or per month until mandated training is provided. Hospitals must provide personnel training, develop policies to address conscience objections, and comply with emergency contraception/forensic exam protocols. The bill contains no funding, appropriation, or budget allocation changes.

Timelines and procedures are specified for hospital responses, assignment of non‑investigator representatives, reports, departmental decisions, hearings (per department rules), and appeals under the Administrative Procedure Act. Enforcement: first substantiated complaint yields a written warning and required correction; second and subsequent substantiated complaints carry a $1,000 fine either per survivor denied required information/offer of emergency contraception or per month until required staff training is provided. No appropriations or budget allocations are included.

LB680 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §79-1204 to redefine the role and mission of educational service units (ESUs) as statewide educational service providers and to enumerate their responsibilities. Key governmental entities referenced: the State Department of Education (ESUs must act cooperatively in developing and implementing long-range plans with the Department and school districts) and the State Board of Education (which sets minimum accreditation standards for ESUs to ensure taxpayer accountability, statewide equity/adequacy of educational opportunities, and program quality). The bill specifies core service priorities (staff development — including for students in poverty and diverse backgrounds; technology, including distance education; and instructional materials), criteria for core services, contracting authority with nonmember districts, nonpublic schools, other ESUs, and public agencies under the Interlocal Cooperation Act and Joint Public Agency Act, and a prohibition on ESUs regulating school districts except as authorized by other law. No new appropriations or funding allocations are included.

LB681, introduced by the Nebraska Legislature’s Education Committee (Chair Sen. Murman; members Conrad, Hughes, Juarez, Lonowski, Meyer, Sanders), amends section 85-931, R.R.S. Neb., to redefine "graduate degree programs." It codifies three categories: first professional degrees (e.g., dentistry, medicine, law, architecture), master's degrees—now subdivided into listed professional programs (engineering, education, nursing, allied health, architecture specialties, etc.) and general academic/occupational programs (mathematics, sciences, business, fine arts, etc.)—and doctoral degrees (e.g., Ph.D., Ed.D., D.A.). The bill repeals the original section. No state agencies beyond the Legislature/Education Committee are referenced, and there are no appropriations or funding changes.

LB682 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §79-770 to require school districts, at a parent or guardian's request, to issue a certificate of attendance to students receiving services under the Special Education Act who are 17 and have not completed their individualized education program. The certificate permits a one-time participation in the high school graduation ceremony with diploma recipients; districts must continue providing special education services and may allow a later ceremony if the student subsequently earns a diploma. The bill cross-references graduation requirements ( §79-729) and high school equivalency ( §79-730) and repeals the original section. No state agency funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Summary: LB686 prohibits governmental entities and officials from knowingly maintaining lists, records, or registries of privately owned firearms or firearm owners, except records kept during criminal investigations, prosecutions, or as otherwise required by law. It bars payment card networks from requiring or incentivizing merchant category codes (MCCs) that distinguish firearm retailers and prohibits covered entities from assigning such MCCs. The Attorn… 
LB686 prohibits governmental entities and officials from knowingly maintaining lists, records, or registries of privately owned firearms or firearm owners, except records kept during criminal investigations, prosecutions, or as otherwise required by law. It bars payment card networks from requiring or incentivizing merchant category codes (MCCs) that distinguish firearm retailers and prohibits covered entities from assigning such MCCs. The Attorney General is given exclusive authority to investigate alleged violations, issue written notices, and, if noncompliance continues after 30 business days, file for injunctions. Courts may enjoin violations; failure to comply 30 business days after an injunction can lead to civil fines up to $1,000 per violation (assessed based on violator resources and constitutional harm). Fines are stayed pending appeal. A statutory defense exists if an MCC was required by law. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: Key points affecting government agencies and enforcement: - Prohibits government entities from maintaining lists/registries of privately owned firearms or owners, except records kept during criminal investigations/prosecutions or as otherwise required by law. - Bars payment card networks and "cover… 
Key points affecting government agencies and enforcement:

- Prohibits government entities from maintaining lists/registries of privately owned firearms or owners, except records kept during criminal investigations/prosecutions or as otherwise required by law.
- Bars payment card networks and "covered entities" from requiring, incentivizing, or assigning merchant category codes that distinguish firearm retailers from other merchants.
- Vest enforcement exclusively in the Attorney General: AG investigates allegations, issues written notice, and requires cessation within 30 business days. If not remedied, the AG may seek an injunction; continued noncompliance 30 business days after an injunction can lead the AG to seek civil fines up to $1,000 per violation (amounts to consider violator’s finances and constitutional harm). Fines are stayed pending appeal. The AG’s remedies are exclusive.
- Provides a defense if a merchant category code was legally required.
- No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB689 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §§79-930 and 79-992 (School Employees Retirement Act and Class V School Employees Retirement Act). Key agency actions:

- Nebraska Public Employees Retirement Systems (NPERS): the director may determine whether a member has satisfied the 180‑day post‑separation period to be treated as terminated; members have 45 days to submit evidence and may appeal the director’s decision to the NPERS board within 30 days. The board’s decision is final and not subject to court review.
- Retirement board / administrator (Class V): parallel authority to make 180‑day determinations with identical 45‑day evidence and 30‑day appeal timelines; board determinations final.
- School districts and participating employers: clarified when returning as temporary, substitute, or volunteer constitutes a termination, when contributions and service credit must resume, and exceptions for limited intermittent or authorized work.

No changes to appropriations, funding, or budget allocations. Original sections are repealed.

LB68 requires coverage and reimbursement rules for FDA‑approved, self‑administered hormonal contraceptives. It directs private insurers (individual/group sickness and accident, hospital/medical/surgical, and self‑funded employee benefit plans to the extent not preempted by federal law) to reimburse in‑network providers or dispensing entities per unit: first prescription up to a three‑month supply if prescribed; subsequent refills up to a twelve‑month supply even if the enrollee was not covered at first dispensing. Under the Medical Assistance Act, "the department" responsible for the medical assistance program must ensure a one‑time dispensation prescription for a twelve‑month supply of such contraceptives. The bill references the federal Food and Drug Administration and preserves provider discretion and limits on cost‑sharing. No appropriations, funding increases, or budget allocations are specified.

Requires insurers, hospital/medical policies, and self-funded employee benefit plans to reimburse in‑network providers per unit for FDA‑approved self‑administered hormonal contraceptives: first prescription up to a 3‑month supply; subsequent refills up to a 12‑month supply even if the enrollee wasn’t covered at first dispensing. Clarifies providers aren’t forced to prescribe 12‑month supplies and plans may not impose cost‑sharing for switching methods before a dispensed supply is exhausted. Also directs "the department" administering the medical assistance (Medicaid) program to ensure one‑time dispensation of a 12‑month supply. No appropriations, funding changes, or budget allocations are included.

LB692 amends the School District Property Tax Limitation Act by specifying administrative duties for "the department" (the agency responsible for calculating school district tax authority). The department must annually calculate and certify each district's property tax request authority using a multi-step formula: adjust prior-year property tax request for any prior overages, add prior-year non-property-tax revenue minus prior-year special building fund investment income, apply the district's base growth percentage, then subtract current-year non-property-tax revenue (with any categories lacking June 1 data deemed equal to the prior year) and correct known documentation errors. The bill also limits what unused request authority may be carried forward—excluding increases resulting from base growth percentage increases under §79-3405—and requires the department to calculate and report unused authority to each school board. Original sections are repealed. No appropriations or funding changes are included.

No specific state agency or funding appropriation is named.

LB696 amends the Professional Landscape Architects Act and primarily affects the State Board of Landscape Architects. Key agency-related changes:

LB697 amends the Pharmacy Practice Act. Key agency changes:

- Board of Pharmacy: membership set at eight members — five actively practicing pharmacists (one hospital-based), one pharmacy technician, and two public members.
- Compounding: required to follow USP chapters 795 and 797 as of Jan. 1, 2023; limited to practitioner medical orders, research/teaching/analysis, or office-use compounding by outsourcing facilities operating under 21 U.S.C. §353b or Neb. §71-470. Hospital pharmacies may compound for hospitals within the same health system or formal network. FDA-identified withdrawn or noncompoundable products are prohibited.
- Public health clinics (delegated dispensing permits): allow clinic workers or licensed clinicians to dispense formulary drugs/devices without onsite pharmacists only if strict conditions are met (initial dispensing by licensed clinician or pharmacist, onsite/affiliated practitioner prescriptions, contraceptive refill limits, director‑approved patient information, prepackaging/labeling requirements, and documented availability of a delegating or on‑call Nebraska pharmacist).

No funding or appropriation changes.

No agencies are newly created and no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB699 amends §77-6831 of the ImagiNE Nebraska Act. Key agency actions and fiscal provisions:

- Tax Commissioner: issue rules, forms, certificates; determine and certify eligibility for personal property exemptions to taxpayers and affected county assessors by Aug. 1; administer sales/use tax exemption procedures.
- Director: collect an administrative fee equal to 0.5% of incentives (excluding personal property exemptions).
- State Treasurer: receive collected fees and credit them to a newly created ImagiNE Nebraska Cash Fund.
- Department of Economic Development: administer the ImagiNE Nebraska Cash Fund; fund may also receive other amounts appropriated by the Legislature.
- State investment officer: invest fund balances under the Nebraska Capital Expansion Act and Nebraska State Funds Investment Act.
- Direct payment permits issued under §77-2705.01 on agreement execution; taxpayers must file exemption claims with Tax Commissioner and county assessors.

No specific appropriation amounts are set.

Adds that when a contractor buying materials under the cited subdivisions has elected to be taxed as the consumer of building materials (per §77-2701.10(2) or (3)): if the contractor already paid sales or use tax, they must certify the amount to the taxpayer and the taxpayer may claim a refund as if they paid the tax; if the contractor did not pay sales or use tax, the contractor’s purchases are treated as tax-exempt as if purchased by the taxpayer. No state agencies, departments, or funding/appropriations are mentioned or changed.

LB69 amends statutes governing the Commission on African American Affairs. Key agency-related changes:
- Commission composition: 14 Governor‑appointed members of African ancestry; one initial appointee must identify as an immigrant or new American and one as a young professional (18–24). Commissioners limited to two full four‑year terms. Names must appear on the commission website.
- Governance: Commission elects its chair; an executive board (chair + four members) may enter contracts up to $2,000 each and supervise commission initiatives.
- Funding/administration: Commission may receive and administer state, federal, and other funds, employ staff and set compensation, and must be provided an office for executive management.
- Duties: Work with state and federal agencies and keep the Governor’s office apprised. Reporting requirements now must include budget, funding sources, expenditures, grants, and public funds allocated.
Additions: Added provisions require initial commission appointments to include one immigrant/new American and one young professional (18–24). The commission must list all commissioners on its website. New required public content covers program areas (health and wellness; criminal justice/public safety, includi… 
Added provisions require initial commission appointments to include one immigrant/new American and one young professional (18–24). The commission must list all commissioners on its website. New required public content covers program areas (health and wellness; criminal justice/public safety, including police-community relations and services for formerly incarcerated individuals; housing and community development, including partnerships with housing agencies; education/career partnerships with schools), metrics/KPIs, public feedback and community needs assessments, and future strategic goals. Importantly, the commission must publicly disclose financial information — budget, funding sources, expenditures, grants received, and public funds allocated — enhancing transparency but not specifying new appropriations or budget increases.

LB704 amends procedures for the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) in IV-D child support cases. DHHS must review support orders and refer cases to the county attorney or other authorized attorney for filing of modification applications in district court when verifiable financial information meets Supreme Court guideline-variation or health-coverage criteria. For a noncustodial parent newly known to be incarcerated more than 180 days, DHHS must: initiate review within 15 business days, send notice to both parents and the correctional facility administrator, require financials within 30 days, complete review and notify parties within 120 calendar days, and—if a decrease is denied—offer a conference (scheduled within 30 days) with a 30-day final determination post-conference. Determinations are not contested cases under the Administrative Procedure Act. No funding or appropriation changes.
Additions: Adds procedures for the department (child support enforcement) when a noncustodial parent is incarcerated: the department must require parties to submit financial information (within 30 days of notice, also to the facility administrator per §47‑1003), complete its review within 120 days of learning… 
Adds procedures for the department (child support enforcement) when a noncustodial parent is incarcerated: the department must require parties to submit financial information (within 30 days of notice, also to the facility administrator per §47‑1003), complete its review within 120 days of learning of the incarceration, and notify parties per §43‑512.13. If a reduction is denied, the department must offer the incarcerated parent a conference within 30 days (in‑person or virtual) with specified first‑class mail notice contents and timing (including ability to submit evidence or waive the conference). Within 30 days after the conference the department issues a final determination and may refer the matter to the county attorney or authorized attorney; notices go to the facility address and facility administrator. Final determinations are not treated as contested cases under the Administrative Procedure Act. No funding or appropriation changes are made.

The bill assigns the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) to operate the medical cannabis registry. The Nebraska Medical Cannabis Commission must collaborate with DHHS, the Department of Agriculture, and the Department of Revenue on cultivation, processing, distribution, transportation, testing, and sale regulation. The Department of Economic Development (DED) will administer the Medical Cannabis Business Equity Fund, provide technical assistance/mentorship and mentorship pairings, and operate a business development grant program for social equity/disproportionately impacted applicants; the Fund may receive gifts, bequests, appropriations, and be invested per law. Employees of the Department of Correctional Services (DCS) are ineligible for medical cannabis licenses; DCS must provide treatment/counseling for sentenced persons. Financial changes: creation of a Medical Cannabis Control Fund; initial license fees split 50/50 between that Fund and local treasurers (school funds); permissive transfers to the General Fund; bond/insurance premiums paid from the General Fund. DOT: aircraft sales/use tax proceeds go to the Aeronautics Capital Improvement Fund; related highway tax distributions retained. DMV must receive court notices for clean‑slate and impoundment/license actions. Vehicles of DHHS, DCS, Department of Agriculture, and the Military Department are exempted from standard state lettering.

Summary of added provisions by agency (concise):

- Department of Health and Human Services: Defined as the “Department” for the patient program; establishes/maintains the patient/caregiver registry, issues registry cards, sets confidentiality, surrender/destruction rules, and may adopt rules for registered-caregiver entities.

- Department of Economic Development: Administers the Medical Cannabis Business Equity Fund (gifts/Legislative appropriations permitted), provides technical assistance, grants, mentorship, and a business development grant program for social equity/disproportionately impacted areas.

- Department of Revenue: Allocates sales/use tax revenue from medical cannabis sales: 50% to the Medical Cannabis Control Fund, 25% to the Medical Cannabis Business Equity Fund, 25% to the Cannabis Community Reinvestment Fund. Also collaborates with the commission.

- Department of Agriculture: Required to collaborate with the commission on regulation of cultivation, processing, testing, etc.

- Department of Correctional Services: Employees of jails or the Department are disqualified from holding licenses; cannabis prohibited in correctional facilities.

- Department of Motor Vehicles: Must be notified of certain sealed adjudications; clean-slate orders do not alter commercial CDL obligations.

- Department of Transportation and Military Department: No substantive mentions or funding changes in the added text.

LB706 requires law enforcement dispatch to screen calls for mental-health indicators, flag "Mental Health Priority" calls, notify and, when safe and practicable, dispatch an APS social worker to accompany officers. APS social workers must lead interactions using de‑escalation and trauma‑informed care.

Agencies and duties:
- Nebraska Commission on Law Enforcement and Criminal Justice (the commission): set minimum standards, accept agency policies, may issue a model policy, perform annual compliance reviews and report to the Governor and Legislature — limited to existing appropriations (including awarded grants) — and recommend improvements.
- Law enforcement agencies: adopt written dispatch/APS‑accompaniment policies and provide them to the commission.
- Department of Health and Human Services is identified as having duties in the bill (text excerpt does not specify details).
Sanctions and fiscal effects:
- Agencies with a pattern of noncompliance become ineligible for loans, grants, funds, or donations administered by the commission until corrected.
- The Council (per amended §81‑1403) may revoke/suspend officer certification for willful failure to comply; fines and training‑center tuition/fee remittances continue to be directed to the State Treasurer and relevant cash funds. No new appropriations are provided.
Additions: Requires law enforcement dispatchers to use a checklist/questionnaire to screen for mental‑health issues, flag such calls as "Mental Health Priority," use a designated code, notify the nearest unit plus an APS social worker, and share mental‑health info with responders. Unless unsafe, officers respo… 
Requires law enforcement dispatchers to use a checklist/questionnaire to screen for mental‑health issues, flag such calls as "Mental Health Priority," use a designated code, notify the nearest unit plus an APS social worker, and share mental‑health info with responders. Unless unsafe, officers responding must be accompanied by an APS social worker, who shall lead interactions using de‑escalation and trauma‑informed care.

Each agency must adopt a written dispatch/APS policy and file it with "the commission," which will set minimum standards and may issue a model policy. The commission will annually review compliance within its existing appropriations (including any grants), report results to the Governor and Legislature (electronically), make recommendations, and may bar noncompliant agencies from receiving commission‑administered loans, grants, funds, or donations until corrected.

Summary: The bill assigns administration of the Good Life District Economic Development Act primarily to the Department of Economic Development (DED) and the Department of Revenue (Tax Commissioner). DED is authorized to review and approve project/district applications, receive applicant materials, transmit approved district maps, retailer lists and ownership updates to the Department of Revenue, adopt rules, and terminate districts that fail investment b… 
The bill assigns administration of the Good Life District Economic Development Act primarily to the Department of Economic Development (DED) and the Department of Revenue (Tax Commissioner). DED is authorized to review and approve project/district applications, receive applicant materials, transmit approved district maps, retailer lists and ownership updates to the Department of Revenue, adopt rules, and terminate districts that fail investment benchmarks. When a district is terminated, unencumbered funds in its economic development fund are recaptured to the State Treasurer for credit to the General Fund. The Tax Commissioner must allocate and remit specified portions of state sales tax (generally 50% for categories defined after Oct. 1, 2025) to cities monthly, deducting or offsetting refunds, and provide detailed monthly reports to cities and DED. Both agencies may share confidential information to administer the Act. The bill contains no explicit appropriations or departmental budget allocations.
Additions: - The Department of Economic Development (DED) and Department of Revenue (DOR) may share confidential information and DED may adopt rules to implement the Good Life Transformational/Good Life District Economic Development Acts. - Beginning Oct. 1, 2025, the Tax Commissioner will allocate "allocated… 
- The Department of Economic Development (DED) and Department of Revenue (DOR) may share confidential information and DED may adopt rules to implement the Good Life Transformational/Good Life District Economic Development Acts.

- Beginning Oct. 1, 2025, the Tax Commissioner will allocate "allocated sales taxes" (50% of certain state sales taxes) to cities as local revenue for Good Life District programs. Allocations include: 50% from new-to-market retailers in the district; 50% from existing district retailers/applicants up to a $5M annual cap (with limited exceptions); and 50% of state sales taxes paid on qualifying new development costs. The Tax Commissioner remits monthly (after deducting refunds and offsetting any uncovered refunds from local remittances), provides confidential parcel-level reports to the city and DED, and deposited funds for project areas into trustee bank accounts. Unencumbered amounts are subject to recapture to the General Fund. The state sales tax rate is set to 5.5% effective Oct. 1, 2025.

LB709 gives the Department of Revenue explicit implementation and enforcement roles. Section 3 authorizes the Department of Revenue to adopt and promulgate rules and regulations to carry out the newly created Adoption Tax Credit Act. Separately, the amendment to section 77-2715.07(7)(d) makes the residence-purchase tax credit subject to recapture by the Department of Revenue if the claimant disposes of or stops using the residence as a primary home within five years. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department are included.
Additions: Creates the "Adoption Tax Credit Act." Creates the "Adoption Tax Credit Act." For taxable years beginning (or deemed to begin) on or after January 1, 2026, Nebraska will allow a refundable state income tax credit equal to 10% of a taxpayer's federal adoption expenses tax credit (26 U.S.C. §23) for taxpayers eligible for the federal credit. The Department of Revenue is authorized to adopt and promulgate rules and regulations to implement the Act. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department are specified in the added text.

LB70 assigns several procedural and administrative responsibilities to the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) in adoption proceedings. DHHS (or a licensed child‑placement agency) must conduct required preplacement or postplacement adoptive home studies per department rules, including national criminal history and central‑registry checks; the department sets fees for home studies and may waive costs. Judges may direct petitioners to request DHHS to check the child‑abuse central registry. DHHS provides the medical history form to be filed with adoption reports and must be sent the original medical history after decree. For children committed to DHHS, prospective adoptive parents must be given the opportunity to read the department’s case file; DHHS must exclude legally protected material, provide a signed verification of access for filing with the court, and allow postfinalization review upon written request. No appropriations or budget allocations are specified.
Additions: Summary (Department of Health and Human Services relevance): The underlined additions clarify who may be adopted by a "second adult person" (minors and adult children, including those with a sole legal parent), set consent and petition requirements, and require an adoptive home study except in limi… 
Summary (Department of Health and Human Services relevance):

The underlined additions clarify who may be adopted by a "second adult person" (minors and adult children, including those with a sole legal parent), set consent and petition requirements, and require an adoptive home study except in limited circumstances (no new study if the sole legal parent adopted the child under six months earlier and the second adult was included in that prior study, unless the court orders otherwise). Courts may order new home studies or background checks as needed. The text limits adoptions so a person cannot have more than two legal parents and requires a spouse to join when applicable. It also addresses parental support liability.

No references to the Department of Health and Human Services, nor any changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations, are included.

LB711 amends multiple provisions of the Tax Equity and Educational Opportunities Support Act, chiefly changing certification and reporting dates and related administrative duties of the Nebraska Department of Education. The department must determine and certify state aid amounts, school general-fund budget authority, and applicable allowable reserve percentages on or before June 15, 2025, and on or before March 1 each year thereafter, and must report necessary funding levels to the Governor, the Appropriations Committee, and the Education Committee. Certified state aid remains budgeted non‑property‑tax receipts and is distributed in ten monthly payments (Sept–Jun) with small-payment exceptions. The State Board retains appeal authority for new‑schools adjustment determinations; Director of Administrative Services and Auditor of Public Accounts receive certifications. Any certifications completed before the bill’s effective date for FY2025‑26 are void. The act takes effect immediately (emergency).

LB713 amends School Employees Retirement Act definitions and return-to-work rules, affecting the Public Employees Retirement Board and the Nebraska Public Employees Retirement Systems (NPERS) and its director, and referencing the State Department of Education, Board of Trustees of the Nebraska State Colleges, Board of Regents of the University of Nebraska, and community college boards. Key agency-related changes: removes the "prior service" definition; clarifies when a member has incurred a termination of employment; specifies that members who return as regular employees must immediately resume contributions and accrue service credit; allows return as temporary, substitute, or volunteer without voiding termination if no retirement application/benefit was filed or paid; limits post-retirement interim work to eight days per month without affecting termination status; authorizes the NPERS director to determine 180-day compliance with appeal rights to the Public Employees Retirement Board (final). No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are made. Original sections 79-902 and 79-930 are repealed.

LB714 (operative Jan. 1, 2026) revises motor vehicle tax and fee collection and allocations. The department (DMV) will annually determine taxes/fees and notify registrants. County treasurers retain 2% of collected motor vehicle tax and 2% of motor vehicle fee for administrative costs. The State Treasurer will receive 1.3% of motor vehicle tax proceeds for credit to the Vehicle Title and Registration System Replacement and Maintenance Cash Fund. Remaining motor vehicle tax proceeds are allocated by tax district: generally 40% to counties, 37% to local school systems/districts, and 23% to cities/villages, with specified exceptions (nonmunicipal districts and counties containing a metropolitan-class city). Motor vehicle fees fund the newly created Motor Vehicle Fee Fund; the State Treasurer distributes it quarterly (70% to counties, 30% to municipalities) pro rata based on recent Highway Allocation Fund allocations. Funds are investable by the state investment officer and restricted to roads, bridges, and streets.

The bill assigns the Department of Health and Human Services (department) these duties: assess market rates using an approved 45 C.F.R. 98.45 methodology and adjust child-care reimbursement every odd-numbered year at no less than the 75th percentile; reimburse nationally accredited providers and programs rated Step Up to Quality step two or higher at higher rates; administer state social services and participate in the federal child care assistance/Subsidy programs (with specified income eligibility thresholds and a 10% earned-income disregard after 12 months); promulgate rules for provisions becoming operative July 1, 2025; and adopt an annual fixed-rate schedule (effective Oct 1) for provider reimbursement, allowing tiered rates for higher-quality ratings. Funding: Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) funds shall cover costs of prior income-eligibility changes through Sept. 30, 2026; if insufficient, TANF funds may be used; no General Funds (except administration) for those costs. The department shall collaborate on an independently funded evaluation if private funds are available.

LB73 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §81-1414.07 to revise mandatory annual continuing-education requirements for certified law enforcement officers (excludes noncertified conditional officers). Training hours are set as the greater of: 32 hours for officers serving in counties with population ≥40,000 or 20 hours for officers in counties <40,000 (population by latest federal decennial census or revised certified count). Required topics include de-escalation, mental health, substance abuse, a minimum of two hours of anti-bias/implicit-bias training, firearms, officer wellness, legal updates (including legislative, First and Fourth Amendment issues), vehicular-pursuit policy review, and agency-determined training. Officers first certified in a year and those retiring in good standing that year are exempt. Continuing education may be delivered by law enforcement agencies, colleges, conferences, seminars, or online. The act becomes operative January 1, 2026; no funding or appropriation changes are included.
Additions: Adds a population-based distinction for required hours: county population is measured by the most recent federal decennial census or the most recent revised certified count from the United States Bureau of the Census. For officers in counties under 40,000 the requirement is twenty hours; officers in… 
Adds a population-based distinction for required hours: county population is measured by the most recent federal decennial census or the most recent revised certified count from the United States Bureau of the Census. For officers in counties under 40,000 the requirement is twenty hours; officers in counties of 40,000 or more are subject to the alternate (greater) standard referenced. Also adds that a law enforcement officer who is not employed but seeks to maintain professional status is treated as serving in the officer’s county of residence for purposes of subdivision (1)(b). No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations.

LB74 amends section 49-1446.03 of the Nebraska Political Accountability and Disclosure Act to expand and clarify permissible committee expenditures. Authorized expenditures include continued campaign office operation; events for campaign workers/constituents; public-opinion activities; repayment of pre-election campaign loans; informational communications; limited gifts of acknowledgment (≤ $50 per individual); and meals, lodging, and travel tied to an officeholder’s candidacy. It additionally authorizes conference fees, meals, lodging, and travel for an officeholder’s minor children and staff when involved in duties of the officeholder, and explicitly permits the candidate committee for the Governor to pay conference fees, meals, lodging, and travel for the Governor, the Governor’s staff, and the Governor’s immediate family when related to gubernatorial duties. The bill repeals the original section. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

Summary: - Defines "Department" to mean the Department of Labor (and "Commissioner" as Commissioner of Labor). - Assigns the Nebraska Department of Labor to calculate and publish, by October 15 each year starting 2026, the minimum wage rate that will take effect the following January 1. - Provides that employees may submit Wage and Hour Act complaints to the department; the department will forward credible complaints to the appropriate county attorney o… 
- Defines "Department" to mean the Department of Labor (and "Commissioner" as Commissioner of Labor).

- Assigns the Nebraska Department of Labor to calculate and publish, by October 15 each year starting 2026, the minimum wage rate that will take effect the following January 1.

- Provides that employees may submit Wage and Hour Act complaints to the department; the department will forward credible complaints to the appropriate county attorney or pursue its own enforcement and must develop forms and promulgate rules to implement this process.

- States all records and information obtained by the department under the bill are confidential and disclosable only by court order.

- Requires employer posting to include advisement and instructions on submitting complaints to the department.

- No appropriations, funding, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: The added provisions give the Department of Labor (Commissioner) expanded enforcement authority over employers of tipped employees: employers must retain for at least three years employee records (name, address, occupation, rate and amount of pay per period, daily and weekly hours), keep them on-sit… 
The added provisions give the Department of Labor (Commissioner) expanded enforcement authority over employers of tipped employees: employers must retain for at least three years employee records (name, address, occupation, rate and amount of pay per period, daily and weekly hours), keep them on-site or at a suitable location, and make them available to the Commissioner by appointment (including on-demand if stored out-of-state). Employers must provide sworn statements on Department-prescribed forms and may not refuse access, falsify records, withhold information, retaliate against employees who complain or testify, or pay below required rates. Records obtained by the Department are confidential and disclosable only by court order. Employees with a reasonable belief of a Wage and Hour Act violation may submit a complaint to the Department “in a manner prescribed by the Department” (using Department forms); the Department will develop forms/rules and will forward credible complaints to county attorneys or pursue enforcement itself. No funding or appropriation changes are included.

Summary: LB79 requires the trial court, on a defendant’s motion in civil cases involving a commercial motor vehicle requiring a commercial driver’s license, to dismiss any claim of the defendant’s direct negligence if the defendant stipulates the alleged negligent person was their employee or independent contractor and was acting within the course and scope of employment or as an independent contractor. LB79 requires the trial court, on a defendant’s motion in civil cases involving a commercial motor vehicle requiring a commercial driver’s license, to dismiss any claim of the defendant’s direct negligence if the defendant stipulates the alleged negligent person was their employee or independent contractor and was acting within the course and scope of employment or as an independent contractor. If those stipulations are made and the person’s negligence is found to have caused the damages, the defendant’s liability is limited to respondeat superior. The bill references the definition of commercial motor vehicle in section 60-316. No state agencies are assigned new duties or funding; no appropriations or budget changes are included.
Additions: Creates a defendant-triggered dismissal mechanism in civil suits involving a commercial motor vehicle that requires a commercial driver's license: if the defendant stipulates the alleged wrongdoer was the defendant’s employee or independent contractor and was acting within the scope of employment/co… 
Creates a defendant-triggered dismissal mechanism in civil suits involving a commercial motor vehicle that requires a commercial driver's license: if the defendant stipulates the alleged wrongdoer was the defendant’s employee or independent contractor and was acting within the scope of employment/contract, the court must dismiss any direct-negligence claim against the defendant. Liability then is adjudicated solely under respondeat superior. “Commercial motor vehicle” is defined by reference to section 60-316. No state agencies or departments are named and no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are affected.

This bill assigns several specific duties to the Department of Agriculture:

- Restricted entities (or their agents/trustees/fiduciaries) that rely on a CFIUS determination or national security agreement must annually certify compliance to the Department of Agriculture by January 15, 2026, and each January 15 thereafter (sec. 76-3709(2)(b)).  
- Any person may notify the Department of Agriculture (or the Attorney General) of suspected violations; the Department is charged with investigating alleged violations (sec. 76-3712).  
- If the Director of Agriculture has reasonable suspicion of a violation, the director must refer the matter to the Attorney General or outside counsel for enforcement (sec. 76-3712).  
- The Director of Agriculture, Attorney General, and retained outside counsel are responsible for determining whether a person is subject to or in violation of the act (sec. 76-3715).

No changes to funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department are included.

No new funding, appropriations, or budget allocations for the Department of Agriculture are included.

DHHS must provide written notice of investigation results and registry decisions to subjects, notify the Commissioner of Education when a subject is a school employee, and notify appropriate military installations when a subject is a military family member. Summary: LB82 adopts the Cosmetology Licensure Compact into Nebraska law and amends several sections of the state's Cosmetology Practice Act. It creates a Compact Commission (with an Executive Committee) to administer a multistate licensure system and a centralized Data System. Member States' State Licensing Authorities remain the primary regulators, select one delegate to the Commission, handle complaints and discipline within their borders, and must sub… 
LB82 adopts the Cosmetology Licensure Compact into Nebraska law and amends several sections of the state's Cosmetology Practice Act. It creates a Compact Commission (with an Executive Committee) to administer a multistate licensure system and a centralized Data System. Member States' State Licensing Authorities remain the primary regulators, select one delegate to the Commission, handle complaints and discipline within their borders, and must submit licensure and adverse-action data to the Commission. The Commission may adopt rules, hire staff, lease property, initiate legal actions, and convene meetings. Funding authorities include levying annual assessments on Member States, charging fees to licensees for multistate licenses and renewals, accepting grants/donations, and establishing a budget with annual financial reviews. The bill contains no specific Nebraska appropriation.
Additions: Creates a Cosmetology Licensure Compact establishing a multistate Compact Commission and Executive Committee to administer multistate cosmetology licenses. State Licensing Authorities in Member States retain primary licensing, disciplinary, investigatory, and enforcement responsibilities and must su… 
Creates a Cosmetology Licensure Compact establishing a multistate Compact Commission and Executive Committee to administer multistate cosmetology licenses. State Licensing Authorities in Member States retain primary licensing, disciplinary, investigatory, and enforcement responsibilities and must submit uniform license and adverse-action data to a Commission-operated Data System. The Commission may adopt rules, hire staff, lease/purchase property, contract services, maintain a budget, borrow, accept gifts/grants, and cooperate with law enforcement and courts. Funding: the Commission may levy annual assessments on Member States (allocated by formula), charge fees to licensees, accept donations/grants, and must secure funds before incurring obligations; annual financial reviews are required. Judicial venue for Commission actions is federal court in D.C. or where its principal office is located.

LB90 amends statutes governing improvement districts in cities of the first class, focusing on actions by the mayor and city council and the city clerk. Key agency-related provisions:

- City clerk must publish creation notice once weekly for not less than 20 days. Owners representing >50% of front footage may file objections within 20 days to require repeal of the ordinance.  
- Mayor and city council must create districts on petition (3/4 front footage) and may deny formation if water, sewer, or street grading are absent, providing a written explanation to interested parties.  
- Bidding: council must solicit materials suggested by a petition from owners (25%); bid openings are postponed 10 days to allow owner selection.  
- Funding: costs assessed by special assessments (installments up to 20 years) or paid in full within 50 days; council may set interest on installments up to the statutory rate (section 45-104.01). Special assessments constitute the sinking fund for city-issued street improvement bonds payable in up to 20 years.  

Original sections 16-617 through 16-624 are repealed and replaced.
Additions: Adds authority for the mayor and city council (notably of a city of the first class) to create improvement districts that may combine two or more types of work (sidewalks, public ways, public spaces, intersecting improvements) in a single ordinance. Specifies the mayor and city council must follow n… 
Adds authority for the mayor and city council (notably of a city of the first class) to create improvement districts that may combine two or more types of work (sidewalks, public ways, public spaces, intersecting improvements) in a single ordinance. Specifies the mayor and city council must follow notice and bid-advertising steps (see §§16-619, 16-624) when forming districts and contracting work. Funding remains by levy of special assessments on specially benefited property; owners may pay the entire assessed cost within 50 days of levy to be exempt from liens. References issuance and terms of street improvement bonds as authorized by ordinance and §§16-617 and 16-622. No direct new appropriations or departmental budget allocations are created.

LB91 amends Neb. Rev. Stat. §70-650.01 governing transfers of electric distribution systems between public power entities and municipalities. It requires a public power district or public power and irrigation district that has retired or reserved funds for indebtedness to convey its electric distribution system — explicitly distinguished from generating plants and transmission lines — to a city or village upon a duly adopted municipal resolution (subject to 30‑day public notice and a potential referendum). The bill retains: processes for declaratory-judgment determination of what constitutes the distribution system; protections allowing refinancing without enlarging pledged obligations; authority to issue bonds for additional facilities; and the district board’s ability to allocate revenue attributable to additional facilities. Agencies/actors referenced include public power districts, public power and irrigation districts, city and village governing bodies, municipal clerks, and district boards of directors. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB92 creates the Residential Tenant Clean Slate Act, directing Nebraska trial courts to seal (grant "clean slate relief" for) eviction records in specified circumstances—automatic sealing after dismissal, when a writ of restitution is reversed/vacated or never executed, COVID-19 nonpayment evictions between March 13, 2020–June 30, 2021, when a defendant was a minor, or when a judgment violated statutory protections—and allows tenant petitions for sealing after three years in other cases. Procedural requirements assign duties to trial courts: petition filing, notice to prior parties, a 30‑day objection period, hearings if objected to (objector bears burden), and that orders are final and appealable. No state agencies or executive departments are named, and the bill contains no funding, appropriation, or budgetary changes.
Additions: Adds the "Residential Tenant Clean Slate Act," defining terms (tenant, landlord, residential tenancy, eviction proceeding, trial court) and requiring the trial court to immediately issue record-sealing ("clean slate") orders under section 5 when an eviction is dismissed. Gives tenants grounds to pet… 
Adds the "Residential Tenant Clean Slate Act," defining terms (tenant, landlord, residential tenancy, eviction proceeding, trial court) and requiring the trial court to immediately issue record-sealing ("clean slate") orders under section 5 when an eviction is dismissed. Gives tenants grounds to petition the trial court for sealing (including vacated/reversed judgments, unwritten/unexecuted writs of restitution, evictions for nonpayment during the COVID-19 emergency Mar 13, 2020–Jun 30, 2021, named minors, or certain statutory-violation judgments) or to petition after three years from writ/final judgment. Petitions are filed in trial court, served on prior parties (30 days to object); no objection -> grant if criteria met; objections trigger a hearing with the objector bearing the burden. Grants/denials are final and appealable per section 25-1902. No executive agencies or departments are created or mentioned, and no funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.

LB93 amends Nebraska discovery statutes to expand obligations for prosecuting authorities, law enforcement agencies, and courts in criminal cases. Prosecuting attorneys must permit defendants to inspect and copy: law‑enforcement reports related to an investigation; electronic communication devices, computers, and digital information; and disclosure of any prosecution expert’s identity, qualifications, opinions, and bases. Courts may order access and specify time/place/manner for defense testing of physical or digital evidence; they may accept sealed written submissions from prosecutors if witness safety is at risk, preserved for appellate review. The continuing duty to disclose is retained. No agencies receive new funding or appropriations.
Additions: Adds disclosure and discovery requirements for prosecutors and courts in criminal (and ordinance) cases where imprisonment is possible. Key points: - Prosecuting authority must disclose expert witnesses’ names, qualifications, and complete opinions (including bases/reasons). - Section made subject t… 
Adds disclosure and discovery requirements for prosecutors and courts in criminal (and ordinance) cases where imprisonment is possible. Key points:
- Prosecuting authority must disclose expert witnesses’ names, qualifications, and complete opinions (including bases/reasons).
- Section made subject to the continuing duty of disclosure under §29-1918.
- Courts may order prosecutors to make electronic evidence (devices, computers, digital information) available or allow defendants to perform equivalent testing with their experts.
- Defines “computer” (refers to §28-1343), “digital information” (examples listed), and “electronic communication device” (refers to §28-833).
- Parties must promptly disclose additional discoverable evidence previously requested or court-ordered (per §§29-1912–29-1921).

No government agencies beyond “prosecuting authority” and courts are referenced, and there are no funding or appropriation changes.

Summary: The bill directs the Department of Labor, in collaboration with the Department of Economic Development, to establish two grant programs: (1) up to $20 million per fiscal year for local educational institutions/nonprofits to develop and operate digital skills training centers in qualified census tracts; and (2) up to $20 million per fiscal year to cover tuition, materials, transportation, equipment, and child care for low‑income individuals attend… 
The bill directs the Department of Labor, in collaboration with the Department of Economic Development, to establish two grant programs: (1) up to $20 million per fiscal year for local educational institutions/nonprofits to develop and operate digital skills training centers in qualified census tracts; and (2) up to $20 million per fiscal year to cover tuition, materials, transportation, equipment, and child care for low‑income individuals attending those centers. The Department of Labor, with the Department of Economic Development and industry input, must develop standardized curricula and administer applications, eligibility, and prioritization. The Legislature intends to appropriate $50 million annually from the Workforce Development Program Cash Fund to the Department of Labor for grants under the Digital Skills Empowerment Act, and the fund statute is amended to include those grants.
Additions: Adds a Digital Skills Empowerment program led by the Department of Labor in collaboration with the Department of Economic Development. Key duties: - Create two grant programs: (a) grants to local educational institutions/nonprofits to develop digital skills training centers in qualified census tract… 
Adds a Digital Skills Empowerment program led by the Department of Labor in collaboration with the Department of Economic Development. Key duties:
- Create two grant programs: (a) grants to local educational institutions/nonprofits to develop digital skills training centers in qualified census tracts (cap $20M/year); (b) grants to cover tuition/transportation/materials/equipment/child care for low‑income individuals attending those centers (cap $20M/year). Departments must set application requirements and award priorities if funds are insufficient.
- Jointly develop industry‑aligned curricula (core skills, special tracks, bootcamps) with tech industry input.
- Dept. of Labor must partner with employers/tech firms to support apprenticeships, job pipelines, and continued training.
Funding: legislative intent to appropriate $50 million annually from the Workforce Development Program Cash Fund to the Department of Labor beginning FY2025‑26 for grants under this Act.

Summary: - The Department of Health and Human Services (department) shall administer the state's social services program and may contract for services. - The department must participate in the federal child care assistance/subsidy program, implement income-eligibility and transitional-assistance rules, and adopt an annual fixed-rate schedule for child-care reimbursement (effective Oct. 1 each year). - The department shall create a child-care workforce p… 
- The Department of Health and Human Services (department) shall administer the state's social services program and may contract for services.

- The department must participate in the federal child care assistance/subsidy program, implement income-eligibility and transitional-assistance rules, and adopt an annual fixed-rate schedule for child-care reimbursement (effective Oct. 1 each year).

- The department shall create a child-care workforce pilot (Oct. 1, 2025–Sept. 30, 2028), set eligibility parameters, allow 12 months continuous eligibility without cost-share for qualifying employed household members, permit rulemaking (operative July 1, 2025), and permit certain enrollment accommodations.

- The department must submit electronic annual reports (Dec. 1, 2026–2028) detailing county-level monthly enrollments, employment tenure before enrollment, and program expenditures (monthly aid disbursed and average household cost).

- The department shall collaborate with a nonprofit on an independent evaluation of prior income-eligibility changes if privately funded (evaluation due July 1, 2024).

- Funding: Child Care and Development Block Grant funds (and, if insufficient, TANF funds) shall cover costs from the 2021 eligibility changes through Sept. 30, 2026; General Funds may not be used for those costs except administration.
Additions: The Department of Health and Human Services must create and administer a pilot within the federal Child Care Subsidy program to provide child care assistance to the child care workforce. The pilot runs October 1, 2025–September 30, 2028. Eligibility: households ≤85% of state median income, an applic… 
The Department of Health and Human Services must create and administer a pilot within the federal Child Care Subsidy program to provide child care assistance to the child care workforce. The pilot runs October 1, 2025–September 30, 2028. Eligibility: households ≤85% of state median income, an applicant/household member listed in the Nebraska Early Childhood Professional Record System, working ≥20 hours/week as (or at) a licensed child care provider, Head Start, or Early Head Start, and meeting federal non‑income requirements. Enrollees remain eligible 12 continuous months with no cost‑share if employment is maintained. DHHS must submit annual electronic reports to the Legislature (Dec 1, 2026–2028) detailing monthly enrollment by county and employment type, tenure before enrollment, and program expenditures (monthly aid disbursed and average household cost). No explicit funding, appropriation, or budget allocation provisions are included.

Summary: LB96 amends §68‑911 to require the Department of Health and Human Services to submit specified state plan amendments, waivers (including Section 1115 waivers), and applications to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Required actions/deadlines include: behavioral‑health community service coverage; school‑based direct reimbursement amendments; providing continuous glucose monitor coverage (implementation deadlines with an Aug. 1… 
LB96 amends §68‑911 to require the Department of Health and Human Services to submit specified state plan amendments, waivers (including Section 1115 waivers), and applications to the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Required actions/deadlines include: behavioral‑health community service coverage; school‑based direct reimbursement amendments; providing continuous glucose monitor coverage (implementation deadlines with an Aug. 1, 2024 eligibility expansion); seeking federal approval to extend postpartum coverage; and, by Oct. 1, 2025, submitting a waiver/state plan amendment to designate two medical‑respite facilities for homeless adults in the Medicaid expansion population. The department must select facilities, report annually to the Health and Human Services Committee, may adopt rules, and the bill directs funding for certain provisions from the Medicaid Managed Care Excess Profit Fund, including an intent that no more than $600,000 be appropriated annually for the CGM expansion.
Additions: No underlined (added) text found in this bill. 
No underlined (added) text found in this bill.

Summary: LB97 centralizes DMV authority for titles, IDs, inspections, electronic/NMVTIS reporting, forms, records (including protected digital images), and license/ID production. It creates two new funds: the Department of Motor Vehicles Cash Fund (administered by the DMV director) to receive DMV-collected fees, county reimbursements, NMVTIS reporting fees, ID‑inspection fees ($10), postage/handling and county fee portions remitted to the State Treasurer;… 
LB97 centralizes DMV authority for titles, IDs, inspections, electronic/NMVTIS reporting, forms, records (including protected digital images), and license/ID production. It creates two new funds: the Department of Motor Vehicles Cash Fund (administered by the DMV director) to receive DMV-collected fees, county reimbursements, NMVTIS reporting fees, ID‑inspection fees ($10), postage/handling and county fee portions remitted to the State Treasurer; and the Department of Motor Vehicles Ignition Interlock Fund to receive portions of interlock fees and to cover installation/removal/maintenance for indigent persons. Fee allocations include a $45 ignition‑interlock permit split $5 to the DMV Cash Fund and $40 to the Ignition Interlock Fund; an $11 replacement split $2.75 to counties and $8.25 to the DMV Cash Fund; 24/7 permit fees follow similar splits. License‑plate production fees (up to $8) go to the Highway Trust Fund until the 2029 issuance cycle, then to the License Plate Cash Fund. Both DMV funds may transfer to the General Fund; investment earnings on DMV Cash Fund balances are credited to the General Fund beginning October 1, 2024.
Additions: Summary (Department of Motor Vehicles): - Establishes a $10 fee for each identification inspection, remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Department of Motor Vehicles Cash Fund; no ID-inspection fee if ownership is evidenced by a U.S. Government Certificate to Obtain Title. - Requires… 
Summary (Department of Motor Vehicles):

- Establishes a $10 fee for each identification inspection, remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to the Department of Motor Vehicles Cash Fund; no ID-inspection fee if ownership is evidenced by a U.S. Government Certificate to Obtain Title.  
- Requires applicants for bonded certificates of title to provide certified-mail notice to lienholders; titles extinguish liens if no response within 30 days.  
- Allows optional 2- or 3-year vehicle registrations (paying fees and taxes for each year up front, including fees under §§60-3,141 and 60-3,156).  
- Authorizes DMV to mail license plates/registration certificates (implementation by director on/before Jan 1, 2029), charge postage/handling (remitted to DMV Cash Fund), and shifts all fees from the 2029 plate cycle to the License Plate Cash Fund.  
- Updates ignition interlock permit issuance: DMV must review records for eligibility, prior convictions, ALRs, and no-drive periods before issuing.

Summary: LB98 amends definitions of "all-terrain vehicle" and "utility-type vehicle" in multiple statutes (sections 60-103, 60-135.01, 60-305, 60-358.01, and 60-6,355), affecting the Motor Vehicle Certificate of Title Act, the Motor Vehicle Registration Act, and references in the Nebraska Rules of the Road. Key changes: ATVs are defined as motorized off‑highway devices ≤50 inches wide, traveling on three or more nonhighway tires, designed for operator onl… 
LB98 amends definitions of "all-terrain vehicle" and "utility-type vehicle" in multiple statutes (sections 60-103, 60-135.01, 60-305, 60-358.01, and 60-6,355), affecting the Motor Vehicle Certificate of Title Act, the Motor Vehicle Registration Act, and references in the Nebraska Rules of the Road. Key changes: ATVs are defined as motorized off‑highway devices ≤50 inches wide, traveling on three or more nonhighway tires, designed for operator only or operator plus one passenger; UTVs are devices ≤74 inches wide, ≤180 inches long (including bumper), traveling on four or more nonhighway tires. Vehicles modified with after‑market equipment beyond statutory requirements are ineligible for registration under the Motor Vehicle Registration Act. Original sections are repealed and the bill takes effect immediately by emergency clause. No funding or appropriation changes.
Additions: The added text consists only of short conjunction/numbering fragments ("(3) and (3) and (iii) and"). It does not reference any government agencies, departments, funding, appropriations, or budget allocations and contains no substantive policy or fiscal changes.

Summary: The bill amends Nebraska's treatment-and-corrections statutes to (1) define "Department" as the Department of Correctional Services and "Director" as the Director of Correctional Services and to tie "committed offender" and "facility" to department-operated facilities; (2) define "restrictive housing" as out-of-cell time of less than ten hours per day; (3) require the department to adopt rules establishing levels of restrictive housing, criteria… 
The bill amends Nebraska's treatment-and-corrections statutes to (1) define "Department" as the Department of Correctional Services and "Director" as the Director of Correctional Services and to tie "committed offender" and "facility" to department-operated facilities; (2) define "restrictive housing" as out-of-cell time of less than ten hours per day; (3) require the department to adopt rules establishing levels of restrictive housing, criteria and procedures for placement, and individualized transition plans developed with the committed offender; (4) limit restrictive-housing placements to no more than fifteen consecutive days and bar placement of members of vulnerable populations except for immediate segregation pending classification; and (5) authorize the department to develop secure mental-health housing that provides meaningful social interaction and programming. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included.
Additions: For the Department of Correctional Services: the added provisions (1) limit restrictive housing—no inmate may be held more than 15 consecutive days and no more than one inmate may be placed in a single-occupancy cell unless all inmates voluntarily agree in writing; (2) appear to require "ten hours p… 
For the Department of Correctional Services: the added provisions (1) limit restrictive housing—no inmate may be held more than 15 consecutive days and no more than one inmate may be placed in a single-occupancy cell unless all inmates voluntarily agree in writing; (2) appear to require "ten hours per day" (context implies a minimum daily period, likely out-of-cell time); and (3) add/clarify definitions for populations relevant to custody and treatment, including developmental disability, serious mental illness (defined as biologically based conditions that substantially limit life activities, with examples such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depression, OCD, etc.), and traumatic brain injury. No funding, appropriations, or budget allocations are included in the added text.

Summary: LB9 expands regulatory, enforcement, and tax authority primarily for the Nebraska Tax Commissioner, with roles for the Attorney General, Governor, State Treasurer, and peace officers. Key agency changes: - Tax Commissioner: new reporting and audit authorities for manufacturers, importers, stamping agents, and retailers; extended deficiency-notice periods (3 years, 6 years for fraud); rulemaking; license suspension/revocation; civil/administrativ… 
LB9 expands regulatory, enforcement, and tax authority primarily for the Nebraska Tax Commissioner, with roles for the Attorney General, Governor, State Treasurer, and peace officers. Key agency changes:

- Tax Commissioner: new reporting and audit authorities for manufacturers, importers, stamping agents, and retailers; extended deficiency-notice periods (3 years, 6 years for fraud); rulemaking; license suspension/revocation; civil/administrative penalties (Tobacco Products Tax Act penalties up to $5,000); authority to seize/forfeit contraband cigarettes and tobacco products and direct destruction or law-enforcement use. Immunity provided for the commissioner, staff, and peace officers for seizures.
- Attorney General: may seek injunctions for violations and calculate escrow shortfalls.
- Governor: advises/consents to commissioner hires.
- Compensation and enforcement expenses: staff paid from tobacco-related revenue; administrative expenses may be paid by General Fund warrants but not to exceed 4% of collections. Effective January 1, 2026.
Additions: Adds definitions tying "nicotine analogue" and "alternative nicotine product" to section 28-1418.01 and imposes a tax on alternative nicotine products equal to 20% of the first owner's purchase price or the first owner's sale price. Empowers the Tax Commissioner to examine returns, notify deficienci… 
Adds definitions tying "nicotine analogue" and "alternative nicotine product" to section 28-1418.01 and imposes a tax on alternative nicotine products equal to 20% of the first owner's purchase price or the first owner's sale price. Empowers the Tax Commissioner to examine returns, notify deficiencies (generally within 3 years, 6 years for fraud/evasion/large omissions), and deliver notices by mail or personal service. Grants the Tax Commissioner authority to suspend or revoke licenses issued under sections 28-1420 to 28-1429 and to impose administrative penalties up to $5,000 after notice and hearing under the Administrative Procedure Act; appeals follow that Act. Declares untaxed tobacco products contraband and authorizes seizure by the Tax Commissioner, the commissioner's agents/employees, or any peace officer on the commissioner's direction; forfeited items are to be destroyed or used for law enforcement and then destroyed. No funding or appropriations changes.
